item.title: Your Existing Component Has State, Props, and Variants You'd Have to Reconstruct — Pull the Design System Into Claude Design First So Redesigns Start From Reality
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run /design-sync in Claude Code before opening Claude Design and your redesign canvas starts from your actual components, tokens, and variants — not the tool's placeholder defaults.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `/design-sync` in a Claude Code session before opening Claude Design, and your redesign canvas starts from your actual components, tokens, and variants — not the tool's placeholder defaults.**
The more common workflow is Claude Design → Claude Code: sketch something in the design tool, export it, integrate it. The reverse direction is less discussed but often more useful: you have a component in production and you want to explore redesign options before committing implementation time.
The problem without `/design-sync` is that Claude Design doesn't know about your design system. It generates something that works visually but uses generic default typography, placeholder spacing, and made-up color values — none of which match your tokens. You end up spending a cleanup pass in Claude Code after every iteration.
**The workflow:**
1. In a Claude Code session in your repo, run: ``` /design-sync ``` This reads your design system from the codebase (tokens, component definitions, Tailwind config, MUI theme, or CSS custom properties) and pushes them to Claude Design.
2. Open Claude Design. Your tokens and component variants now appear as the starting context.
3. Describe the redesign — layout changes, information hierarchy, mobile/desktop behavior. Claude Design now generates from your palette and your spacing scale, not generic defaults.
4. Export the redesign. Claude Code receives the export and applies it to the specific component, with existing props, state handling, and test coverage preserved.
**What gets lost in the reverse direction** (the limitation to plan for): the component's behavioral complexity doesn't transfer. Event handlers, complex state machines, and async data patterns don't appear in the design surface. The exported layout is accurate; the logic is not. Plan for Claude Code to reconcile the new layout against the existing component implementation, not paste-replace it.
**When to skip it and stay in Claude Code:** if the change is purely behavioral (swapping a sort order, changing an API call), or if it's a one-line style change (a color swap, a padding bump), the round-trip overhead isn't worth it. The design tool earns its overhead when you're deciding among three different layout directions and want to see them all before writing any code.
**Sources:** [Anthropic: Claude Design now stays on brand for daily work](https://claude.com/blog/claude-design-stays-on-brand-for-daily-work) · [VentureBeat: Anthropic ships Claude Design overhaul with code round-trips](https://venturebeat.com/technology/anthropic-ships-major-claude-design-overhaul-with-design-system-imports-code-round-trips-and-a-fix-for-its-token-burning-problem) · [Practitioner review: Claude Design tested on a real project](https://ice-ice-bear.github.io/posts/2026-04-22-claude-design/)

item.title: vLLM v0.34.0 Removes Model Runner V1 and Changes Default Block Size — Three Breaking Changes to Check Before Upgrading; GitHub Copilot Retires 6 Models Dec 14
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: vLLM v0.34.0 (Nov 16) drops V1 runner, sets default block size to 64, requires huggingface_hub 2.0+. GitHub Copilot retires Claude Fable 5 and five others on December 14.
item.content:encoded:
**vLLM v0.34.0 (November 16) silently breaks three common configurations. GitHub Copilot retires Claude Fable 5 and five other models December 14.**
Two breaking-change deadlines this week.
## vLLM v0.34.0 (November 16)
If you serve models with vLLM, three changes in v0.34.0 will break existing setups without startup warnings:
- **Model Runner V1 removed.** The flag `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0` now fails at startup. Custom logits processors written against the V1 API need to be migrated to the V2 sampler module. The vLLM team published a [Model Runner V2 migration guide](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-03-24-mrv2) in March. - **Default block size: 16 → 64.** The KV cache now sizes from actually-free GPU memory after warmup (extensible KV cache is on by default). If you sized memory budgets assuming the old 16-block default, benchmark memory usage before promoting. Use `--no-enable-extensible-kv-cache` to restore the previous static-allocation behavior during testing. - **huggingface_hub ≥ 2.0.0 required.** Existing environments with older releases will fail on import. - ROCm 7.2 images are discontinued; AMD users need ROCm 10.0.
**Limit worth flagging:** extensible KV cache sizing is no longer static — if your GPU has variable free memory across restarts (from other processes), cache capacity will vary between runs. Worth testing for consistency in production environments.
## GitHub Copilot model retirements — December 14
GitHub is removing six models from all Copilot experiences on December 14. Per the GitHub changelog:
| Retiring model | Suggested replacement | |---|---| | Claude Fable 5 | Claude Fable 5.2 | | Claude Haiku 4.5 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | | Gemini 3.8 Flash | Gemini 4 Flash | | Gemini 4 Argon | Gemini 4 Pro | | Grok 4.6 | Grok 5 | | Kimi K3 | TBA |
If you pin model names in Copilot policies, CI scripts, or in GitHub Actions workflows that call the Copilot API, test against the replacements before December 7.
**Why it matters:** A vLLM upgrade that changes KV cache behavior or fails at startup is expensive to debug in production. The Copilot retirements affect any team that pins model IDs by name in automation — a silent fallback to a default model on December 14 is a behavior change, not an error.

item.title: Your Dense Retriever Misses Keywords Your Users Type Exactly — `EnsembleRetriever` Combines BM25 and Vector Search With Reciprocal Rank Fusion to Cover Both Gaps
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangChain's EnsembleRetriever merges a BM25 keyword retriever with a dense vector retriever using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Install rank_bm25, combine four objects, beat either retriever alone on mixed queries.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** build a hybrid retriever that ranks keyword-heavy queries and semantic queries well, without choosing between them.
- BM25 catches exact keywords that semantic search misses; dense vectors catch synonyms and paraphrases that BM25 misses — combining them raises recall on both query types simultaneously. - Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges the two ranked lists without requiring you to reconcile incompatible similarity scores from different spaces. - `EnsembleRetriever` applies RRF by default with four lines of setup; adjust the `weights` parameter based on your query distribution and validate with RAGAS or DeepEval.
Dense vector search handles paraphrases and meaning-based queries well but misses exact-match signals — a user asking for "RFC 7807" or a specific function name won't get great results from embedding similarity alone. BM25 (keyword search) handles exact matches and term frequency well but misses synonyms and reformulations. Hybrid search at query time combines both and re-ranks using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which typically outperforms either retriever alone on mixed query types.
LangChain's `EnsembleRetriever` runs both retrievers in parallel and merges the results with RRF by default. Official docs at [python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/ensemble_retriever/](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/ensemble_retriever/).
**Install:** ```bash pip install rank_bm25 langchain-community langchain-huggingface ```
**Code:** ```python from langchain_community.retrievers import BM25Retriever from langchain.retrievers import EnsembleRetriever from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
docs = [...] # your Document list
bm25_retriever = BM25Retriever.from_documents(docs) bm25_retriever.k = 4
embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5") faiss_store = FAISS.from_documents(docs, embeddings) dense_retriever = faiss_store.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 4})
# EnsembleRetriever merges results with RRF # weights control contribution strength, not a threshold hybrid = EnsembleRetriever( retrievers=[bm25_retriever, dense_retriever], weights=[0.5, 0.5] )
results = hybrid.invoke("your query here") ```
**What RRF does:** each retriever returns its own ranked list. RRF scores each document as `1 / (rank + k)` from each list (k=60 is the standard default), then sums the scores. A document that ranks 2nd in BM25 and 3rd in vector search scores higher than one that ranks 1st in only one list — rewarding breadth of evidence across retrieval methods.
**When to adjust weights:** 0.5/0.5 is a reasonable starting point. In highly technical corpora with exact identifiers (API names, error codes, function signatures), lean BM25 (0.6–0.7). For conversational queries and paraphrases, lean dense (0.3/0.7). Measure the difference on your actual queries with RAGAS or DeepEval rather than guessing.
**Key limits:** - BM25 is a bag-of-words method — it has no sense of "near" or "related"; misspellings and morphological variants miss. - Hybrid search requires the full document set in memory for BM25 (via `rank_bm25`). For large corpora, consider a vector database that supports native hybrid search (Qdrant, Weaviate, Elasticsearch) instead of maintaining a separate in-memory BM25 index. - `EnsembleRetriever`'s default RRF uses k=60; at very small corpora (under ~100 documents) this parameter matters more and may benefit from tuning. - BM25 import path: use `langchain_community.retrievers.BM25Retriever` (not `langchain.retrievers`), which requires `langchain-community` installed separately.
**Sources:** [LangChain EnsembleRetriever docs](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/ensemble_retriever/) · [LanceDB: Hybrid Search combining BM25 and semantic search with LangChain](https://lancedb.substack.com/p/hybrid-search-combining-bm25-and) · [LangChain Open Tutorial: EnsembleRetriever](https://langchain-opentutorial.gitbook.io/langchain-opentutorial/10-retriever/03-ensembleretriever)

item.title: Your 100-Package Monorepo Loads Every CLAUDE.md Into Context — `claudeMdExcludes` Keeps the Packages You Never Touch Out of Scope
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: claudeMdExcludes skips CLAUDE.md files for packages you never touch; worktree.sparsePaths sparse-checks out only relevant directories on session start. Both are committable settings that cut context noise in large monorepos.
item.content:encoded:
**`claudeMdExcludes` in `.claude/settings.json` strips CLAUDE.md files for packages you never touch; `worktree.sparsePaths` sparse-checks out only relevant directories when a subagent starts a worktree.**
In a monorepo with 50+ packages, every Claude Code session discovers and loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories as it reads files in them. A backend session touching `apps/api` may still load configuration from `packages/mobile` and `tools/legacy-*` as Claude explores the codebase — noise from code you never want it near.
`claudeMdExcludes` cuts this. Add it to `.claude/settings.json`:
```json { "claudeMdExcludes": [ "**/packages/legacy-*/**", "**/tools/vendor-scripts/**", "**/apps/mobile/**" ] } ```
Matching CLAUDE.md files are silently skipped. Patterns follow gitignore-style glob rules. The setting is array-mergeable across scopes: a project-level list sets the team baseline; individual developers add local overrides in `~/.claude/settings.json` without overwriting the project defaults. Managed policy CLAUDE.md files (org-level) cannot be excluded.
**What it won't do.** `claudeMdExcludes` only skips CLAUDE.md configuration files — not source files. Claude can still read and edit any file in an excluded package; it won't load that package's configuration. For true source-file exclusion, add deny rules under `permissions.denyList`. The root-level CLAUDE.md always loads regardless; this setting only affects subdirectory files.
For worktree sessions, `worktree.sparsePaths` pairs with this. When Claude creates a worktree via the Agent tool's `isolation: "worktree"` parameter, git checks out the whole repo by default — a 10 GB monorepo writes all packages. `worktree.sparsePaths` uses git sparse-checkout to write only the directories you list:
```json { "worktree": { "sparsePaths": [ "apps/api", "packages/shared", "packages/database" ] } } ```
Root-level files (`.claude/`, `package.json`, lockfiles) always come through regardless. This cuts worktree creation from minutes to seconds on large repos.
**Setup for a 100-package monorepo:** 1. Commit a project `.claude/settings.json` with `claudeMdExcludes` covering legacy, vendored, and unrelated platform packages. 2. Add `worktree.sparsePaths` with the packages each working team touches. List entries merge across scopes, so individuals can add paths in local settings without affecting teammates. 3. Keep the root CLAUDE.md focused on cross-cutting conventions — per-package CLAUDE.md files carry the specialized rules, and they load only when Claude works in that directory.
**Sources:** [Large codebases — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases) · [GitHub issue #4904: File filtering configuration request](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/4904) · [Large projects guide — claude-code-handbook](https://joeyyu23.github.io/claude-code-handbook/en/book2-advanced/18-large-projects)

item.title: Your Background Agent Re-Pays Full Input Tokens on Every Turn When Gaps Exceed 5 Minutes — Set "ttl": "1h" on the System Prompt Block
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The default 5-minute prompt cache TTL expires between turns in agents waiting on CI jobs or human review. Set "ttl": "1h" on the system prompt block to stay warm for an hour at 2x write cost.
item.content:encoded:
**Background agents with inter-turn gaps over 5 minutes silently lose their prompt cache hits — the system prompt re-charges on every turn, paying full input token cost.**
Claude's prompt cache has two TTLs: 5-minute (the default) and 1-hour (opt-in, 2× cache write cost). An interactive chat session almost never hits the 5-minute ceiling. A background agent waiting for a CI pipeline to finish, a human reviewer to sign off, or a batch job to complete often does.
```python # default: cache expires 5 minutes after last write system = [{"type": "text", "text": your_system_prompt}]
# 1-hour TTL: stays warm across long inter-turn pauses system = [ { "type": "text", "text": your_system_prompt, # e.g. 10k tokens of project context "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"} } ] response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", system=system, messages=messages ) ```
**When the 1-hour TTL pays off:** The cache write costs 2× the base input token price. For a 10,000-token system prompt, the break-even is two cache reads per hour. Any agent that runs three or more turns in a session — waiting 10 minutes between each — saves 90% on system prompt tokens from turn two onward. If your agent runs fewer than two turns per hour on average, the 5-minute default stays cheaper.
**Spot a TTL miss:** Check `cache_creation_input_tokens` in the usage block on each turn. If you see a creation charge every turn when you expected hits, the cache expired between turns — the signal to switch to the 1-hour TTL.
**Limit:** The 1-hour TTL only helps when the system prompt stays constant across turns. A system prompt that includes a live timestamp, session ID, or other dynamic context changes every turn regardless of TTL — no TTL prevents that re-write. Keep dynamic values in the `messages` array, not in the cached system block. The 1-hour option is also unavailable on some older Bedrock regions; check the platform docs for regional availability.
**Sources:** [Prompt caching — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Prompt caching in production: patterns that cut API costs — dev.to](https://dev.to/akram_bakhouche/prompt-caching-in-production-the-4-patterns-that-cut-my-anthropic-bill-and-when-not-to-bother-1h5e)

item.title: Every Claude Code Design Implementation Reinvents Your Component API — A Design Section in CLAUDE.md Ends That
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add a design system block to CLAUDE.md listing your component paths, token file location, and icon set — Claude Code reads it before touching a file and stops re-inventing what already exists in your codebase.
item.content:encoded:
**Add a "Design system" block to CLAUDE.md listing your component names, token file, and naming conventions — Claude Code reads project memory before touching a file and stops re-inventing the library you already built.**
When Claude Code implements a design from a handoff bundle or a description, it defaults to whatever feels standard — a bare `<Button>` where you have `<PrimaryButton variant="cta">`, or hardcoded hex values where you have CSS custom properties. The fix is a standing design system section in CLAUDE.md that every session inherits.
```markdown ## Design system
Component library: `src/components/ui/` Token file: `src/styles/tokens.css` — CSS custom properties: --color-primary, --color-surface, --color-text-muted, --spacing-4, --radius-md Icon set: Heroicons v2 (`@heroicons/react/24/solid` or `/24/outline`)
When implementing any UI: 1. Use existing components from `src/components/ui/` before writing new ones 2. Reference CSS custom properties from tokens.css — never hardcode hex values 3. For layout use Tailwind classes; for brand color use the custom properties above 4. If a component doesn't exist and needs creating, put it in `src/components/ui/` with a named export, following the naming pattern already there ```
**What this changes in practice:** With this section present, the first draft of any design implementation uses `--color-primary` instead of `#1a56db`, your existing `<Card>` instead of a new `div` with the same styles, and your icon set rather than whatever appeared in Claude Code's training. Corrections shrink from layout-level to detail-level.
**Pair it with per-task context:** When handing off a Claude Design bundle, add `Implement using the components and tokens in CLAUDE.md` to the prompt. Claude Code reads both the bundle structure and the project brief together.
**The limit to plan around:** CLAUDE.md is manually maintained. Rename a token or move a component directory and the file falls out of sync — Claude Code will continue generating the old path until you update the entry. If you use `/design-sync` to push your design system into Claude Design, update CLAUDE.md in the same commit that changes the token names, so both sides stay aligned.
This is the complement to the per-session brand spec in Claude Design (which anchors Claude Design's output to your tokens). CLAUDE.md anchors Claude Code's implementation to the components that already exist.
**Sources:** [CLAUDE.md project memory — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) · [Bridging Claude Design and Claude Code — DEV Community](https://dev.to/hrekov/bridging-claude-design-and-claude-code-3jbk) · [Claude Design to Claude Code workflow — flowpoint.ai](https://flowpoint.ai/blog/claude-design-to-claude-code)

item.title: Code Review Runs Generic Rules on Every PR Until You Add a REVIEW.md — Here's What to Put in It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code Review looks for REVIEW.md at your repo root before it starts. If the file exists, those rules augment its default behavior — give it your actual codebase conventions, not generic ones.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code Review checks for a `REVIEW.md` at your repo root before it runs. Without one, it applies generic rules. With one, it applies yours.**
The file is plain Markdown. Write it like instructions for a thorough reviewer who knows nothing about your team's conventions:
```markdown # Review rules
- This codebase uses Prisma. Flag any raw SQL or manual query construction. - Database migrations live in `prisma/migrations/`. A PR that edits schema.prisma without a new migration file is incomplete. - All React components must import types from `@/types/` — no inline `any`. - Price formatting must use `lib/currency.ts`. Do not call `Intl.NumberFormat` directly. - Never approve a commit that removes a test without an inline comment explaining why. - API routes under `app/api/` must validate request bodies with Zod before accessing them. ```
The structure that works:
1. **Scope constraints** — which files or patterns Code Review should focus on 2. **Known failure modes** — the bugs your team actually ships (not hypothetical ones) 3. **Conventions a linter can't catch** — file ownership, library choices, naming patterns 4. **Never-approve rules** — your absolute lines for security, data, or test coverage
**Where to find what belongs in this file:** Your last five rejected PRs. The patterns that keep appearing in your code reviews as human comments. Anything your linter flags but doesn't block.
**The limit:** REVIEW.md rules are additive — they extend Code Review's defaults, not replace them. There is no mechanism to disable a built-in rule you disagree with. If a default rule is noisy for your codebase (say, it flags a pattern you use deliberately), the only current mitigation is noting the exception in REVIEW.md so Claude Code treats it as intentional.
Also worth knowing: Code Review runs as a neutral GitHub check, so it can't block a merge on its own — it surfaces findings for human review. What REVIEW.md does is make those findings relevant to your actual codebase, not a generic one.
**Sources:** [Claude Code Review — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review) · [Set up Code Review — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14233555-set-up-code-review-for-claude-code) · [Automated PR review in GitHub Actions — DEV Community](https://dev.to/whoffagents/github-actions-claude-code-automated-pr-review-on-every-commit-510p)

item.title: Claude Ship Launches: Code Review Moves to GA, PR Steward and Claude Approvals Hit Beta
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic's Claude Ship suite launched November 23: Code Review is now generally available, while PR Steward (auto-fixes failing checks) and Claude Approvals (team-policy merges) are in public beta.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Ship landed November 23: Code Review is now generally available; PR Steward (auto-fixes failing checks) and Claude Approvals (merges under a team policy file) are in public beta. The `/ship` command drives the full PR cycle from Claude Code.**
**The three components:**
- **Code Review (GA):** Reviews a PR on open, on each push, or on demand with `@claude review`. Posts findings as a neutral GitHub check — it can't block a merge on its own. Skips draft PRs; forks require a manual `@claude review` comment. - **PR Steward (beta):** Receives Code Review's findings, attempts to fix failing checks, and pushes an amendment commit. For the common cases where Code Review spots something fixable, Steward does the fix without a manual round-trip. - **Claude Approvals (beta):** Evaluates a PR against a policy file you write and stamps approval when conditions are satisfied. Repository branch-protection rules still govern the actual merge — this doesn't bypass your required-reviewer count.
**The `/ship` command:** Paid plan users can run `/ship` from Claude Code to push the current branch, open a PR, trigger review, and work through feedback in one flow. It counts as regular Claude Code usage.
**Limits to know:** Anthropic reports an average cost of $15–25 per Code Review run, billed separately from plan usage. Both PR Steward and Claude Approvals are public beta and subject to change. Anthropic explicitly warns that Code Review may miss security flaws; it is advisory, not a replacement for human review. Code Review and Claude Ship are available on Team and Enterprise plans; the `/ship` command extends to paid individual plans.
**Why it matters:** Automated review catches the boilerplate problems — missing migrations, stale tests, type escapes — before the human reviewer opens the PR. That shifts the human review to judgment calls instead of pattern matching.
**Sources:** [Claude Ship launch — TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes) · [Claude Code Review docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review) · [Set up Code Review — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14233555-set-up-code-review-for-claude-code)

item.title: Your Knowledge Base Re-Embeds Everything When One Document Changes — Track Content Hashes So Only Altered Records Rebuild
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Qdrant's incremental update tutorial builds a sync pipeline that stores a content hash and pipeline version on each vector — only documents whose hash changed get re-embedded on the next run.
item.content:encoded:
**A sync pipeline that re-embeds only changed documents: store a content hash in each vector's payload, compare on each run, and skip unchanged records. Qdrant's official tutorial builds this end-to-end with a Colab notebook.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Run a sync job that re-embeds only the documents that changed since the last run, skips unchanged records entirely, and deletes vectors for documents that were removed from the source — without re-scanning the whole collection.
**Three-bullet takeaway:** - Store a content hash and pipeline version as payload metadata on each vector — if the incoming doc's hash matches the stored value, skip re-embedding and move on - Upsert by stable document ID (a hash of the document path, for example) — Qdrant replaces the whole point on upsert, so a re-run with an unchanged document lands with the same vectors, wasting one embed call but staying correct - Handle deletes explicitly: a naive sync that only processes "active" documents leaves stale vectors from removed docs that keep showing up in retrieval results — query all stored IDs, diff against your active set, delete the orphans
**The core pattern in Python:**
```python from qdrant_client import QdrantClient from qdrant_client.models import PointStruct import hashlib
client = QdrantClient("https://your-cluster.qdrant.io", api_key="...")
def content_hash(text: str) -> str: return hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
def sync_document(doc_id: str, text: str, existing_hashes: dict): h = content_hash(text) if existing_hashes.get(doc_id) == h: return # unchanged — skip
vector = embed(text) # your embedding call client.upsert("my_kb", points=[ PointStruct( id=doc_id, vector=vector, payload={"content_hash": h, "pipeline_version": "1.0"} ) ]) existing_hashes[doc_id] = h
def remove_deleted(active_ids: set, collection: str): all_points, _ = client.scroll(collection, with_payload=["_id"]) stale = [p.id for p in all_points if p.id not in active_ids] if stale: client.delete(collection, points_selector=stale) ```
The official Qdrant tutorial walks through the full pipeline with Qdrant Cloud's free embedding inference and a runnable Colab notebook.
**Limit:** Upserts are only safe for idempotent operations when you use stable, source-document-derived IDs. If the database uses store-generated keys, retrying a failed upsert creates duplicate records. Also: the `pipeline_version` field is how you trigger a full re-embed when you swap embedding models — bump the version and every record whose stored version doesn't match will re-embed on the next sync pass.
**Sources:** [Incremental Embedding Updates — qdrant.tech](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/tutorials-operations/incremental-embedding-updates/) · [Maintaining index freshness — DEV Community](https://dev.to/beefedai/maintaining-index-freshness-incremental-updates-for-vector-databases-16eb) · [Qdrant upsert without recreating collection — oneuptime.com](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-08-28-how-to-upsert-new-qdrant-points-without-recreating-the-collection/view)

item.title: Your DPO Fine-Tune Needs a Finished SFT Run Before It Can Start — ORPO Folds Both Passes Into One Free Colab GPU
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: ORPO (Odds Ratio Preference Optimization) combines instruction tuning and preference alignment in one training pass, removing the SFT checkpoint requirement and the reference model that DPO depends on.
item.content:encoded:
**ORPO trains instruction following and preference alignment in a single pass, removing the SFT checkpoint that DPO requires as a prerequisite — Unsloth's free Colab runs the full pipeline on a T4 GPU.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:**
- Understand why DPO needs two training stages and what ORPO removes - Prepare a preference dataset (prompt, chosen, rejected) from an existing Hub dataset - Run a complete ORPO fine-tune on Llama 3 8B from a base model on a free Colab T4
## The DPO prerequisite problem
DPO computes its alignment loss relative to a reference model — a frozen copy of the SFT-trained checkpoint. That means you need to:
1. SFT-train a base model on instruction pairs first 2. DPO-train the resulting checkpoint against chosen/rejected preference pairs
Skipping step 1 and running DPO against a raw base model usually performs poorly because the reference model's outputs are not well-calibrated for the preference signal.
**ORPO removes the reference model.** It adds a log-odds ratio penalty to the standard SFT cross-entropy loss in the same backward pass: the model simultaneously learns to generate the target output AND to prefer the chosen response over the rejected one — without maintaining a separate frozen checkpoint.
## The concrete walk-through
The free T4 Colab notebook is linked directly from [Unsloth's ORPO guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide/preference-dpo-orpo-and-kto).
**1. Install Unsloth and load the base model**
```python %%capture !pip install "unsloth[colab-new] @ git+https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth.git"
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Meta-Llama-3-8B", # base model, not instruct max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, ) model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=16, ...) ```
**2. Load a preference dataset**
ORPOTrainer expects `prompt`, `chosen`, and `rejected` columns. `mlabonne/orpo-dpo-mix-40k` on the Hub is a cleaned UltraFeedback mix that works without modification.
**3. Train with ORPOTrainer**
```python from trl import ORPOTrainer, ORPOConfig trainer = ORPOTrainer( model=model, args=ORPOConfig(max_steps=200, beta=0.1), train_dataset=dataset, tokenizer=tokenizer, ) trainer.train() ```
The `beta` parameter weights the ORPO penalty against the SFT loss. The original paper uses 0.1; watch both loss components in the training log and adjust if one dominates.
## Limits
ORPO requires a preference dataset upfront — if you don't have human-rated pairs, you'll need to generate or curate them (sample multiple outputs, rate them). Training runs slower per step than SFT alone since both losses compute in every backward pass. And there is no stable SFT fallback: if alignment training goes wrong early, the model hasn't learned instruction following from a stable intermediate checkpoint.
**Sources:** [Unsloth DPO, ORPO & KTO guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide/preference-dpo-orpo-and-kto) · [Fine-tune Llama 3 with ORPO — HuggingFace blog (mlabonne)](https://huggingface.co/blog/mlabonne/orpo-llama-3) · [ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model — arXiv:2403.07691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691)

item.title: Ollama Now Pulls Any GGUF Directly from HuggingFace Hub — One Command, Any Quant
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Ollama's hf.co:// prefix pulls any GGUF from HuggingFace Hub without manual download or conversion. Specify the quantization as a tag; alias the long name with `ollama cp` for daily use.
item.content:encoded:
Ollama has a native bridge to HuggingFace Hub: prefix any model pull with `hf.co/` and it fetches the GGUF directly — no manual download, no format conversion, no intermediate files.
**The pattern:**
```bash ollama pull hf.co/{namespace}/{repo}:{quantization-tag} ```
For example:
```bash ollama pull hf.co/bartowski/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M ollama pull hf.co/mradermacher/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-GGUF:Q5_K_M ollama pull hf.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B-GGUF:Q4_K_M ```
Ollama reads the repo's GGUF filenames, matches the tag you specified, and streams the file directly into your model library — same as a named model from the official registry.
**Finding the right tag:** On any HuggingFace model page, the Files tab shows the GGUF variants. The filename before `.gguf` usually becomes the Ollama tag: `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf` → tag `Q4_K_M`. When in doubt, omit the tag and Ollama picks a default (usually a mid-range quant if one exists).
**Aliasing long names:**
```bash ollama pull hf.co/bartowski/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M ollama cp hf.co/bartowski/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M llama3.1-8b ollama run llama3.1-8b ```
**Three limits to know before you rely on this:**
- **GGUF must already exist in the repo.** Ollama does not quantize on the fly from safetensors. If a model ships only in HF's native format with no GGUF variants, the pull will fail. Check the Files tab before writing the command into scripts. - **Tag names are repo-specific.** Some repos use `q4_k_m` (lowercase), others `Q4_K_M`, others `Q4KM`. The pattern is consistent within a repo but not across repos — copy the exact casing from the filename. - **Private repos require an HF token.** Set `HUGGING_FACE_HUB_TOKEN` in your environment before pulling a gated or private model; public models work without authentication.
The pattern that survives vendor removal: "pull any GGUF from a hosted registry with one command by specifying the quantization as a tag."

item.title: Claude Design Outputs React — Here's the Workflow When Your Stack Is Svelte, Vue, or Tailwind
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Design's component sync is React-only. For Svelte, Vue, or plain Tailwind codebases, the working pattern is: build the visual design in Claude Design, export a standalone artboard as HTML, then give Claude Code the HTML to implement in your actual stack.
item.content:encoded:
Claude Design's design-to-code sync works by bundling components as React — that's the mechanism behind the one-click "Add to code" flow. If your project is Svelte, Vue, Tailwind/plain HTML, or anything non-React, that button produces code you can't use directly.
The working pattern for non-React stacks is two steps: treat Claude Design as a visual specification tool, then hand the output to Claude Code for implementation.
**Step 1: Build the design in Claude Design**
Design the component or screen in Claude Design exactly as you would for any project. Use your brand spec document (pasted at session start) to keep colors, type, and spacing consistent. Don't worry about the generated React code — you're using Claude Design as a visual canvas, not a code generator.
When the artboard looks right, export it: **Share → Export → Standalone HTML**. This gives you a self-contained HTML file with inline CSS — no React dependency, no build step required.
**Step 2: Implement in your stack with Claude Code**
Open Claude Code, attach the exported HTML file, and use a prompt like:
``` Attached is a Claude Design artboard export (standalone HTML). Implement this component in [Svelte / Vue 3 / vanilla HTML+Tailwind]. Match the visual design exactly: colors, spacing, typography, hover states. Use our existing token names where they correspond — primary is `--color-primary`, etc. Do not use React. ```
Claude Code reads the HTML's inline styles and structure, then produces idiomatic code for your actual stack. The result needs a review pass, but the visual fidelity is high because you're giving it exact pixel values and computed styles, not a screenshot or a written description.
**What this workflow doesn't give you:**
- **No live sync.** Changes to the artboard don't propagate to your codebase; each iteration is a fresh export and a new Claude Code prompt. - **No design token awareness.** Claude Design doesn't read your token file. If your Svelte component uses `$primary` and the artboard used `#1a56db`, the translation requires an explicit instruction in the prompt. - **Component hierarchy isn't preserved.** The exported HTML is a flat, computed render. Nested component structure has to be inferred or instructed in the Claude Code prompt.
The pattern is worth it for initial implementation — it closes the visual gap faster than describing a design from scratch. Use it for the first pass; iterate in code after.

item.title: Claude Design Resets Its Visual Context Every Session — A Brand Spec Document Anchors Outputs to Your Tokens Instead of AI Defaults
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Design has no session memory. A one-page brand spec document pasted at session start anchors hex values, fonts, border radii, and component rules so outputs match your design system instead of AI defaults.
item.content:encoded:
**Without a brand spec, every Claude Design session starts from AI defaults: a generic sans-serif, blue-ish primary, and rounded "AI aesthetic." A one-page reference pasted at session start anchors outputs to your actual tokens.**
Claude Design has no persistent memory between sessions. The design system you established last week is gone unless you explicitly bring it in. The simplest fix is a brand spec document — a text file that describes your design decisions precisely enough that Claude Design can follow them without seeing your codebase.
**What to put in the spec:**
```markdown # Brand Spec — [Project Name]
## Colors Primary: #1a56db (CTAs and active states only) Surface: #f8fafc (page background), #ffffff (card background) On-primary text: #ffffff Danger: #e02424 Text primary: #111827, secondary: #6b7280
## Typography Font: Inter (web), system-ui (fallback) — never Arial or generic sans-serif Heading: weight 600, tracking -0.02em Body: weight 400, 1.6 line-height
## Components Buttons: rounded-lg (8px radius), no drop shadows, padding 10px 20px Cards: rounded-xl (12px), border 1px #e5e7eb, no gradient backgrounds
## Anti-patterns No glassmorphism, gradient fills, or decorative patterns No default blue (#3b82f6) — use our primary (#1a56db) No "AI aesthetic" gradients on hero sections ```
Paste this at the start of every session, before any design prompt. Outputs that deviate can be corrected by citing the specific spec rule.
**Two limits to plan around:** The spec is manually maintained — if your codebase tokens change, update the spec separately. Claude Design still can't read your actual token file; it's working from your text description. When the spec drifts from the code, generated output drifts too.
**Where to store it:** Keep it as `docs/brand-spec.md` in your repo. Claude Code can read it and pass the content when it invokes a design session — or reference it from your CLAUDE.md so any session can find it without being told.
**Why it matters for the handoff:** A brand spec reduces the gap between what Claude Design generates and what Claude Code implements. Without one, every imported component needs manual token substitution. With one, the first draft is usually close enough that Claude Code's corrections are small and predictable.
**Sources:** [Claude Design overview — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/claude-design) · [Claude Design produces AI slop unless you tell it not to — The Adpharm](https://www.theadpharm.com/insights/claude-design-without-the-ai-slop-look) · [Build a Design System in Claude Design — Mindstudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/build-design-system-claude-design-no-ai-aesthetics)

item.title: Your Vector Search Ignores the Date and Source Fields You Stored — LangChain's SelfQueryRetriever Parses Natural-Language Constraints Into Pre-Filters Before Similarity Search Runs
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Vector similarity ignores date ranges, source filters, and categories. LangChain's SelfQueryRetriever uses an LLM to parse natural-language constraints into structured pre-filters before similarity search runs.
item.content:encoded:
**If your RAG retriever returns results from the wrong time period or wrong source, the problem is not the embeddings — vector similarity has no way to honor "from last week" or "from the blog" unless you filter first. SelfQueryRetriever uses an LLM to infer the filter from the user's question before the search runs.**
**What you will be able to do after this:** Build a retriever that narrows the search space by structured metadata (date, source, category, author) before vector similarity runs — so "Python tutorials from the last two weeks" retrieves the right documents even when older ones have higher embedding similarity.
**Three takeaways:** - Dense search ranks by cosine distance alone. A document from two years ago on the same topic outscores a fresh one unless you filter by date before searching. - SelfQueryRetriever adds one LLM call per query to generate the filter. That call adds latency and cost — if your filters are predictable, passing `search_kwargs={"filter": {...}}` directly is cheaper and more reliable. - Filter syntax differs by vector store: Chroma uses `$gte`, `$lte`, `$eq`, `$contains`; Pinecone uses `$gt`, `$lt`; FAISS does not support metadata filtering natively. Test on your store before relying on this in production.
**Walk-through:**
```python from langchain.retrievers.self_query.base import SelfQueryRetriever from langchain.chains.query_constructor.base import AttributeInfo from langchain_chroma import Chroma from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
# 1. Documents must carry metadata at ingest time from langchain_core.documents import Document docs = [ Document( page_content="How to use pgvector for RAG", metadata={"source": "blog", "date": "2026-11-15", "category": "rag"} ), # ... ] vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(docs, embedding_function)
# 2. Describe each metadata field to the retriever metadata_field_info = [ AttributeInfo( name="source", description="Where the document came from: 'blog', 'docs', or 'github'", type="string", ), AttributeInfo( name="date", description="Publication date in YYYY-MM-DD format", type="string", ), AttributeInfo( name="category", description="Topic area: 'python', 'typescript', 'rag'", type="string", ), ]
# 3. Build the retriever — LLM parses the question into a filter retriever = SelfQueryRetriever.from_llm( llm=ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6"), vectorstore=vectorstore, document_contents="Technical tutorials and blog posts", metadata_field_info=metadata_field_info, verbose=True, # log the generated filter during development )
# 4. Query naturally docs = retriever.invoke("RAG tutorials from the last two weeks") # LangChain generates: {"date": {"$gte": "2026-11-09"}, "category": "rag"} # That filter runs against metadata before similarity search ```
**What to watch for:** The LLM-generated filter must match your metadata keys exactly — a mismatch silently returns no results rather than raising an error. Log with `verbose=True` during development to confirm the generated filter. For Chroma specifically, the `$gte` date comparison works only if dates are stored as ISO strings in consistent format; mixed formats produce incorrect ordering.
**Sources:** [LangChain: How to do self-querying retrieval — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/self_query/) · [MongoDB self-querying tutorial — mongodb.com/docs](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/ai-integrations/langchain/self-query-retrieval/) · [Advanced RAG techniques Part 7 — medium.com/@roberto.g.infante](https://medium.com/@roberto.g.infante/advanced-rag-techniques-with-langchain-part-7-843ecd3199f0)

item.title: Your RAG Index Has No Idea When Source Documents Change — LangChain's Indexing API Tracks Hashes and Removes Stale Chunks
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: LangChain's indexing API with SQLRecordManager tracks document content hashes. Run index() with cleanup="full" to skip unchanged files and purge stale chunks when source docs are deleted.
item.content:encoded:
**Your RAG index silently serves stale chunks the moment a source document changes — LangChain's `SQLRecordManager` tracks content hashes so re-runs skip what's unchanged and delete what's gone.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** keep a knowledge base in sync with a changing source directory — handling edits, new files, and deletions — without re-embedding everything from scratch.
**Three takeaways:** - `index()` with a record manager hashes every document chunk; unchanged hashes are skipped, changed ones are re-embedded and re-indexed - `cleanup="full"` deletes orphaned vector store chunks when source documents are removed — without it, deleted files stay in retrieval results indefinitely - The record manager's SQLite state file must survive process restarts — commit it or put it in a durable path, or every run re-embeds everything
**Walk-through:**
```bash pip install langchain langchain-openai langchain-community chromadb ```
```python from langchain.indexes import SQLRecordManager, index from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma from langchain_community.document_loaders import DirectoryLoader
# 1. Record manager — run create_schema() once namespace = "chroma/my_docs" record_manager = SQLRecordManager( namespace, db_url="sqlite:///record_manager_cache.sql" ) record_manager.create_schema()
# 2. Vector store vectorstore = Chroma( embedding_function=OpenAIEmbeddings(), persist_directory="./chroma_db" )
# 3. Load all source docs each time loader = DirectoryLoader("./docs", glob="**/*.md") docs = loader.load()
# 4. Incremental index — idempotent, handles adds/edits/deletes result = index( docs, record_manager, vectorstore, cleanup="full", # remove chunks from deleted source docs source_id_key="source", # group chunks by origin file path ) print(result) # {'num_added': 2, 'num_updated': 0, 'num_skipped': 10, 'num_deleted': 1} ```
**Two limits to plan around:** - `cleanup="full"` runs *after* all documents are indexed, so there is a brief window where old and new chunks coexist — schedule indexing runs at low-traffic times if that matters - With Chroma on SQLite there is a known bug where stale chunks survive deletion; enabling WAL mode on the SQLite connection (`isolation_level=None`) mitigates it, but test on your store before relying on deletion in production
**Sources:** [LangChain indexing how-to](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/indexing) · [LangChain blog: syncing data sources to vector stores](https://www.langchain.com/blog/syncing-data-sources-to-vector-stores) · [DEV Community: incremental updates — keeping the knowledge base fresh](https://dev.to/wonderlab/rag-series-19-incremental-updates-keeping-the-knowledge-base-fresh-596c)

item.title: Your Claude Design Handoff Bundle Names Tokens Claude Code Has Never Seen — `/design-sync` Is the Step That Makes Them Match
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run `/design-sync` in Claude Code before exporting a handoff bundle — it uploads your existing design system into Claude Design so the bundle's token names already match your codebase.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `/design-sync` in Claude Code before exporting a handoff bundle — it uploads your existing design system into Claude Design so the bundle's token names already match your codebase.**
When Claude Design exports a handoff bundle, it packages a component structure, layout hierarchy, and a list of design token names. Claude Code reads that token list and builds with those names — `var(--color-brand-primary)`, `spacing-4`, whatever the design file uses. If those names already exist in your codebase, you get clean variable references. If they don't — because you built the design from scratch inside Claude Design — Claude Code generates a new parallel token set that conflicts with or sits alongside the one you've already built.
`/design-sync` closes that gap, and it needs to run before the export.
**Run it from Claude Code:**
```bash /design-sync ```
The command reads your existing design system from the working directory — `tokens.css`, your Tailwind config, component files — and uploads it into the linked Claude Design project. After that, when you create or adjust layouts in Claude Design, it uses your actual token names. The handoff bundle it generates then refers to `var(--color-brand-primary)` exactly as your codebase already defines it, so Claude Code implements against variables that already exist.
**What to verify before syncing:**
- Token names are consistent throughout — mixing `--color-primary` and `--clr-primary` in the same file produces confusion in both directions - Component files are in discoverable paths, not buried in undocumented subdirectories - If `/design-sync` doesn't appear in your command list, run `/update` to refresh skills — it may not appear in older sessions (reported by multiple practitioners)
**The limit to know:** Sync is not live. Rename a token after syncing — say, `--color-primary` becomes `--color-brand-primary` — and the design file keeps the old name until you re-sync. Build the habit of re-syncing after any token rename or design system restructure, before your next handoff export.
One independent reviewer (The New Stack, reviewing Claude Design's June 2026 update) noted that design operations draw from the same usage pool as other Claude work — so frequent re-syncs on a large design system are worth factoring into your planning.
**Sources:** [Claude Design stays on brand for daily work (claude.com/blog)](https://claude.com/blog/claude-design-stays-on-brand-for-daily-work) · [Anthropic ships major Claude Design overhaul — VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/technology/anthropic-ships-major-claude-design-overhaul-with-design-system-imports-code-round-trips-and-a-fix-for-its-token-burning-problem) · [The New Stack: Claude Design overhaul coverage](https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-claude-design-overhaul/)

item.title: Your Unattended Claude Code Agent Still Prompts for Approval When an Edge-Case Tool Call Isn't on Your List — `--dangerously-skip-permissions` Inside a Container Gives True Zero-Prompt Operation
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: `--allowedTools` scopes permissions but still prompts for unlisted tool calls. `--dangerously-skip-permissions` removes all prompts — safely only inside an isolated container where the container itself is the blast-radius boundary.
item.content:encoded:
**`--dangerously-skip-permissions` removes all approval prompts from Claude Code. The safety comes from the container around it, not the flag — and that distinction is what makes it usable in automated pipelines.**
Your headless agent hits a prompt, hangs, and your CI job times out. You add `--allowedTools "Bash,Read,Write,Edit"` and it mostly works — until the agent calls `WebFetch` to verify a URL, or `ListMcpResourcesTool` on a server you forgot to scope. Each unlisted tool is either a hang (if the prompt is interactive) or a denied tool call (if `denyInsteadOfPrompting` is set), and both outcomes break the run in ways that are hard to debug after the fact.
The root issue is that an allowlist can't anticipate every tool a capable agent reaches for. `--dangerously-skip-permissions` (or its equivalent permission mode `bypassPermissions`) bypasses the approval layer entirely — no prompts, no denies, every tool call runs.
**Why this is safe inside a container but not outside**
The flag does not sandbox anything. It does not restrict network access, revoke credentials, or limit what Claude Code can read. What makes it safe to use is what you put around it: an isolated container or VM with: - Only the environment variables the task needs (not your full CI token set) - A firewall or network policy that blocks unapproved egress - A clean checkout, not your workstation with `~/.aws` and `~/.npmrc` mounted in
Anthropic's own dev container (`github.com/trailofbits/claude-code-devcontainer`) ships a firewall that blocks unapproved outbound connections, which is why the flag is usable in that image. Without that boundary, you're giving the agent your full machine's network and credential access.
**Running it:**
```bash # Docker one-liner: clean container, project mounted read/write, no other creds # Use your base image of choice (Node LTS works; check the official sandbox docs # for the Anthropic-maintained devcontainer image) docker run --rm \ -v $(pwd):/workspace \ -w /workspace \ -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY \ node:22 \ bash -c "npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code && \ claude --dangerously-skip-permissions --print \ 'Run the test suite and fix any failures.'" ```
Replace the unbounded network with a custom bridge that permits only `api.anthropic.com` and your project's services — that's the firewall step that makes this defensible. Docker's own Claude Code sandbox doc (`docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/agents/claude-code/`) ships a pre-wired version if you want a ready-made starting point.
**What to pass in and what to keep out**
A common mistake is running the container with the full CI environment forwarded in. If your pipeline exports `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `DATABASE_URL`, those are visible to anything the agent runs. Pass only what the specific task needs. For a test-and-fix agent, that's usually just `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
**One thing `denyInsteadOfPrompting` still adds**
Even with `bypassPermissions`, keeping `denyInsteadOfPrompting: true` in your project settings is worthwhile: it documents intent and blocks any tool the agent shouldn't have if you later run the same session interactively rather than in bypass mode.
