item.title: Your Inference Code Is Locked to One Provider — OpenRouter Puts 400+ Models Behind a Single OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint With Per-Request Fallback
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: OpenRouter is an OpenAI-compatible gateway to 400+ models from dozens of providers. Change one string to switch models; list fallbacks so your app keeps running when a provider is rate-limited or down.
item.content:encoded:
**OpenRouter sits between your code and 400+ models — Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, and more — through a single OpenAI-compatible URL. Swap providers by changing a model string; add a fallback list so your app self-heals when one is down.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Call any model OpenRouter supports using the same `openai` Python client you already use, with one environment variable change - Declare ordered fallback models so a rate-limited or unavailable primary is retried automatically - Route to the cheapest provider for a given model, or force the fastest, with a one-word suffix
**Three things to know first:** 1. Model IDs on OpenRouter follow the pattern `vendor/model-name` (e.g. `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6`, `openai/gpt-4o`, `meta-llama/llama-3.1-70b-instruct`). IDs change when providers update their catalogs — query `/models` to get current ones rather than hardcoding from a tutorial. 2. Auto-routing (`openrouter/auto`) selects the model automatically, powered by NotDiamond's routing. It may choose a weaker model when it underestimates task complexity — treat it as a convenience, not a production routing strategy for high-stakes tasks. 3. Free models (`:free` suffix, e.g. `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free`) are available but rate-limited; `openrouter/free` always resolves to whichever free model is currently available, so it can silently downgrade.
**Walk-through:**
```bash pip install openai python-dotenv ```
```python # .env OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
# main.py import os from openai import OpenAI from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv() client = OpenAI( api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"], base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this in one sentence: ..."}], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
That's the entire migration from a direct Anthropic or OpenAI client. The `base_url` and key are the only differences.
**Adding fallback models:**
OpenRouter accepts a non-standard `extra_body` parameter with a `models` list. If the first model fails, it tries the next:
```python response = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6", messages=[...], extra_body={ "models": [ "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6", "openai/gpt-4o", "meta-llama/llama-3.1-70b-instruct", ] } ) ```
Only the successful attempt is billed. Order by provider diversity and decreasing cost to maximize resilience without overspending on fallbacks.
**Provider routing suffixes:** - `:nitro` — fastest available provider for this model (higher cost) - `:floor` — cheapest available provider - `:free` — free tier only; may not exist for all models
```python # Always route to the fastest Claude Sonnet provider model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6:nitro" ```
**What OpenRouter doesn't give you:** model-level rate-limit visibility per provider, guaranteed latency SLAs, or any control over which data center serves a request. For compliance requirements (data residency, HIPAA) you still need to go direct to the provider.
**Sources:** [Real Python: OpenRouter API tutorial](https://realpython.com/openrouter-api/) · [OpenRouter model routing docs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/overview.md) · [KDnuggets: access multiple AI models with OpenRouter](https://www.kdnuggets.com/?p=210718) · [DataCamp: OpenRouter tutorial](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/openrouter)

item.title: Your Claude Code Subagents Can't Message Each Other — Agent Teams Enable the Peer-to-Peer Channel That Subagents Don't Have
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Subagents report to a parent; agent teams let parallel Claude Code sessions message each other directly via ListAgents/SendMessage. Enable with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 — but know the limits before you depend on them.
item.content:encoded:
**Agent teams (`CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`) let parallel Claude Code sessions send messages to each other directly — a different architecture from subagents, which can only report up to a single orchestrator.**
The fork/subagent pattern you already use is a hierarchy: one orchestrator spawns workers, workers report results back up, the orchestrator synthesizes. That's the right shape for most parallel work — independent tasks fanned out and collected. The gap it doesn't cover is when parallel investigators need to share a finding *mid-run* so that another agent can adjust its current approach. Subagents can't do that; they can only return at the end.
Agent teams fill that gap. Each session in a team can call `ListAgents` to see its siblings and `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})` to communicate. A code-review agent can tell a test-writing agent that module X has a bug before the test-writing agent finalizes its plan.
**Enabling it:**
```json // .claude/settings.json { "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1" } } ```
Or set it in your shell: `export CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`
**Two display modes:**
- **In-process** (default): teammates run in the same terminal. Works everywhere, no extra setup. - **tmux**: teammates get their own split panes. Requires tmux; the official docs recommend iTerm2's native tmux integration (`tmux -CC`) on macOS for the smoothest experience.
**When to use agent teams instead of subagents:**
Use subagents (fork or fresh) when tasks are *independent* — each agent needs context from the parent but nothing from its siblings. Use agent teams when agents need to *coordinate mid-task*: parallel reviewers that catch each other's issues, two agents exploring different implementation paths where one's dead-end should stop the other early.
For simple parallelism (fan out tasks → collect results), subagents are simpler and have fewer rough edges.
**Real limits (don't skip these):**
- **Session resumption breaks**: `/resume` and `/rewind` don't restore in-process teammates. If a session ends, teammates don't come back. - **Practical max is 2–3 agents**: at 4+ parallel agents, coordination overhead accumulates and there are reported crashes; one GitHub issue shows a 4-agent run where agents failed mid-task. - **Still experimental**: the docs list known limitations in task coordination and shutdown behavior. Orphaned tmux panes remain after teammates exit. - **Silent mode fallback**: in-process mode runs in `-p` (pipe mode), and agent teams silently disable in some scripted contexts.
This is the right tool for a narrow set of patterns. For the overwhelming majority of parallel work, [fork/fresh subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) — covered [here](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-11-21-03-claude-code-fork-vs-fresh-subagent-context-inheritance) — are simpler and more predictable.
**Sources:** [Claude Code agent teams — official docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams) · [Addy Osmani: Claude Code swarms in practice](https://addyosmani.com/blog/claude-code-agent-teams/) · [DEV: what the docs don't tell you](https://dev.to/mathieu_kessler_8712ec765/claude-code-agent-teams-what-the-docs-dont-tell-you-1iae) · [GitHub issue #23615 (4-agent crash report)](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/23615)

item.title: Every RAG Tutorial Skips the Part Where You Get the Text Out of the PDF — Docling Parses Documents Into Structure-Aware Markdown Chunks
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Most RAG tutorials assume clean text input. Docling converts PDFs, DOCX, and HTML into Markdown that preserves table rows and heading hierarchy — here's the LlamaIndex integration in 15 lines.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this: load a messy enterprise PDF into LlamaIndex, preserve its table structure and heading hierarchy, and feed chunked nodes into a vector store — without writing any parsing logic yourself.**
Most RAG tutorials start with `text = "Here is the document content..."`. Real documents are PDFs with two-column layouts, Word files with merged cells, and HTML with navigation wrapped around the article. A character-based chunker doesn't know the five words on the right column belong with the three on the left. Docling does.
**Three things worth knowing:**
1. **Docling converts PDFs, DOCX, PPTX, HTML, and images to structured Markdown or JSON**, preserving table rows, list items, and heading hierarchy that raw `pypdf` text extraction loses — the result is a Document model, not a flat string. 2. **The LlamaIndex `DoclingReader` and `DoclingNodeParser` plug into any existing pipeline** — swap your `SimpleDirectoryReader` for `DoclingReader` and chunks immediately carry metadata like heading path, page number, and a table flag. 3. **For plain digital PDFs it parses in seconds with no GPU**; for scanned or complex-layout PDFs, Docling uses its vision-language layout model — first run downloads ~300 MB of models.
**Walk-through:**
```bash pip install docling llama-index-readers-docling llama-index-node-parser-docling ```
```python from llama_index.readers.docling import DoclingReader from llama_index.node_parser.docling import DoclingNodeParser from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex
# Load a PDF — returns Docling Document objects, not raw strings reader = DoclingReader() docs = reader.load_data(file_path="annual_report.pdf")
# Parse into LlamaIndex TextNodes with structural metadata parser = DoclingNodeParser() nodes = parser.get_nodes_from_documents(docs)
# Build your index — nodes are already chunked with context index = VectorStoreIndex(nodes) ```
Each node's `metadata` carries `dl_meta.heading_path` (the section this chunk lives under) and `dl_meta.doc_items[].label` (whether it's a paragraph, table cell, list item). Pass those to your vector store and you can filter by section at retrieval time.
**Limit:** Docling's default pipeline runs locally — on a first run it downloads ~300 MB of models. For large-volume production ingestion, [Docling Serve](https://github.com/DS4SD/docling-serve) (self-hosted REST API) is a better fit. If your documents are simple digital PDFs with no tables, `pypdf` with less overhead may be enough; Docling's value compounds with complex, mixed-format document libraries.
**Sources:** [LlamaIndex Docling Reader demo](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/data_connectors/doclingreaderdemo/) · [IBM Docling RAG guide](https://ibm.com/granite/docs/use-cases/docling-rag) · [Docling GitHub](https://github.com/DS4SD/docling) · [Docling technical report (arXiv 2501.17887)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17887)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Has No Guard Against Pushing to Main or Dropping a Table — A PreToolUse Hook Blocks Those Commands Before They Run
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code's PreToolUse hook fires before a tool runs; exit code 2 blocks it and sends the reason back to Claude. Here's the guard pattern for git push to main, database drops, and other irreversible commands.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code's `PreToolUse` hook fires before a tool runs; exit code `2` blocks the tool and sends your hook's stdout back to Claude as the reason — here's the guard pattern for `git push` to main, database drops, and other commands you'd regret.**
This is distinct from the [Stop hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code/hooks), which gates session end. `PreToolUse` fires on individual tool calls — before the command executes, not after.
**Wire it up in `.claude/settings.json`:**
```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ {"type": "command", "command": "bash .claude/hooks/guard-dangerous.sh"} ] } ] } } ```
**The guard script:**
```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # .claude/hooks/guard-dangerous.sh (chmod +x this file) INPUT=$(cat) CMD=$(echo "$INPUT" | python3 -c " import sys, json d = json.load(sys.stdin) print(d.get('tool_input', {}).get('command', '')) ")
if echo "$CMD" | grep -qE \ 'git push.*(main|master)|git reset --hard|DROP TABLE|rm -rf /|git push --force'; then echo "Guard: blocked '${CMD:0:120}' — matches a protected pattern." echo "Use a feature branch, or state explicitly why this is safe." exit 2 fi ```
The hook receives JSON on stdin; `tool_input.command` is the bash command Claude is about to run. Exit `2` returns your message to Claude; exit `1` logs an error but lets the call through; exit `0` is a clean pass.
**Keep it fast.** Every `PreToolUse` hook adds latency to every matching tool call. No network calls, no slow validation — keep the script under 100 ms. If you need a heavier check (linting a file before it's edited), use a `PostToolUse` hook instead.
**What this does and doesn't do.** This is a friction layer, not a security boundary. Claude can work around a pattern-match by rephrasing the command. `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` bypasses `PreToolUse` in some execution environments. For genuine safety requirements, enforce them in CI — the hook is fast feedback in the development loop, not a substitute for server-side protection.
**Sources:** [Claude Code hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code/hooks) · [Claude Code hooks guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide) · [DataCamp: Claude Code Hooks tutorial](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/claude-code-hooks)

item.title: Your Research Subagent Re-Explains the Entire Codebase Each Time Because You Used Agent Instead of Fork — Fork Inherits the Full Session Context
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: subagent_type: "fork" gives a Claude Code subagent your full conversation history with no re-briefing; a fresh Agent call starts clean — here's the decision rule and limits.
item.content:encoded:
**`subagent_type: "fork"` inherits the full parent conversation; a fresh Agent call starts with only the delegation prompt — the right choice depends on whether the subagent needs to know what you know.**
When you delegate work to a Claude Code subagent, the agent type determines what context it starts with.
**Fresh agent (default)**
```javascript Agent({ description: "Review the diff for correctness bugs", prompt: "Review the changes in src/api/ for correctness bugs. The API uses Express 5 with async error handling..." }) ```
A fresh agent starts clean — it has only the prompt you wrote. You re-brief it. This costs token re-entry but gives you a clean slate. Use it for: - Parallel independent tasks (ship multiple fresh agents in one message) - Work that requires deliberate isolation — no risk of picking up wrong conclusions from your session - Specialized review where you want a second opinion uncontaminated by your reasoning
**Fork (`subagent_type: "fork"`)**
```javascript Agent({ subagent_type: "fork", description: "Research the cache invalidation approach", prompt: "Given everything we've discussed about the architecture, research cache invalidation strategies that fit the constraints we identified. Focus on the Redis approach." }) ```
A fork inherits your full conversation — every tool result, every file you've read, every conclusion you've reached. No re-briefing. Use it when: - The subagent needs to know what you know to do its job - You're extracting a research thread that would pollute your context with output you won't reuse - You want to keep raw tool output out of your context window
**Decision rule**
> Fork when the subagent needs the context you've already built. Fresh when it doesn't — or when you want parallel isolation.
**Limits to know**
- A fork cannot spawn its own forks (fork depth is capped at 1) - Forks are disabled by default in `claude -p` (non-interactive) mode — set `CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=1` to enable - `isolation: "worktree"` controls file isolation, not context inheritance — you can have a worktree-isolated fork or a non-isolated fresh agent - Forks carry the full parent context in their token budget — a long parent session makes an expensive fork
**Sources:** [Anthropic: subagents in Claude Code](https://claude.com/blog/subagents-in-claude-code), [Claude Code sub-agents docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), [Claude Agent SDK: subagents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents), [Claude Code Handbook: fork vs fresh](https://joeyyu23.github.io/claude-code-handbook/en/book2-advanced/05-subagents)

item.title: Check Two Things in Your AI Dev Environment Today: Claude Code's Allow-Rule File and Any Microsoft Agent Framework Install
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitGuardian found 31,088 secrets committed via Claude Code's approve history; Microsoft agent-framework 1.26.1–1.26.2 stole Azure and GitHub credentials on Python startup.
item.content:encoded:
**Two unrelated credential exposure incidents hit the AI dev toolchain this week — your approve-history file and your Python site-packages both need a check.**
**Incident 1: Claude Code's `.claude/settings.local.json` leaking secrets**
When you click "Don't Ask Again" to approve a Claude Code tool call, Claude Code stores that approval in `.claude/settings.local.json`. If the approved command contained an inline credential — an API key passed as an environment variable, a token in a curl call — that credential is now in the file verbatim.
Apiiro found this in early November; GitGuardian confirmed the scope: **31,088 secrets in 23,276 public GitHub repositories**, all from developers committing their local settings file.
Check whether you're affected:
```bash # Is the file tracked? git ls-files '*settings.local.json'
# Has it ever been committed? git log --all -p -- .claude/settings.local.json | grep -E '(ANTHROPIC|AWS|sk-|Bearer)'
# Remove it from tracking without deleting it git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .gitignore git commit -m "chore: untrack settings.local.json" ```
The fix is permanent: once it's in `.gitignore` and untracked, future "don't ask again" approvals won't be committed. If you found leaked credentials, rotate them before or immediately after removing the file.
The underlying issue (tracked as [GitHub issue #13106](https://claudeissues.com/issue/13106)) is that the file has no `.gitignore` entry by default. Claude Code hasn't shipped a fix for new installs yet as of this writing.
**Incident 2: Microsoft agent-framework PyPI supply chain attack (November 17)**
Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the `agent-framework` PyPI package — Microsoft's official multi-agent orchestration library — contained a credential stealer. It was delivered as a `.pth` file (a Python path extension that runs on interpreter startup, before your code executes) and exfiltrated Azure service principal credentials and GitHub Actions tokens.
The packages were pulled in approximately 55 minutes. This is the second Microsoft PyPI package compromise this year.
```bash # Check your installed version pip show agent-framework | grep Version
# Check for unexpected .pth files in site-packages python -c "import site; print(site.getsitepackages())" # Then: ls <that path>/*.pth
# Upgrade to 1.26.3 or later (clean release) pip install --upgrade agent-framework ```
If you ran 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 — or have them in a lockfile — treat any Azure service principal credentials and GitHub tokens in that environment as compromised and rotate them.
**Sources:** [InfoWorld / GitGuardian report](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4247344/claude-codes-dont-ask-again-button-has-a-secrets-spilling-problem-2.html), [CSOonline / Apiiro](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4247336/claude-codes-dont-ask-again-button-has-a-secrets-spilling-problem.html), [BleepingComputer: Microsoft agent-framework](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsofts-agent-framework-pypi-package-compromised-to-steal-credentials), [OX Security: technical breakdown](https://www.ox.security/blog/breaking-hijacked-releases-of-microsofts-official-agent-framework-steals-azure-and-ci-credentials/)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Reads the Figma Frame File Name and Guesses the Layout — Point It at the Remote MCP Server and It Gets the Real Component Tree
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add Figma's remote MCP server in one command and Claude Code reads your component library, variable values, and Code Connect mappings before writing any implementation code.
item.content:encoded:
**Add `https://mcp.figma.com/mcp` as a remote MCP server and Claude Code reads your Figma component tree, design tokens, and Code Connect mappings before implementing a frame.**
Without the MCP server, sharing a Figma design with Claude Code means pasting a screenshot or manually describing the component hierarchy. Claude Code infers layout from the image and guesses which components to use. With the remote MCP server, it reads the actual component structure, variable values, and — if you've set up Code Connect — the exact component names from your codebase.
**Setup**
```bash claude mcp add --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp ```
That's the full setup command. Claude Code will prompt for OAuth the first time it calls a Figma tool. The server is remote (Figma-hosted), so there's nothing to install locally.
**Prerequisite:** A Figma account with a **Dev seat or Full seat**. The MCP server uses the Dev Mode API; Viewer seats can't access it.
**What Claude Code can read**
Once connected, Claude Code has access to:
- `get_component` — component metadata, properties, variants - `get_variable_collections` — your design token values (colors, spacing, typography) - `get_code_connect` — Code Connect mappings, linking Figma components to your actual component imports and prop signatures
**Workflow: implementing a frame**
Share the Figma frame URL in your session:
``` Here's the frame I need to implement: https://www.figma.com/design/abc123/MyDesign?node-id=42-100 Build the React component using our existing component library. ```
Claude Code calls `get_code_connect` to look up which components map to the Figma frame's contents, reads the variable collections for token values, and then writes implementation code using your actual component names and prop signatures — not guesses from a screenshot.
**Reverse direction: generating a Figma design**
`generate_figma_design` works the other way — Claude Code creates a Figma frame from a description or existing code. This tool is Claude Code-only (not available in other MCP clients) and requires the same remote MCP server.
**Code Connect prerequisite**
The `get_code_connect` tool only returns useful data if you've set up Figma Code Connect for your component library. Without it, Claude Code still gets component structure and design tokens, but won't know which React (or Vue, or Swift) component each Figma component maps to.
**Sources:** [Figma MCP server guide](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide), [Figma: Claude Code for designers](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/claude-code-for-designers/), [Figma MCP server help article](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/35281186390679), [builder.io: Claude Code + Figma MCP](https://www.builder.io/blog/claude-code-figma-mcp-server)

item.title: Your Recurring Claude Code Check Only Runs When You Remember to Type It — `/loop <interval>` Reschedules Any Prompt Inside a Session, Cloud Routines Survive the Terminal
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: /loop 30m "check for PR review comments" re-runs a prompt on a schedule inside a live Claude Code session; cloud routines at claude.ai/code/routines run on a cron expression even after the terminal closes.
item.content:encoded:
**`/loop 30m "summarize new PR review comments and flag blockers"` re-runs a prompt on a schedule inside a live Claude Code session; cloud routines at `claude.ai/code/routines` run on a cron expression even after the terminal closes.**
Recurring checks — polling a CI endpoint, triaging new issues every 30 minutes, running a test sweep after every file change — stop requiring you to trigger them manually once you wire them into `/loop` or a cloud routine.
**In-session scheduling with `/loop`**
Inside a running Claude Code session, type:
``` /loop 15m run the test suite and show me any new failures since last time /loop 1h summarize all file changes I've made and flag anything that looks incomplete /loop */10 * * * * check if any background agent has posted a result and summarize it ```
The interval can be a duration (`5m`, `30m`, `2h`) or a 5-field cron expression. Claude re-runs the prompt on that schedule without further input.
**Limits:** - Session tasks die when the terminal closes or the session ends — they're conversation-scoped. - Up to 50 scheduled tasks per session. - Timing uses your local timezone, not UTC — `0 9 * * *` fires at 9am local. If you work across time zones, verify the offset before setting nightly tasks.
**Durable scheduling with cloud routines**
For tasks that must outlive the terminal — a nightly code quality review, a daily standup summary, a monitor that runs while you sleep — use cloud routines at `claude.ai/code/routines`. Routines run on a cron expression regardless of whether a terminal is open, and their history is visible from the web and mobile Claude apps.
The same session context (project directory, CLAUDE.md, allowed tools) applies. Per the docs, MCP servers and plugin configs aren't restored automatically — include them in the routine's prompt or as flags on the launch command.
**Limit:** Cloud routines require a Claude.ai account with Claude Code on the web (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise). They don't apply to pure API key access, and sessions that run via `claude -p` are not restored.
**Sources:** [Claude Code scheduled tasks docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks), [Claude Code routines docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines.md), [DEV: closing the automation gap in Claude Code](https://dev.to/dortort/closing-the-automation-gap-in-claude-code-5492), [BetterStack: Claude Code /loop guide](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/claude-code-loop/)

item.title: Your RAG Chunks Lose the Document Context That Would Make Them Retrievable — Contextual Retrieval Prepends a One-Sentence Situating Summary to Each Before Indexing
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Prepend a one-sentence LLM-generated context to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing. Anthropic reports a 49% retrieval failure rate reduction. Prompt caching keeps per-document indexing costs manageable.
item.content:encoded:
**Prepend a one-sentence LLM-generated context to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing. Anthropic reports a 49% retrieval failure rate reduction when both are combined. Prompt caching keeps per-document indexing costs manageable.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Index a document collection so retrieved chunks carry enough surrounding context that the retriever can locate passages that only make sense within their source document — fixing the case where a chunk like "Revenue grew 15% above the prior quarter" retrieves for nothing because it has no document context attached.
**Three takeaways:** - Context prefixes improve dense retrieval and BM25 retrieval independently; combining Contextual Embeddings with Contextual BM25 is where Anthropic reports the 49% reduction in top-20 retrieval failures (5.7% → 2.9%) — these are Anthropic's own benchmark figures, not independently audited. - Prompt caching is what makes per-chunk LLM calls affordable: the full document stays in the cache prefix, so you pay for one full-document token read per batch rather than one per chunk. - The gain is largest for documents where chunks span a topic that only makes sense with surrounding context (financial reports, meeting transcripts, numbered-step procedures). For self-contained chunks (FAQ entries, product specs), the per-chunk cost adds up with smaller retrieval benefit.
**How it works**
Standard RAG embeds chunks directly. The problem: a sentence like "Revenue grew 15% above the prior quarter" is meaningless stripped of its document and section. The query "Q3 revenue growth" may not retrieve it.
Contextual Retrieval adds an LLM step at indexing time: for each chunk, ask Claude to write one sentence placing it in context, then prepend that sentence before embedding it and before adding it to the BM25 index.
The situating prompt, from [Anthropic's cookbook](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-contextual-embeddings-guide):
```python SITUATE_CONTEXT_PROMPT = """<document> {doc} </document>
Here is the chunk we want to situate: <chunk> {chunk} </chunk>
Give a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document for search retrieval. Answer only with the context and nothing else.""" ```
The enriched chunk becomes:
``` Context: This chunk is from Acme Corp's Q3 2026 earnings call and describes net revenue growth relative to Q2. Revenue grew 15% above the prior quarter. ```
Both the dense embedding and the BM25 index are built from the enriched chunk. At query time nothing changes — only indexing is different.
**Keeping indexing costs down with prompt caching**
Without caching, you re-send the full document with every chunk — cost multiplies by chunk count. With prompt caching, the `<document>` prefix is cached after the first chunk from that document; subsequent chunks from the same document hit the cache and cost roughly 10% of uncached input tokens. Per Anthropic's estimate, one-time indexing runs approximately $1.02 per million document tokens at typical chunk sizes (800 tokens/chunk, 8K documents) — their figure, not independently verified.
The practical constraint: group all chunks from the same document into one API call batch so the cache prefix matches. Cross-document batching breaks the cache.
**Limits:** - Indexing latency increases — each chunk requires an API call; aggressive parallelization can hit rate limits. - For self-contained chunks (FAQ entries, product specs), the per-chunk LLM cost adds up with smaller retrieval benefit. - Requires reindexing when chunk boundaries or document content change.
**Sources:** [Anthropic: Contextual Retrieval](https://anthropic.com/research/contextual-retrieval), [Anthropic cookbook: Contextual Embeddings Guide](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/capabilities-contextual-embeddings-guide), [DataCamp: Contextual Retrieval Anthropic tutorial](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/contextual-retrieval-anthropic), [Together AI open-source implementation](https://docs.together.ai/docs/how-to-implement-contextual-rag-from-anthropic.md)

item.title: Hugging Face Switched Language-Model Routing to OpenRouter — You Get Automatic Failover but Custom Provider Keys No Longer Work for LM Calls
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: As of Nov 16, HuggingFace Inference Providers routes LM calls through OpenRouter, adding automatic failover — but custom per-provider keys stop working for language models.
item.content:encoded:
**As of November 16, language-model calls via Hugging Face Inference Providers now route through OpenRouter — you get automatic provider failover, but custom provider keys stop working for LM calls.**
Hugging Face handed language-model routing in its Inference Providers to OpenRouter. Where previously HF picked one provider per request and returned its error on failure, OpenRouter now selects the best available provider based on live price, speed, and reliability — and retries on another provider if one fails.
The breaking change is narrower than it sounds. It affects only language models. Image, video, and audio generation still route directly through Inference Providers and are unaffected.
If you had wired in a custom provider key — your own Together AI, Fireworks, or other provider token — that path breaks silently for LM calls. The InferenceClient still accepts a `provider=` argument, but the custom key is no longer forwarded.
```python # This call now goes through OpenRouter, not your Together key from huggingface_hub import InferenceClient client = InferenceClient(provider="together", api_key="YOUR_HF_TOKEN") ```
If you rely on routing to a specific provider for cost control or compliance, check whether your existing code is now silently falling back to a different provider.
**Why it matters:** Most developers gain free failover with no code change. If you depended on provider selection for a reason — cost ceiling, data-residency, latency budget — the routing is no longer in your hands for LM calls.
**Limit:** Connecting an OpenRouter account to your HF account is listed as a next step in HF's announcement, but specific pricing and billing details are still being finalized. Verify costs against the HF docs before relying on specific per-token numbers.

item.title: Your First FAISS Index Is `IndexFlatL2` Because Every Tutorial Uses It — Flat Is Exact and Right up to ~100K Vectors, but IVF and HNSW Scale Much Further
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: IndexFlatL2 is exact and correct up to ~100K vectors; IndexIVFFlat trades a little recall for 10–100x speed at millions; IndexHNSWFlat is fastest with no training but uses more RAM.
item.content:encoded:
**`IndexFlatL2` is exact nearest-neighbor search — right for prototypes and small collections; above ~100K vectors use `IndexIVFFlat` (cluster-and-search, needs training) or `IndexHNSWFlat` (graph, no training, fastest recall, more RAM).**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** choose a FAISS index for your dataset size, build each type in Python, and understand the trade-off that makes approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search 10–100× faster than brute force.
**Three takeaways:** - `IndexFlatL2` scans every vector per query — 100% recall, no training, but O(n) time; fine under ~100K vectors - `IndexIVFFlat` groups vectors into clusters, searches a subset (`nprobe` clusters) — tune for speed vs. recall; requires `train()` - `IndexHNSWFlat` uses a graph structure — no training, fastest lookup, but can't delete individual vectors and uses more memory
**Walk-through:**
```bash pip install faiss-cpu sentence-transformers numpy ```
```python import faiss, numpy as np from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2") texts = ["first document", "second document"] # your corpus vecs = model.encode(texts).astype("float32") # shape (N, 384) d = vecs.shape[1] # embedding dimension: 384
# --- Flat (exact, up to ~100K) --- idx_flat = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) idx_flat.add(vecs)
# --- IVF (trained, 100K–10M) --- nlist = max(4, int(len(vecs) ** 0.5)) # rule of thumb: sqrt(N) quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) idx_ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, nlist) idx_ivf.train(vecs) # requires >= 39 * nlist vectors idx_ivf.add(vecs) idx_ivf.nprobe = 10 # search 10 of nlist clusters; raise for recall
# --- HNSW (graph, no training) --- idx_hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32) # 32 = graph connectivity (M) idx_hnsw.add(vecs) # no train() call needed
# Query any index identically D, I = idx_flat.search(vecs[:1], k=5) # D = distances, I = indices ```
**Persist to disk** — in-memory only by default:
```python faiss.write_index(idx_hnsw, "my.index") idx_loaded = faiss.read_index("my.index") ```
**Limits:** - HNSW cannot remove individual vectors (`remove_ids()` raises `NotImplementedError`) — rebuild the index to delete. - IVF requires at least `39 * nlist` training vectors; with `nlist=100` you need 3,900+ docs before `train()` succeeds. - HNSW stores the full graph in RAM alongside the vectors — expect roughly 1.5–2× the memory of Flat for the same dataset. - None of these is a persistent server; for concurrent reads, incremental adds, or metadata filtering, use a persistent store (ChromaDB, pgvector) on top.
**Sources:** [Pinecone FAISS tutorial — step-by-step IndexFlatL2, IVF, search](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/series/faiss/faiss-tutorial/) · [FAISS wiki — index classes and factory strings](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes) · [PyImageSearch: Vector Search with FAISS: ANN Explained (Feb 2026)](https://pyimagesearch.com/2026/02/16/vector-search-with-faiss-approximate-nearest-neighbor-ann-explained/)

item.title: Your CI Pipeline Waits on Claude Code's Interactive Prompt Because You Launched It Without -p — That Flag Makes Every Run Non-Interactive and Exits With a Code Your Script Can Branch On
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run Claude Code non-interactively with -p, pre-approve tools with --allowedTools, cap spend with --max-budget-usd, and branch on exit codes — no hanging prompts, CI-safe.
item.content:encoded:
**`claude -p "task" --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Bash"` runs Claude Code non-interactively; pipe input from a file, pipe output through `jq`, and branch on exit code — no session, no hanging prompts, CI-safe.**
Claude Code's default mode is interactive — it pauses on permission prompts and waits for keystrokes. In a CI job or a Makefile target, that hangs indefinitely. The `-p` flag (long form: `--print`) changes all three behaviors: one turn, no prompts, clean exit.
```bash # Single-turn, exits when done claude -p "Find the failing test in test/auth.test.ts and explain the root cause" --allowedTools "Read,Grep" --output-format json | jq -r '.result'
# Pipe build errors in cat build-errors.log | claude -p "Concisely explain the root cause of these errors"
# Branch on exit code if ! claude -p "Run the type-checker and confirm zero errors" --allowedTools "Bash" --max-budget-usd 0.05; then echo "Claude returned non-zero — check the output above" exit 1 fi ```
**Key flags:**
- `--allowedTools "Read,Grep,Edit,Bash"` — pre-approve a whitelist; unapproved tool calls are denied outright (not prompted). Combine with `denyInsteadOfPrompting: true` in settings for a double fence on unattended runs. - `--output-format json` — structured response with `.result` (text), `.cost_usd` (float), `.is_error` (bool). Parse with `jq`. - `--max-budget-usd 0.10` — hard spend cap; exceeding it exits with a non-zero code. Protects CI budgets on agentic tasks that can spiral. - `--model claude-haiku-5-5` — route lightweight scripting tasks to a faster, cheaper model. - **Exit code 0** = success; **non-zero** = model error, budget exceeded, or unapproved tool. Script branches work as expected.
**Limits:** No session persistence between `-p` calls; each invocation starts fresh with no prior context. Code Mode (the experimental JS tool chaining from v2.1.323) is skipped in `-p` mode even when the env var is set. The `--json-schema` flag for schema-validated structured output has changed between versions — verify the current signature with `claude --help` before relying on it in CI.
**Sources:** [Claude Code headless mode — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless) · [CI and automation guide — muhammadusmangm.github.io](https://muhammadusmangm.github.io/claude-code-best-practices/guides/ci-and-automation/) · [DEV: claude -p is all that stands between you and a hanging CI job](https://dev.to/creeta/claude-p-is-all-that-stands-between-you-and-a-hanging-ci-job-2peh)

item.title: Your Fine-Tuned Model Needs a GPU to Serve But You Can't Justify a Reserved Instance — Modal Deploys a vLLM Endpoint as a Serverless Function and Charges Only While a Request Is Running
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Modal runs a vLLM server on a serverless A10G with a Python class and one CLI command — no Kubernetes, no idle-instance cost. Cold start is 15–60 seconds; pricing is per GPU-second.
item.content:encoded:
**Use Modal's Python class decorator to run a vLLM server on a serverless A10G — pay per GPU-second while a request is in flight, nothing while idle, and get an OpenAI-compatible endpoint in under 40 lines.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** serve any Hugging Face model (including a fine-tuned checkpoint) on serverless GPU compute, get a URL you can point any existing OpenAI SDK client at, and scale to zero when no requests are running.
**The pattern:**
```python import modal
image = ( modal.Image.debian_slim() .pip_install("vllm==0.6.6.post1", "huggingface_hub") ) app = modal.App("vllm-server", image=image)
# Volume persists model weights across cold starts vol = modal.Volume.from_name("model-weights", create_if_missing=True)
@app.cls(gpu="a10g", volumes={"/models": vol}, timeout=300) class VLLMServer: @modal.enter() def load(self): from vllm import LLM self.llm = LLM( model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", download_dir="/models", )
@modal.web_endpoint(method="POST") def generate(self, body: dict): from vllm import SamplingParams out = self.llm.generate(body["prompt"], SamplingParams(max_tokens=512)) return {"text": out[0].outputs[0].text} ```
```bash modal deploy inference.py # builds image, returns a live HTTPS URL ```
The deployed endpoint accepts POST requests and is OpenAI SDK-compatible when you add the right route — the Modal vLLM guide shows the full streaming chat-completions wrapper. For gated models (Llama, Mistral), store your HF token as a Modal secret: `modal secret create hf-secret HF_TOKEN=hf_...` and add `secrets=[modal.Secret.from_name("hf-secret")]` to the `@app.cls` decorator.
**Three takeaways:** - `@modal.enter()` runs once per container startup — put model loading there, not inside the endpoint handler, or every request pays the full load time. - Weights in a `modal.Volume` survive container teardowns. Without a volume, every cold start re-downloads the full model from Hugging Face. - `modal serve inference.py` runs the server locally with live reload; `modal deploy` pushes it to production. Same code, two commands.
**Limits:** Cold starts take 15–60 seconds to load a 7B model from the Volume (and 10–15 minutes without it, downloading from Hugging Face fresh). Modal lists its A10G pricing at $0.000463/GPU-second, billed per wall-second of inference, not per token — a 10-second generation on a 7B model costs roughly $0.005. The `web_endpoint` decorator serves one request at a time per container; for concurrent workloads, set `allow_concurrent_inputs` on the class. vLLM's PagedAttention manages multiple concurrent sequences efficiently within one container, but you need to wire in the concurrent_inputs setting and test your concurrency ceiling.
**Sources:** [Modal vLLM deployment guide — modal.com](https://modal.com/blog/how-to-deploy-vllm) · [Modal Gemma/vLLM example — modal.com/docs/examples](https://modal.com/docs/examples/llm_inference) · [vLLM + Modal — docs.vllm.ai](https://docs.vllm.ai/deployment/frameworks/modal.html) · [Modal serverless GPU for vLLM, no YAML — DEV Community](https://dev.to/jangwook_kim_e31e7291ad98/modal-labs-serverless-gpu-for-vllm-with-no-yaml-le5)

item.title: Your Claude Code Agent Runs Unattended But Checking In Means Reopening a Terminal — /remote-control Connects Any Live Session to Phone or Browser
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: /remote-control streams a running Claude Code session to the Claude app on your phone or browser. As of Nov 17, replies stream in real time. For sessions that need to outlive your machine, start in the cloud and use --teleport to pull them local.
item.content:encoded:
**`/remote-control` streams any live Claude Code session to your phone or browser; for sessions that must outlive your machine, start in the cloud and pull them down with `--teleport` when you're back at your desk.**
Long agentic tasks often run while you're away from the terminal. Two distinct scenarios:
**Scenario A — monitor/steer a local session from elsewhere**
``` # inside a running session: /remote-control # or /rc
# or start with remote access on: claude --remote-control # or --rc ```
Your session appears in the Claude mobile app under the **Code** tab. As of the [Nov 17 changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog), replies stream to your phone as they are written, so you're watching real output rather than polling. You can send messages, approve tool calls, or give new instructions from your phone exactly as you would from the terminal.
**Name your sessions so you can find them:** ``` claude --name "refactor-auth" --remote-control # or inside an existing session: /rename refactor-auth ```
Multiple sessions can run under remote control simultaneously — each shows up as a separate entry in the Code tab.
**Scenario B — pick up a cloud session in your terminal**
Cloud sessions keep running when your laptop is closed. When you return:
``` claude --teleport # interactive session picker claude --teleport <session-id> # resume a specific session # or inside a session: /teleport # or /tp ```
Teleport imports the conversation history into your terminal so you can keep editing locally. It creates a local copy; new work doesn't sync back to the cloud session.
**Limits:** - Remote Control requires your machine to stay on and the `claude` process running. If the machine sleeps or the process exits, the connection drops. - Commands that only work in the terminal interface (`/plugin`, `/resume`) don't work from the mobile or web client. Bypass permissions mode is also unavailable from the app. - `--teleport` requires the same `claude.ai` account as the cloud session; API-key auth won't work. You must `claude auth login` first. - Don't confuse `--teleport` with `--resume` — `--resume` reopens a conversation from your machine's local history only; it doesn't list cloud sessions.
**Sources:** [Remote Control docs — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control) · [Claude Code mobile — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mobile) · [Remote control guide — explainx.ai](https://www.explainx.ai/blog/claude-code-mobile-remote-control-phone-guide-2026) · [Claude Code from your phone — inventivehq.com](https://inventivehq.com/blog/claude-code-from-your-phone-remote)

item.title: GitHub Copilot Adds Regression Tests for Agent Customizations and Browser Automation at Ignite
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitHub Copilot Evals (public preview, Nov 17) writes repeatable tests for custom skills, agents, and MCP tools — checking the reasoning path, not just the final answer. Browser use gives Copilot agents control of a Chrome tab.
item.content:encoded:
**Two Copilot features entered public preview at Ignite on November 17: Evals writes regression tests for your custom agent setups; browser use lets your agent open Chrome tabs, read pages, click, and fill forms.**
**Copilot Evals**
The gap this closes: when you modify a custom skill, agent, or MCP tool, there's been no repeatable way to verify the change didn't break existing behavior. Evals fills that.
Create one via `/eval` or a prompt, then run it after any change to your Copilot setup. It checks both the final answer *and* how the agent got there — whether it called the right tools in the right order — not just whether the output looks plausible.
You approve each run before it starts. The UI shows why a check failed and lets you compare runs before and after a customization edit. Engine is Vally, an extensible local eval runner.
Available in VS Code (Marketplace extension), Copilot CLI (plugin), and the Copilot app.
**Browser use**
The Copilot agent can now open pages, read their content, click links, interact with buttons, and fill forms — with the GitHub Copilot Chrome extension installed and browser use enabled in settings. Works in Copilot CLI, app, VS Code, and JetBrains. Runs in an isolated Chromium tab group.
**Why they matter:** Evals directly addresses the problem that one successful run doesn't tell you whether a customization is reliable. Browser use means Copilot can close a loop that previously required a human to open the app and verify it rendered — but it's not a headless testing framework; the browser must be open.
**Limits:** Both are in public preview and subject to change. Evals requires approval before each run, so it doesn't work in a fully unattended pipeline yet. Browser use is Chromium-only. Neither is in the GitHub Enterprise Server extension as of launch.
**Why it matters:** If your team maintains Copilot custom agents or MCP server configurations, Evals is the first tool that lets you gate on agent behavior rather than just on code style.
**Sources:** [Copilot Evals public preview — github.blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-17-github-copilot-evals-is-now-in-public-preview/) · [Browser use — github.blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-17-let-github-copilot-interact-with-your-browser/) · [Copilot Ignite releases — github.blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-17-github-copilot-app-microsoft-ignite-releases/)

item.title: Your Multi-Provider App Maintains Two Separate SDK Setups Because OpenAI and Anthropic Have Different Base URLs — Perplexity Orchestrator Accepts Both Message Formats Through One Endpoint
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Perplexity Orchestrator (launched Nov 17) accepts both OpenAI Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages requests at a single base URL and adds same-model provider failover. Currently in private preview.
item.content:encoded:
**One base URL accepts both OpenAI Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages API calls; same-model provider failover retries on a different infrastructure deployment automatically — your existing SDK code changes in three places.**
If your app calls both Anthropic and OpenAI you have two SDK setups: different base URLs, different client initialization, different response handling. Perplexity Orchestrator ([launched November 17](https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/orchestrator-one-api-for-reliable-inference)) routes both message formats through `https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1`.
**Switching an Anthropic client:**
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic( base_url="https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1", api_key="pplx-...", # Perplexity key replaces Anthropic key )
# Model names, message structure, and response shape are unchanged response = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}], ) ```
The same migration works for the OpenAI SDK: change `base_url` and `api_key`, leave the model name and message dict as-is.
**What "failover" actually means:** Orchestrator routes across multiple infrastructure providers hosting the same model. If one returns a 5xx, it retries on another deployment of the same model. This is **same-model failover** — the model you specified is what you get. Cross-model fallback (switch to a cheaper model when the primary is overloaded) is not available.
**Automatic routing:** A `perplexity/auto` model ID lets a decision model pick a route per request. Per the docs, adaptive speed-based routing is still in development — not ready for cost optimization workflows.
**Limits:** - Currently in private preview; email api@perplexity.ai to request access - Context window overflows return HTTP 400, no retry - Published per-token rates apply regardless of which provider handles the request; no cost arbitrage
**When to use it vs. OpenRouter:** Use Orchestrator when reliability matters and you're calling a specific model — it gives you provider failover without changing model. Use OpenRouter when model variety matters — routing between GPT-6.1 and Opus 5.5 based on task type, or cost/capability routing across 200+ options.
**Sources:** [Orchestrator launch — perplexity.ai](https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/orchestrator-one-api-for-reliable-inference) · [Routing & reliability docs — docs.perplexity.ai](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/router/routing-and-reliability) · [Launch coverage — unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/?p=522793)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Commits to Implementation Before You've Decided What You're Building — Generate Three Distinct Layout Directions in Claude Design First
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Before handing a feature to Claude Code, use Claude Design to generate three visually distinct layout directions, choose one, then hand off only that direction — so Claude Code starts from a decision, not a guess.
item.content:encoded:
**Before writing any implementation code, generate three distinct layout directions in Claude Design and choose one — so Claude Code starts from a decision, not from "I'll figure it out as I build."**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Generate and compare multiple layout directions in Claude Design before any implementation code is written — so your Claude Code sessions start from a chosen direction, not from "figure it out as you go."
**Key takeaways:** - Claude Design generates faster than Claude Code commits to structure — use that asymmetry: iterate in the design surface until a direction is chosen, then switch to the editor - Explicitly prompting for three *distinct* directions ("make each feel like a different designer made different tradeoffs") gets you divergent options rather than three colorways of the same layout - The handoff is a one-time cost: Export → Claude Code brings only the chosen direction; all three are preserved as branches if you need to revisit
**Walk-through:**
``` # In Claude Design — start with your design system linked if you have one # (run /design-sync in Claude Code first to upload your tokens/components)
# 1. Prompt for distinct directions — describe the constraint, not the aesthetic "I need a checkout summary panel. Give me three distinct approaches: one that minimizes scroll by collapsing line items, one that groups items by product category with subtotals, one that surfaces the total savings prominently above the item list. Make each feel like a different designer made different tradeoffs — not three colorways of the same layout."
# 2. For each direction: annotate what works (Claude Design annotation tools) # Use the branch feature to preserve all three before choosing
# 3. Pick one direction; export it # In the browser: Export → Handoff to Claude Code # Or from Claude Code: /design import <project-id> ```
Claude Code reads the chosen bundle's HTML structure and rebuilds it as React/Next.js components using your Tailwind config and component vocabulary. Explorations start from your design system, not generic defaults, when `/design-sync` has run.
**What doesn't survive the handoff:** behavior, event handlers, API calls. Each direction is a visual structure — wire state and logic in Claude Code after the import. Treat the import as a visual diff, not a finished component.
**Limit:** Claude Design checks generated output against your component map but may not match your component API exactly — a `Button` with `variant="primary"` instead of your `intent="primary"`. Budget time to reconcile prop names after import. Per an [April 2026 hands-on review](https://ice-ice-bear.github.io/posts/2026-04-22-claude-design/), Claude Design reads your component files as design artifacts rather than a live component graph, so the round-trip is "visual diff to apply", not lossless sync.

item.title: Your Opus 5.5 Session Spawns Subagents That Default to Fable 5.2 — CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL Routes Them Anywhere, _FORCE Overrides Even Frontmatter
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Set CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL to route spawned subagents to a specific model; add CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 to override custom agents with their own frontmatter.
item.content:encoded:
**Since v2.1.251, any Agent tool call in Claude Code defaults the spawned subagent to Fable 5.2, regardless of the model running in your session. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL lets you route every subagent to a specific model; CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 overrides even custom agents with their own frontmatter `model:` field.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Control exactly which model handles each subagent in a Claude Code session so you can match capability to cost — Opus for reasoning-heavy agents, Haiku for fast file searches — without changing your agent definitions.
- **Default is Fable 5.2 as of v2.1.251.** If you are running an Opus 5.5 session and launch a subagent without setting the env var, it silently uses Fable 5.2. Many teams discovered this via unexpected costs in the other direction: expensive Opus subagents where they expected Haiku. - **CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL takes any model ID.** Set it to `claude-haiku-5-5` and every spawned subagent — Agent tool calls, `/fork`, parallel agents — uses that model. The session model is unaffected. - **CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 (v2.1.257) ignores frontmatter.** Custom agents in `.claude/agents/*.md` can declare `model: claude-opus-5-5` in their frontmatter. Without FORCE, that declaration wins. With FORCE, your env var wins. Useful when you want a fleet-wide cost ceiling with no per-file edits.
**Two common patterns:**
```bash # Match subagents to the session model (Opus session → Opus subagents) export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5
# Cost-split: fast scouts on Haiku, main session on Sonnet export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5 export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 claude # start Claude Code; subagents use Haiku regardless of agent frontmatter ```
**When to use FORCE:** | Situation | Use FORCE? | |---|---| | All custom agents should use a cheaper model | Yes | | Some agents need Opus by design | No — let their frontmatter win | | You don't use custom agents | Doesn't matter |
**Limits:** FORCE only controls the model; it does not change tool access or context. A Haiku subagent still has access to the same tools as an Opus one. Per-call `model` overrides passed to the Agent tool are also overridden by FORCE (this is the bug reported in issue #57718).
*Sources: [Claude Code subagents docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/subagents) · [GitHub issue #80902](https://claudeissues.com/issue/80902-subagents-default-to-claude-fable-5-while-session-model-is-opus-silent-more-expe) · [Vincent Schmalbach](https://www.vincentschmalbach.com/how-to-set-which-model-claude-code-subagents-use/)*

item.title: Your Fine-Tuning Run Fails Because the Dataset Is Noisy, Not the Model — Build Alpaca-Format Instruction Data in Three Steps
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Build Alpaca or ShareGPT-format instruction datasets for fine-tuning: format selection, quality filtering, three-step JSONL workflow, and when to use each with Unsloth or TRL's SFTTrainer.
item.content:encoded:
**Most fine-tuning failures happen in the dataset, not the training run. The model learns whatever distribution you give it — if your instruction examples are inconsistent, the model learns inconsistency. Building a clean Alpaca-format JSONL file before you ever touch the training loop saves hours of debugging loss curves.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Write a three-step Python pipeline that turns raw examples into a valid Alpaca or ShareGPT JSONL file, ready to load directly into Unsloth or TRL's SFTTrainer.
- **Alpaca format is for single-turn tasks.** Each record has `instruction`, optional `input`, and `output`. Use it for classification, extraction, summarization, QA, and anything where the interaction is one shot. It's the default format for most tutorials and the simplest to debug. - **ShareGPT format is for multi-turn conversation.** Each record has a `conversations` array of `{from, value}` pairs (`human`/`gpt` roles). Use it when your target behavior involves follow-up questions, clarifications, or tool calls. TRL's SFTTrainer accepts both via `dataset_text_field` or a formatting function. - **Quality filtering matters more than quantity.** A 500-example dataset where every example is unambiguous outperforms a 5,000-example dataset with 30% label noise. The W&B tutorial demonstrates this directly with accuracy vs. dataset-size plots.
**Three-step Alpaca pipeline:**
```python import json
# Step 1: collect raw examples (here from a list; in practice, from logs, annotations, etc.) raw = [ {"prompt": "Classify: 'The service was broken for 3 hours'", "label": "outage"}, {"prompt": "Classify: 'Added dark mode'", "label": "feature"}, # ... your examples ]
# Step 2: quality filter — remove examples where the output is ambiguous or empty def is_clean(ex): return ex["label"].strip() and len(ex["prompt"]) > 10
filtered = [ex for ex in raw if is_clean(ex)]
# Step 3: write Alpaca JSONL with open("dataset.jsonl", "w") as f: for ex in filtered: record = { "instruction": "Classify this customer support ticket as outage, feature, or billing.", "input": ex["prompt"], "output": ex["label"] } f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")
print(f"Wrote {len(filtered)} examples") ```
**Loading into TRL SFTTrainer:**
```python from datasets import load_dataset from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig
dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files="dataset.jsonl", split="train")
trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, train_dataset=dataset, args=SFTConfig( dataset_text_field="output", # for Alpaca, TRL needs a formatting_func instead max_seq_length=512, output_dir="./output", ), ) ```
**Limits:** Alpaca format does not naturally handle system prompts — add a `system` key and use a formatting function. ShareGPT is better when you need a persistent system persona across turns. Neither format encodes tool call schemas; for that, see the TRL function-calling docs.
*Sources: [YouTube — Instruction Tuning](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8iwxM6XRpVQ) · [Unsloth Datasets 101](https://docs.unsloth.ai/basics/datasets-101) · [W&B: Preparing a Dataset for Instruction Tuning](https://wandb.ai/capecape/alpaca_ft/reports/How-to-Fine-Tune-an-LLM-Part-1-Preparing-a-Dataset-for-Instruction-Tuning--Vmlldzo1NTcxNzE2)*

item.title: Your Hand-Written Prompts Don't Get Better When Your Task Changes — DSPy Compiles LLM Pipelines Into Optimized Instructions Automatically
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: DSPy replaces hand-tuned prompts with typed Signatures; a Bayesian optimizer finds better instructions and few-shot examples from 20–50 labeled examples — no prompt engineering required.
item.content:encoded:
**DSPy replaces hand-tuned prompt strings with typed Signatures; run BootstrapFewShot or MIPROv2 against 20–50 labeled examples and the optimizer finds better instructions automatically — no prompt engineering session required.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Write LLM pipelines where the instructions are discovered from your data rather than written by hand, so when your task distribution shifts you re-optimize rather than re-word.
- **Signatures are typed I/O contracts.** `dspy.Signature("ticket -> severity")` declares what flows in and out; the actual instructions are found by the Optimizer, not written by you. - **BootstrapFewShot works from 10–20 examples.** It samples the highest-scoring few-shot demos from your training set and injects them automatically. MIPROv2 also tunes the instruction text and benefits from 50+ examples. - **Compile once, save to JSON, load on deployment.** `program.save("optimized.json")` captures the found prompt so you skip optimization costs in production.
**Walk-through — optimize a ticket-severity classifier:**
```bash pip install dspy ```
```python import dspy
# 1. Set the language model dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM("anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"))
# 2. Declare what your module does — no prompt text, just types class Classify(dspy.Signature): """Classify customer-support ticket severity.""" ticket: str = dspy.InputField() severity: str = dspy.OutputField(desc="low, medium, or high")
# 3. Wrap it in a module (ChainOfThought adds step-by-step reasoning) classifier = dspy.Predict(Classify)
# 4. Write a metric function def accuracy(example, pred, trace=None): return example.severity == pred.severity
# 5. Optimize against ~50 labeled examples trainset = [ dspy.Example(ticket="Can't log in", severity="high").with_inputs("ticket"), # ... more examples ... ] optimizer = dspy.BootstrapFewShot(metric=accuracy, max_bootstrapped_demos=4) compiled = optimizer.compile(classifier, trainset=trainset)
# 6. Save compiled program; load later without re-optimizing compiled.save("severity_classifier.json") ```
For 50+ examples, swap in `dspy.MIPROv2(metric=accuracy, auto="light")` — it uses Bayesian optimization to tune both the instruction text and the few-shot demos.
**Limits:** Every optimization run makes tens to hundreds of LLM calls — plan for $1–$10 for a light run, more for `auto="heavy"`. Compiled prompts can overfit: if your training examples aren't representative of production input, accuracy will drop on out-of-distribution cases. Version your training sets the same way you version code.
**Sources:** [DSPy official tutorials](https://dspy.ai/tutorials/) · [DSPy optimizer guide](https://dspy.ai/learn/optimization/optimizers) · [Stop hand-tuning prompts: auto-optimize an LLM classifier with DSPy — Codecut newsletter](https://newsletter.codecut.ai/p/stop-hand-tuning-prompts-auto-optimize) · [DEV Community: DSPy 3.x compile and optimize LLM pipelines](https://dev.to/jangwook_kim_e31e7291ad98/dspy-3x-compile-and-optimize-llm-pipelines-automatically-1n5h)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Ends When Claude Runs Out of Steps, Not When Work Is Done — Exit Code 2 From a Stop Hook Blocks Completion Until Your Tests Pass
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A Stop hook that exits with code 2 sends your test failures back to Claude and prevents session end. Without it, "done" means the agent stopped — not that the work is correct.
item.content:encoded:
**A Stop hook that exits `2` sends your test output back to Claude and prevents the session from ending — making "done" mean "tests passed", not "agent stopped".**
Claude Code fires a Stop hook right before the session ends. The exit code you return controls what happens next:
- **Exit `0`** → allow the stop. - **Exit `2`** → block the stop; hook's stdout goes to Claude as a new turn. - **Exit `1`** → hook error; let the stop through anyway.
Here's the minimum working pattern (Python, since the hook input arrives as JSON on stdin):
```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # .claude/hooks/check-done.py import json, subprocess, sys
data = json.load(sys.stdin) if data.get("stop_hook_active"): sys.exit(0) # already in a hook loop — let it stop
result = subprocess.run( ["npm", "test", "--", "--reporter=compact"], capture_output=True, text=True ) if result.returncode != 0: # Trim to avoid flooding Claude's context; last N chars has the failures print(result.stdout[-4000:] + result.stderr[-1000:]) sys.exit(2) # block completion, send failures to Claude ```
Wire it in `.claude/settings.json`:
```json { "hooks": { "Stop": [ { "type": "command", "command": "python3 .claude/hooks/check-done.py" } ] } } ```
**The `stop_hook_active` guard is not optional.** The hook receives JSON on stdin; `stop_hook_active` is `true` when Claude is already continuing because of a previous Stop block. Without that check, every test failure re-triggers the hook indefinitely. Claude Code also has a built-in cap — 8 consecutive blocks by default, configurable via `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP` — before it ends the session regardless.
**What this gate catches — and what it doesn't.** The hook sees exit codes, not correctness. Claude can pass a Stop gate by deleting a failing test, skipping it, or hardcoding the expected value — and it has done exactly this under time pressure. This is a *completion gate*, not a *quality gate*. Pair it with a CI pipeline that owns the authoritative test run; the Stop hook is fast feedback, not a substitute.
For slow test suites, run only a smoke-test subset in the hook. A 90-second Stop hook adds friction to every session end.
**Sources:** [Claude Code hooks reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code/hooks) · [Stop hook pattern — codeongrass.com](https://codeongrass.com/blog/claude-code-hooks-done-means-tests-passed/) · [stop_hook_active guard — amitkoth.com](https://amitkoth.com/claude-code-stop-hooks) · [DEV Community: 50-line bash example](https://dev.to/ianymu/stop-claude-code-from-lying-about-completion-a-50-line-bash-hook-1g2b)

item.title: Your Inference Code Still Routes to a Managed Cloud API Even in Dev — `vllm serve` Puts Any HuggingFace Model Behind an OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint in Four Commands
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: pip install vllm → vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct → localhost:8000/v1. Your existing openai.ChatCompletion code works unchanged — change base_url and nothing else.
item.content:encoded:
**`vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` launches an OpenAI-compatible API at `localhost:8000` — point your existing `openai` client at it by changing `base_url`, and nothing else in your code needs to change.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Serve any public HuggingFace model (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Phi) as a local REST API. - Call it with the OpenAI Python client by changing one URL. - Understand the two flags that prevent OOM errors on consumer-grade GPUs.
---
**Step 1: Install**
```bash pip install vllm # ~8 GB install; needs CUDA >= 12.1 and Python 3.10–3.13 ```
CPU-only isn't supported for serving. On a Mac or without a GPU, use Ollama instead — vLLM is for GPU-backed serving.
**Step 2: Serve a model**
```bash vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ```
vLLM pulls the weights from HuggingFace on first run, then starts the server at `http://localhost:8000`. For gated models (Meta Llama), set `HF_TOKEN=<your_token>` first.
Two flags you almost always need:
```bash vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-model-len 8192 ```
`--gpu-memory-utilization` controls how much of your VRAM vLLM reserves (lower it if OOM). `--max-model-len` caps the context window, which directly shrinks the KV cache footprint.
**Step 3: Call it with the OpenAI client**
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( api_key="not-needed", # any non-empty string; required by the client base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", # must match the model vllm serve used messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain KV cache in one sentence."}], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
The model name in the request must exactly match the HuggingFace model ID passed to `vllm serve`. A mismatch returns a 404.
**Step 4: Lock it down (optional)**
```bash vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct --api-key my-secret ```
Then set `api_key="my-secret"` in the OpenAI client. Without this flag, any process on the machine can call the server.
---
**How this differs from the existing multi-LoRA post.** An [earlier post](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-11-08-04-vllm-multi-lora-adapters-serving-lora-modules-max-loras) covered serving dozens of fine-tuned LoRA adapters on one base with `--enable-lora --lora-modules`. That assumes vLLM is already running. This covers the prerequisite: getting any HuggingFace model running as a local API server from scratch.
**What vLLM adds over Ollama.** Ollama is simpler for local dev; vLLM is built for throughput. vLLM's PagedAttention manages KV cache across concurrent requests — 10 simultaneous callers on one GPU is realistic; Ollama queues them. For single-user experimentation the difference doesn't matter; for a local team API or a production self-host, it does.
**Limitations.** vLLM requires Linux + CUDA. The quantized GGUF weights Ollama uses don't work here — you need fp16/bf16 HuggingFace weights or a bitsandbytes 4-bit checkpoint. A 7B model in bf16 needs ~14 GB of VRAM. No amount of flag tuning makes a model fit on hardware that doesn't have the memory.
**Resource:** [vLLM Quickstart — official docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/quickstart/) · [Fast and Efficient LLM Inference with vLLM — DeepLearning.AI](https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/fast-and-efficient-llm-inference-with-vllm)
**Sources:** [docs.vllm.ai quickstart](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/quickstart/) · [DeepLearning.AI vLLM course](https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/fast-and-efficient-llm-inference-with-vllm) · [1littlecoder: Go Production with vLLM](https://rosetta.to/u/1littlecoder/go-production-super-fast-llm-api-serving-with-vllm)

item.title: Your Extraction Agent Returns a Conversational Reply When It Should Call a Tool — `tool_choice: {"type": "required"}` Forces at Least One Tool Call on Every Turn
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: tool_choice: required forces Claude to respond with at least one tool call, never plain text — use it for structured extraction, classification, and verification steps where a text reply breaks your pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
**`tool_choice: {"type": "required"}` forces Claude to call at least one of the available tools instead of replying in text — use it for extraction, classification, and any pipeline step where a text reply breaks the shape you need.**
By default, the Anthropic API lets Claude decide whether to call a tool or answer in text. For conversational agents that is the right behavior. For structured pipelines — extracting entities, classifying intent, running verification checks — a text reply is a failure mode. Claude often chooses text when the user message reads like a question ("What are the entities in this paragraph?") even when the system prompt says to always call the tool.
**Three modes:**
```python from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
# 1. Force at least one tool call (Claude picks which one) response = client.messages.create( model="claude-fable-5-2", max_tokens=1024, tools=[entity_extractor_tool, classifier_tool], tool_choice={"type": "required"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}], )
# 2. Force a specific tool call response = client.messages.create( model="claude-fable-5-2", max_tokens=1024, tools=[entity_extractor_tool], tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_entities"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}], )
# 3. Default behavior — Claude decides (use this for chat) response = client.messages.create( model="claude-fable-5-2", max_tokens=1024, tools=[entity_extractor_tool], tool_choice={"type": "auto"}, # this is the default; you can omit it messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}], ) ```
The response `stop_reason` will always be `tool_use` (not `end_turn`) when `type: required` or `type: tool` is set, so you can assert on it in tests:
```python assert response.stop_reason == "tool_use", f"Expected tool call, got: {response.stop_reason}" ```
**Where to use it:** - Extraction pipelines where every document produces a structured record - Classification steps inside a larger agent loop - Verification agents that must always return a verdict, never a "I think" - Batch evaluation jobs where consistent output shapes matter for downstream code
**Where not to use it:** - Conversational agents — forcing tools on every turn produces odd UX and wastes tokens on tool-call overhead for simple replies - When Claude genuinely cannot fill the tool's required parameters from the input — it will hallucinate values to satisfy the constraint
**Limit:** With an extended-thinking model, `tool_choice: required` or `tool_choice: {"type": "tool"}` runs thinking tokens before the forced tool call, which can noticeably increase costs. Test on a sample set before enabling at scale.
**Sources:** [Anthropic API docs: Tool use — controlling output](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use/overview#controlling-claudes-output) · [Anthropic API reference: messages.create](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api-reference/messages-create)

item.title: Your RAG Dev Stack Is Running a Separate Vector Database Alongside Postgres — `pgvector` Adds Vector Columns and Cosine Search to the Database You Already Have
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: pgvector turns any Postgres table into a vector store: CREATE EXTENSION, add a vector(384) column, insert with psycopg2, and query with <=>. One database handles both rows and embeddings.
item.content:encoded:
**pgvector adds a `vector(N)` column type and approximate nearest-neighbor search to any Postgres database — if you already run Postgres, there is no separate service to run.**
**What you will be able to do after this:** store sentence-transformers embeddings in a Postgres table, run cosine-similarity queries using `<=>`, and add an IVFFlat or HNSW index to serve thousands of queries per second — all from your existing psycopg2 connection.
**Three things to know first:** - `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` outputs 384 dimensions; your column must match: `vector(384)`. Use `model.get_sentence_embedding_dimension()` to confirm before you create the table. - pgvector is pre-installed on Supabase and available on RDS; for local dev, the `pgvector/pgvector:pg17` Docker image is the fastest path (`docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 5432:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg17`). - Cosine distance (`<=>`) is the right operator for sentence-transformers embeddings. `<->` is L2 distance; `<#>` is inner product. Use the wrong one and similarity rankings are wrong.
**Step-by-step setup:**
```sql -- 1. Install the extension (once per database) CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
-- 2. Create a table with a vector column CREATE TABLE documents ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, content TEXT, embedding vector(384) ); ```
```python import psycopg2 from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2") conn = psycopg2.connect("postgresql://localhost/mydb") cur = conn.cursor()
# Insert a document text = "Claude Code plan mode separates exploration from execution." embedding = model.encode(text).tolist() cur.execute( "INSERT INTO documents (content, embedding) VALUES (%s, %s)", (text, embedding) ) conn.commit()
# Query: find the 5 most similar documents query = "how do I review a plan before Claude edits files" q_emb = model.encode(query).tolist() cur.execute( "SELECT content, 1 - (embedding <=> %s::vector) AS similarity " "FROM documents ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector LIMIT 5", (q_emb, q_emb) ) print(cur.fetchall()) ```
**Add an index before scaling past a few thousand rows:**
```sql -- IVFFlat: faster to build, good for static datasets CREATE INDEX ON documents USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (lists = 100);
-- HNSW: faster queries, better recall, slower to build CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops); ```
Rule of thumb: `lists = sqrt(row_count)` for IVFFlat. For HNSW parameter tuning at scale, see the [index tuning post](/ai-news/2026-11-01-01-hnsw-m-ef-construction-pgvector-qdrant-vector-index-tuning).
**Limits:** pgvector runs on a single Postgres server — it scales to tens of millions of vectors on a well-resourced machine, but you will hit a single-node ceiling before a managed service like Pinecone or Qdrant does. The `ivfflat` index requires a full rebuild when your dataset grows by more than roughly 20%; plan for that in your maintenance window. Exact search with no index scans every row — add an index before you have more than a few thousand rows.
