**AgentMon Live is an open-source Claude Code plugin that streams every tool call, bash command, and file write to a live dashboard — one install command and zero configuration.**
Claude Code sessions are powerful but hard to watch. The session reports what it did after the turn ends, not while it's running. If a session touches the wrong file, skips a test run, or quietly fails mid-task, the first sign is usually the broken state it left behind.

Once active, it opens a dashboard panel showing: - Every tool call as it fires (read, write, bash, MCP) - Files touched in the current session - A "Done Gate" that runs at session end — if a file was changed but its tests have not re-run since, Claude Code is prompted to finish the work or explain what remains
This matters most on long-running sessions with broad file scope, agentic workflows that run unattended, or any codebase where unexpected changes are hard to spot quickly.
**Limits:** The dashboard only captures what appears in the tool log — a logic error that never triggers a tool call is invisible here. The project is recent and the interface will evolve. Codenotary also sells a separate enterprise monitoring product at a separate price; this open-source plugin is not that tier.

item.title: Every RAG Tutorial Assumes You Already Know What a Vector Store Retrieves — Here's the Minimal Working Pipeline That Makes Each Step Visible
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A minimal RAG pipeline — chunk documents, embed with sentence-transformers, store in FAISS, retrieve top chunks, pass to an LLM — fits in 50 lines of Python. Here's the full walkthrough.
item.content:encoded:
**A minimal RAG pipeline — chunk documents, embed with sentence-transformers, store in FAISS, retrieve top chunks, pass to an LLM — fits in 50 lines of Python.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Build and run a working RAG pipeline from documents to answered questions, with every step (chunk → embed → store → retrieve → prompt) explicit in your code.
Three takeaways: - The mental model of RAG's data flow and what each stage contributes - A reference implementation you can run and modify - The two specific failure modes that trip up first builds
**Walk-through**
LangChain engineer Lance Martin's freeCodeCamp tutorial covers the full pipeline from indexing through query translation. The companion Jupyter notebooks (github.com/langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch) are the working code, with each notebook isolating one stage.
```python from langchain_community.document_loaders import TextLoader from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
# 1. Load and chunk your documents loader = TextLoader("./docs.txt") docs = loader.load() splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50) chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)
# 2. Embed into FAISS embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2") vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embeddings) retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 4})
# 3. Retrieve + prompt chain prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template( "Answer based only on this context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}" ) chain = ( {"context": retriever, "question": lambda x: x} | prompt | llm | StrOutputParser() ) result = chain.invoke("What is covered in the docs?") ```
**Two failure modes for first builds:**
1. **chunk_overlap too small.** Overlap is what prevents an answer from splitting across two adjacent chunks and being missed by both. Start at 10–15% of chunk_size — `chunk_overlap=50` on a `chunk_size=500` is the floor, not the default.
2. **k too low.** Retrieving 4 chunks works for single-topic questions; a broader question needs 6–10. Set k too low and your answer exists in the index but never reaches the prompt.
The freeCodeCamp video spends its first 25 minutes on exactly these two steps — indexing and retrieval — before touching generation.
**Sources:** [Learn RAG From Scratch — freeCodeCamp / Lance Martin (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sVcwVQRHIc8) · [rag-from-scratch Jupyter notebooks — langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch](https://github.com/langchain-ai/rag-from-scratch)

item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Has 200 Lines but Claude Code Still Gets the ORM Wrong — Put the Constraints Your Linter Can't See, Leave Out the Rules It Already Enforces
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Every line in CLAUDE.md should change Claude's behavior — commands in code blocks, arch invariants, repeated corrections. Formatting rules your linter enforces belong there, not here.
item.content:encoded:
**Put the constraints Claude can't read from your code — commands in code blocks, arch invariants, repeated corrections. Leave out formatting rules your linter already enforces.**
A 200-line `CLAUDE.md` that repeats your ESLint config and Prettier settings gives Claude nothing it can't read from `.eslintrc`. The file earns its keep only on constraints that exist nowhere else in the codebase.
**What belongs:**
**Commands, in code blocks.** Write runnable commands in fenced code blocks, not prose sentences. The DataCamp CLAUDE.md guide notes that commands in prose get improvised; a command inside a code fence runs verbatim. Keep a `## Commands` section at the top with your build, test, and lint commands.
**Constraints linters can't enforce.** `All prices are stored in cents — never use floats for monetary values.` `The /api directory is a Cloudflare Worker, not Next.js — no Node APIs.` These span the whole codebase and can't be inferred from a local read.
**Corrections you've made more than once.** The Grind Engineer guide's heuristic: if you've corrected the same mistake twice in one project, the third time is a CLAUDE.md entry. After the second correction, not the first.
**Architectural facts that don't appear in any single file.** `The database uses append-only writes; never issue UPDATE or DELETE outside migrations.` Claude will infer this eventually — CLAUDE.md lets it start there.
**What doesn't belong:**
**Formatting rules your linter already enforces.** If Prettier handles indentation and ESLint catches unused imports, adding those to CLAUDE.md just crowds out the constraints the linter can't see.
**Long step-by-step procedures.** A 12-step deployment runbook compresses away under `/compact`. Link instead: `See docs/deploy.md for the deployment runbook.`
**Structure tips:** Put the most important rules first — under `/compact`, Claude summarizes from the top and rules near the bottom disappear first. Use clear section headers (`## Commands`, `## Architecture`, `## Never do this`). Root `CLAUDE.md` applies globally; subdirectory files load only when Claude works in that path — critical rules placed only there may not apply.
**Limit:** On Claude 5 models, over-specified CLAUDE.md files backfire. Instructions written for Claude 3/4 about output formatting often confuse the current generation, which handles those decisions better without guidance. Run `/claude-api prompt-audit` periodically to surface stale entries before they degrade sessions.
**Sources:** [Writing the best CLAUDE.md — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/writing-the-best-claude-md) · [CLAUDE.md: The Complete Guide — Grind Engineer](https://grindengineer.substack.com/p/claudemd-the-complete-guide-to-claude) · [What to include and skip — AI Nexus Daily](https://ainexusdaily.vercel.app/article/2026-06-21-what-to-put-in-your-claudemd-and-what-to-leave-out) · [Claude Code memory docs — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Has Already Rewritten Four Files by the Time You Notice the Approach Is Wrong — Run /plan to Lock In the Strategy Before Any Edits Start
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code's /plan command is a read-only phase where Claude proposes the full approach before touching any file — redirect it once instead of reverting after.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code's `/plan` command opens a read-only phase: Claude proposes the approach as a text artifact before it has write access to anything. Redirect once here instead of reverting after.**
The default Claude Code flow is effective for small changes, but for a multi-file refactor, a schema migration, or anything where the right sequence matters, the first edits often reveal a misunderstanding about the architecture — after several files have already been touched. Plan mode puts that discovery earlier.
### How it works
Type your task description, then type `/plan` before submitting (or press `Shift+Tab` from the input field — this cycles through available modes, one of which is plan mode). Claude reads your files, proposes a step-by-step approach, and stops. It has not written anything.
You can: - Ask questions about the plan in the same session - Tell it the approach is wrong ("Don't modify the base class — extend it instead") - Ask it to consider a constraint it missed ("The API version must stay at v2") - Request an alternative ("What if we used a migration script instead of modifying the model?")
Once you're satisfied, reply "looks good" or "proceed" and Claude executes from that plan.
### When to use it
Plan mode earns its time on: - **Multi-file refactors** where edit order matters (renaming an interface used in 12 places, restructuring a service layer) - **Schema changes** that require a migration + model update + test update in a specific sequence - **Integrations** where the wrong approach will require substantial cleanup (adding a third-party SDK, switching authentication strategy)
For a single-file fix or a one-line change, it adds friction with no benefit.
### What a plan review looks like
``` > Refactor the auth service to use JWTs instead of sessions. All existing tests must pass.
/plan ```
Claude produces something like: 1. Read `src/auth/service.ts`, `src/middleware/session.ts`, and all files importing them 2. Identify all session-dependent paths 3. Add a JWT sign/verify utility in `src/auth/jwt.ts` 4. Replace session creation in `service.ts` with JWT issuance 5. Update `session.ts` middleware to validate JWTs 6. Update affected tests
You review step 2 and notice it missed `src/websocket/handlers.ts`, which also uses sessions. You say so. Claude revises the plan to include it. Then you let it execute.
That revision costs 10 seconds. Catching it after execution would cost a failed test run, a revert, and a second run.
**Limits:** A plan can still be wrong or overconfident about what a file contains — it is a proposal based on what Claude can read, not a guarantee. Unusual project structures or implicit dependencies (env-var–driven behavior, runtime configuration) can fool it. Plan mode is a Claude Code CLI feature; it is not available in the web interface or Workbench. If you are using Claude Code as an SDK-driven headless agent, the equivalent is a plan-turn → approve-turn → execute-turn structure in your loop, not this slash command. A very long plan across many files can fill the context window before execution begins, leaving less room for the actual edits; for very large scopes, break the plan into phases.
**Sources:** [Claude Code plan mode — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/claude-code-plan-mode) · [Plan Mode task delegation — CodeSignal](https://codesignal.com/learn/courses/advanced-claude-code-features/lessons/plan-mode-task-delegation) · [Claude Code best practices — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md)

item.title: Your 7B Model Weighs 14 GB in Float16 and Requires a Cloud GPU — llama.cpp Quantizes It to Q4_K_M at 4 GB and Runs at Full Token Rate on a Laptop CPU
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: llama.cpp's two-step workflow converts any HuggingFace checkpoint to FP16 GGUF then quantizes it; Q4_K_M shrinks a 7B to ~4 GB and runs on a laptop CPU with no cloud GPU required.
item.content:encoded:
**llama.cpp converts any HuggingFace checkpoint to GGUF, then a one-line `llama-quantize` call shrinks it to Q4_K_M — roughly 4 GB for a 7B model — and runs on a laptop CPU with no cloud GPU required.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Run any publicly available model locally without cloud costs, quantize a fine-tuned checkpoint for edge or offline deployment, and choose between quant levels based on your actual accuracy vs. RAM tradeoff rather than a tutorial's default.
- Float16 GGUF is the intermediate format, not the final one — always convert from the original weights first, then quantize; re-quantizing an already-quantized file compounds error across two lossy passes - An importance matrix (`imatrix`) reduces the perplexity hit at Q4 and below by calibrating per-layer quantization against representative text from your domain; skip it at Q8_0 where the gap is small - Q4_K_M is the practical default: ~4 GB for a 7B model, well-preserved reasoning ability, and runs on most consumer hardware; Q8_0 is near-lossless at ~7.6 GB when you need higher fidelity
---
### Walk-through: Llama 3.2 3B to Q4_K_M
```bash # 1. Build llama.cpp (macOS/Linux; for Windows use CMakePresets or WSL) git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j$(nproc) pip install -r requirements/requirements-convert-hf-to-gguf.txt
# 2. Download a model (Llama 3.2 is gated — accept Meta's license on HF first) huggingface-cli login huggingface-cli download meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct --local-dir ./models/llama3-3b
# 3. Convert to FP16 GGUF (always from original weights, never from a prior quant) python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ./models/llama3-3b \ --outfile ./models/llama3-3b-f16.gguf \ --outtype f16
# 4. Build an importance matrix using calibration text # Use domain-specific text for a domain-specific model (code, legal, medical, etc.) curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt \ > calib.txt ./build/bin/llama-imatrix \ -m ./models/llama3-3b-f16.gguf \ -f calib.txt \ -o ./models/llama3-3b.imatrix
# 5. Quantize to Q4_K_M using the imatrix ./build/bin/llama-quantize \ --imatrix ./models/llama3-3b.imatrix \ ./models/llama3-3b-f16.gguf \ ./models/llama3-3b-q4_k_m.gguf \ Q4_K_M
# 6. Test ./build/bin/llama-cli \ -m ./models/llama3-3b-q4_k_m.gguf \ -p "What is GGUF quantization in one sentence?" \ -n 60 ```
| Quant type | 7B size | 3B size | When to use | |---|---|---|---| | Q8_0 | ~7.6 GB | ~3.3 GB | Near-lossless; worth it if RAM allows | | Q4_K_M | ~4.1 GB | ~2.0 GB | Daily driver; best accuracy/size tradeoff | | Q3_K_M | ~3.3 GB | ~1.6 GB | Very tight RAM; noticeable quality drop |
**Once you have the GGUF, Ollama can run it directly** — `ollama run --path ./models/llama3-3b-q4_k_m.gguf` skips the CLI and gives you a chat interface and an OpenAI-compatible local API at `localhost:11434/v1`.
**Limits:** Q4 quantization introduces a real perplexity increase — independent benchmarks show roughly 5–8% on standard evals vs. float16; Q3 and below compound this meaningfully. The imatrix helps but does not eliminate the gap. Calibration text matters: a code model calibrated on Shakespeare prose will produce a worse imatrix than one calibrated on actual code. GGUF format and `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` are updated frequently — script names and quant type names have changed between releases; always use the script from the same commit as the binary you built. llama.cpp's default build targets CPU; for Metal (macOS GPU) or CUDA, pass `-DGGML_METAL=ON` or `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` to CMake.
**Sources:** [llama.cpp quantization guide — ggml-org docs](https://mintlify.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/models/quantizing-models) · [GGUF quantization for fast and memory-efficient inference — The Kaitchup](https://kaitchup.substack.com/p/gguf-quantization-for-fast-and-memory) · [How to Convert Models to GGUF Format — Analytics Vidhya](https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/blog/2024/10/convert-models-to-gguf-format/) · [GGUF quantization concept deep-dive — Mistral AI](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/cookbooks/concept-deep-dive-quantization-methods-gguf)

item.title: Your Subagents All Inherit the Default Tools and Scope — A .claude/agents/*.md File With YAML Frontmatter Gives Each One Its Own System Prompt, Toolset, and Model
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Drop a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter into .claude/agents/ and Claude Code routes to that agent automatically — description governs selection, body is the system prompt, tools: limits its reach.
item.content:encoded:
**Drop a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter into `.claude/agents/` and Claude Code treats it as a named subagent type — the `description` field governs when Claude picks it, the body is its full system prompt, and `tools:` hard-caps what it can touch.**
The built-in general-purpose subagent can read, write, and run anything. That scope is intentional for ad-hoc sessions, but too wide when you want a code reviewer that must never commit, a schema inspector that should only read, or a documentation writer that works strictly from your existing files.
Create `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md`:
```yaml --- description: Reviews staged code changes for correctness, test coverage, and regressions. Never modifies files. tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash model: claude-haiku-5-5 --- You are a focused code reviewer. Report issues as: file:line — severity (critical|warning|suggestion) — what and why. Report only what you find. Do not suggest refactors unless asked. ```
Two locations control availability: - **`.claude/agents/<name>.md`** — project-level; present only in this repo - **`~/.claude/agents/<name>.md`** — user-level; available across all projects
The `description` field is the routing key. Claude reads it when deciding whether to use your agent versus the general-purpose fallback. Write it to describe the trigger ("reviews staged changes for correctness") rather than capabilities ("has Grep and Read") — the former matches the moment a reviewer is needed; the latter describes an implementation detail Claude doesn't need to reason about.
The `tools:` list is a hard cap. Omit `Write` and the subagent cannot write files regardless of what the body says — which matters in unattended sessions where a reviewer accidentally patching what it found is a real failure mode.
The `model:` key overrides the session default for this agent only. A quick file scanner that doesn't need heavy reasoning is a good fit for Haiku 5.5; spending Sonnet tokens on it in every loop is avoidable once the agent has its own model setting.
**One real constraint:** a custom agent is addressable by its filename as a `subagent_type` value. If the orchestrating session doesn't explicitly pass the type name, it falls back to the general-purpose agent. Document your custom types in `CLAUDE.md` so the LLM knows to reach for them.

item.title: Your Dense Retriever Returns 100 Candidates But Only 3 Are Actually Relevant — Add a Cross-Encoder Reranker After First-Stage Retrieval to Score Query-Document Pairs Jointly
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Bi-encoders rank by vector similarity alone; a cross-encoder sees query and document jointly for real relevance scoring. Add it after first-stage retrieval and your RAG precision improves measurably.
item.content:encoded:
**Bi-encoders are fast but rank by embedding distance alone — a cross-encoder processes query and document together and scores actual relevance. Run it on your top-100 candidates and pass only the best 5 to the LLM.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Build a two-stage RAG retrieval pipeline where a fast bi-encoder fetches the top-100 candidates and a cross-encoder reranks them to the top-5 most relevant, without changing your existing embedding setup.
**Three things to know first:** - A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently, then scores by cosine similarity — fast (one forward pass per document), but it misses fine-grained lexical overlap. - A cross-encoder concatenates query and document and runs them through the model together — far more precise, but O(n) in your candidate count. That is why you combine them: bi-encoder for recall, cross-encoder for precision. - Independent benchmarks (and the sentence-transformers BEIR evaluation) show reranking from 100 to 5 typically gains 5–8 NDCG@10 points on MS MARCO, with diminishing returns past the top-5.
**Add it to an existing retriever in three steps:**
```python from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
# Load once — keep this alive between requests reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2")
def rerank(query: str, candidates: list[str], top_k: int = 5) -> list[str]: pairs = [(query, doc) for doc in candidates] scores = reranker.predict(pairs) # returns a float per pair ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates), reverse=True) return [doc for _, doc in ranked[:top_k]] ```
Or use the built-in `.rank()` method which does the same thing:
```python results = reranker.rank(query, candidates, top_k=5, return_documents=True) top_docs = [r["text"] for r in results] ```
**Model choices by use case:** - `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2` — 22 MB, runs fine on CPU, good for local dev and CI evals - `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` — stronger across non-English queries; worth the extra size in production - Cohere Rerank API (`rerank-v3.5`) — hosted, no GPU needed, but adds a network round-trip and an API key dependency
**The real constraint:** reranker latency scales with candidate count. At 100 candidates on CPU, `ms-marco-MiniLM` takes roughly 200–400 ms per query — acceptable for a search bar, too slow inside a tight agent loop. Keep candidates ≤ 50 on CPU or move to a GPU or a hosted API for latency-sensitive paths.
**Sources:** [CrossEncoder usage — sbert.net/docs](https://sbert.net/docs/cross_encoder/usage/usage.html) · [Pretrained cross-encoder models — sbert.net](https://sbert.net/docs/cross_encoder/pretrained_models.html) · [RAG reranking with cross-encoders — bigdataboutique.com](https://bigdataboutique.com/blog/rag-reranking-improving-retrieval-quality-with-cross-encoders)

item.title: Your Tool-Using Claude App Shows a Spinner Until Every Call Finishes — `content_block_start` Events Carry the Tool Name the Moment Claude Decides to Call It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: When Claude calls a tool, the streaming API emits content_block_start with the tool name before any input_json_delta events stream — intercept it to surface real-time progress instead of a spinner.
item.content:encoded:
**When Claude calls a tool, `content_block_start` fires with `content_block.name` before any input streams — catch it to show users "Searching for X…" in real time rather than a silent spinner.**
When you use `stream.text_stream` for a plain-text app, `client.messages.stream()` works fine. Add tools and the user experience degrades: nothing visible happens between the user's message and Claude's final answer. Every tool call runs silently.
The raw streaming event sequence for a tool call is: 1. `content_block_start` — `type: "content_block_start"`, `content_block.type == "tool_use"`, `content_block.name == "get_weather"`, `content_block.input == {}` 2. Series of `input_json_delta` events — each carries a `partial_json` string fragment 3. `content_block_stop`
The tool name arrives on step 1, before any inputs stream. Use `stream.stream_events()` to intercept it:
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
tools = [ { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get current weather for a city.", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"], }, } ]
with client.messages.stream( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, tools=tools, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in London?"}], ) as stream: for event in stream.stream_events(): if ( event.type == "content_block_start" and hasattr(event, "content_block") and event.content_block.type == "tool_use" ): # fires immediately — before any input streams print(f"\n⚙ Calling {event.content_block.name}…", flush=True) elif ( event.type == "content_block_delta" and event.delta.type == "input_json_delta" ): # accumulate partial_json if you need the args live pass elif event.type == "text": print(event.text, end="", flush=True) ```
For even finer control — streaming individual parameter values token by token as Claude generates them — set `eager_input_streaming: true` on each tool definition and pass `betas=["fine-grained-tool-streaming-2025-05-14"]` in your request. Without it, `input_json_delta` events arrive in bursts.
**Limits:** `stream.text_stream` is a text-only view; `stream_events()` is required for tool events. `input_json_delta` fragments are partial JSON — not individually parseable; accumulate them into a string and parse on `content_block_stop`. `eager_input_streaming` is a beta feature with a dated API header; check the docs before shipping to production.
**Sources:** [Fine-grained tool streaming — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/fine-grained-tool-streaming) · [Messages streaming reference — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages-streaming) · [Claude API Tool Use Tutorial 2026 — gilricardo.com](https://www.gilricardo.com/blog/claude-api-tool-use-tutorial-2026)

item.title: Your 7B Fine-Tune Requires 24GB of VRAM in Full Precision — Unsloth's Pre-Quantized 4-Bit Checkpoint Runs the Same Training on a Free Colab T4
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: QLoRA runs LoRA adapters on a 4-bit quantized base model, cutting VRAM roughly fourfold. Unsloth's free Colab notebook fine-tunes Llama 3.1 8B on the T4's 15GB in under an hour.
item.content:encoded:
**QLoRA = LoRA adapters on a 4-bit quantized base model, which cuts VRAM roughly fourfold. Unsloth's free Colab T4 notebook fine-tunes Llama 3.1 8B in under an hour without any paid GPU.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** fine-tune a 7–8B open model on the free Colab T4 GPU (~15GB VRAM) using QLoRA and save only the adapter (~100MB), not the full 15GB base model.
**Three-bullet takeaway:** - QLoRA (Quantized LoRA) = standard LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized base; the base weights stay frozen and 4-bit, while only the small LoRA matrices train in fp16 - Unsloth provides pre-quantized `bnb-4bit` checkpoints for Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral — they download and load faster than quantizing on the fly - The free Colab T4 (15GB) fits Llama 3.1 8B QLoRA; the saved adapter is ~100MB and loads onto any copy of the same base at inference time
**Steps:**
```python # In a Colab cell (T4 runtime): suppress noisy pip output %%capture !pip install unsloth
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
# 1. Load the pre-quantized 4-bit checkpoint model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-bnb-4bit", # pre-quantized hub checkpoint max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, # QLoRA: base stays 4-bit throughout training dtype=None, # auto-detect (float16 on T4) )
# 2. Attach LoRA adapters — only these matrices train model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, # rank; increase for harder tasks (try 32–64 on larger GPUs) target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, # 0 = Unsloth's optimised kernel path bias="none", )
# 3. Train with TRL's SFTTrainer from trl import SFTTrainer from transformers import TrainingArguments
trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer, train_dataset=your_dataset, # an HF Dataset with a "text" column dataset_text_field="text", max_seq_length=2048, args=TrainingArguments( per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, warmup_steps=5, max_steps=60, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=True, # T4 is fp16; bf16 for A100/H100 optim="adamw_8bit", # 8-bit Adam saves VRAM on the optimiser states logging_steps=10, output_dir="outputs", save_steps=30, # checkpoint mid-run; free Colab sessions disconnect ), ) trainer.train()
# 4. Save the adapter only — not the 15GB base model.save_pretrained("my_lora_adapter") tokenizer.save_pretrained("my_lora_adapter") ```
Load the adapter at inference time with `PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, "my_lora_adapter")`.
**Limits:** 4-bit quantization introduces a small accuracy penalty. Unsloth reports the gap is "mostly closed" by their dynamic quants — that claim comes from Unsloth and hasn't been independently benchmarked; treat it as vendor-reported until you run your own eval (the previous post on `lm_eval` covers exactly this). Free Colab T4 sessions disconnect after 12 hours or on inactivity; `save_steps=30` checkpoints mitigate loss but don't eliminate it. Llama 3.1 is a gated model on Hugging Face — you must accept Meta's license before the checkpoint will download. Unsloth's official notebook targets Llama 3.1 (8B); for Llama 3.2 (3B) or Qwen 2.5, check the [notebooks index](https://docs.unsloth.ai/get-started/unsloth-notebooks) for the matching bnb-4bit checkpoint name.
**Sources:** [Unsloth fine-tuning guide — docs.unsloth.ai](https://docs.unsloth.ai/get-started/fine-tuning-guide) · [Free Colab Llama 3.1 (8B) QLoRA notebook — Unsloth/GitHub](https://colab.research.google.com/github/unslothai/notebooks/blob/main/nb/Llama3.1_(8B)-Alpaca.ipynb) · [Fine-tune Llama 3.1 with Unsloth — Hugging Face blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/mlabonne/sft-llama3)

item.title: Claude Code's Experimental Code Mode Rewrites How Tools Are Called — One JavaScript Pass Instead of Sequential Round-Trips
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Code Mode (opt-in, v2.1.323+) lets Claude write JavaScript that calls multiple tools in one execution pass. Enable with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 and confirm at the prompt.
item.content:encoded:
**Code Mode (opt-in, v2.1.323+) lets Claude write JavaScript that calls multiple tools in one execution pass instead of sequential round-trips — enable with `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1`.**
Claude Code v2.1.323 (November 12) ships an experimental opt-in feature: Code Mode. Under normal operation, Claude calls tools one by one — read file, wait for result; edit file, wait for confirmation; run test, wait. Under Code Mode, Claude instead writes a small JavaScript program that calls its tools in a single execution pass, batching reads and writes before you review the result.
**Enable it:**
```bash export CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude ```
Confirm when Claude Code offers to switch modes. Unset the variable to revert. For organization-wide disable, there is reportedly a Claude Code enterprise config setting — see the official release notes (note: the dedicated docs page at `code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode` returned 404 as of this writing; details may appear there once the feature exits experimental).
**What changes:** Instead of approving each tool call separately, you review a JS script that describes the full operation before it runs. For multi-file refactors or directory-wide reads, this can surface the complete plan before any change is made. You approve the script; Claude runs it.
**What to watch out for:** You are approving more at once. A script that reads 20 files and edits 15 of them is harder to verify than 15 individual approval prompts you can skip or reject selectively. Build a habit of reading the script's target paths before approving, the same way you'd review a `git diff` before merging.
**What's not confirmed:** Anthropic has not published measurements of token savings or latency improvements. The feature is experimental and may change in subsequent releases. `claude -p` (non-interactive) calls and subagent invocations are reported to skip Code Mode even when the env var is set.
**Sources:** [Code Mode release analysis — clauding.de](https://clauding.de/en/posts/claude-code-code-mode-2-1-323/) · [v2.1.322–323 changes breakdown — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20261113-cc-updates-v2-1-323/) · [Simon Willison on the new JS execution model — simonw.substack.com](https://simonw.substack.com/p/the-new-claude-analysis-javascript)

item.title: Your Agent SDK Loop Keeps Running Until Context Runs Out Because No Cap Was Set — `maxTurns` Limits Tool-Use Turns and `error_max_turns` Signals Truncation
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Set maxTurns on every Agent SDK run call or your unattended loop will keep burning tool calls until it hits a context limit. Check error_max_turns in the result to distinguish a clean finish from a truncated one.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `maxTurns` on every Agent SDK call or a runaway loop will burn tool calls until context runs out — `error_max_turns` in the result distinguishes a clean finish from a cut-short one.**
An agent launched without a turn cap runs until one of three things happens: Claude returns `end_turn` with no pending tool calls, the session context fills up, or a network timeout kills it. For short interactive tasks, that is fine. For unattended or background agents — processing a large directory, running a long refactor — a missing cap means a silent runaway you will not notice until the usage bill arrives.
Add `maxTurns` to your `run` call and check `result.stop_reason` after:
```python from claude_code_sdk import ClaudeCodeOptions, run
result = await run( prompt="Refactor all tests in src/tests/ to use the new fixture API", options=ClaudeCodeOptions(max_turns=20), # tool-use turns only )
if result.stop_reason == "error_max_turns": # Loop was truncated — task likely incomplete logger.warning("Hit turn cap — retry with narrower scope or higher cap") elif result.stop_reason == "end_turn": # Clean finish process(result.text) ```
**What counts as a turn.** `maxTurns` counts tool-use rounds: each time Claude calls a tool and receives the result is one turn. Conversational exchanges with no tool calls do not count. A task that reads 8 files, edits 3, and runs a test command uses roughly 12 turns.
**Picking the right cap.** Two times the median expected tool calls, plus 5 buffer turns, is a reasonable starting point. "Edit one file": 10–15. "Process this directory": 40–80. Too low truncates real tasks; too high defeats the protection. Tune it after you have production traces.
**When the cap triggers.** `error_max_turns` is a clean stop at a turn boundary — not a crash. The result still contains whatever the agent produced up to that point. Inspect it, log the incomplete state, and retry with a narrower scope rather than restarting blind.
The SDK default is `None` — no cap. Set it explicitly on every loop you deploy outside interactive mode.
**Sources:** [Claude Agent SDK — Agent Loop](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop) (official docs); [Claude Code agent loop control surface checklist](https://toolhalla.ai/blog/claude-code-agent-loop-control-surface-checklist) (independent practitioner checklist)

item.title: Your LLM App Traces Show What Happened But Not What Failed — Phoenix Instruments Anthropic API Calls With OpenTelemetry and Scores Each Span for Hallucination With a Built-In LLM Judge
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Arize Phoenix instruments your Anthropic app in three lines via OpenTelemetry, then runs LLM-as-judge hallucination and QA-correctness scores on every span — no test cases required.
item.content:encoded:
**Arize Phoenix traces every Anthropic API call as an OpenTelemetry span and scores them for hallucination and relevance using an LLM judge — adding evaluation to your existing observability in one afternoon.**
**What you will be able to do after this:** - See every `client.messages.create()` call as a span with its full input, output, tokens, and latency — no manual logging required - Run automated hallucination and QA-correctness evals against live traces using an LLM judge, without writing explicit test assertions - Identify which calls failed and why by clicking into flagged spans in the Phoenix UI
---
### Setup (10 minutes)
```bash pip install arize-phoenix arize-phoenix-evals openinference-instrumentation-anthropic uvx arize-phoenix serve # starts Phoenix + UI at localhost:6006 ```
Add these three lines before any Anthropic calls in your application code:
```python from phoenix.otel import register from openinference.instrumentation.anthropic import AnthropicInstrumentor
register(endpoint="http://localhost:6006/v1/traces") AnthropicInstrumentor().instrument() ```
Every subsequent `client.messages.create()` call now emits an OpenInference-formatted span to Phoenix. The span carries the full messages array, model, usage, latency, and stop reason. No changes to your production code path.
---
### Running evaluations
After collecting traces, use Phoenix's eval library to score them. Use Claude as the judge model:
```python import anthropic from phoenix.evals import ( HallucinationEvaluator, QAEvaluator, run_evals, AnthropicModel, ) import phoenix as px from datetime import datetime, timedelta
judge = AnthropicModel(model="claude-haiku-5-5") # cheap; works well as judge evaluators = [HallucinationEvaluator(judge), QAEvaluator(judge)]
client = px.Client() spans_df = client.query_spans( start_time=datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=24), project_name="default", )
eval_df = run_evals( dataframe=spans_df, evaluators=evaluators, provide_explanation=True, ) px.Client().log_evaluations(eval_df) # writes scores back onto spans in the UI ```
Each span now shows a hallucination score and an explanation you can click through. Flagged spans sort to the top. The underlying transport is OpenTelemetry — the same spans Phoenix receives can also go to any OTel-compatible backend by adding a second exporter to `register()`.
---
### Limits to know
Phoenix stores traces locally by default; for persistent storage in production you need Phoenix Cloud or a self-hosted Postgres backend. The UI annotation workflow is built for review sessions, not high-volume automated workflows — the docs note it is not optimized for high-volume trace workflows. License is Elastic License 2.0, which restricts using Phoenix itself as a managed service for third parties; check that before commercializing a build on top of it.
**Sources:** [Arize Phoenix — Anthropic tracing](https://docs.arize.com/phoenix/integrations/llm-providers/anthropic/anthropic-tracing) (official integration docs); [I tried observability and evaluation of LLM apps with Arize Phoenix](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/arize-phoenix-otel-llm-observability-handson/) (independent practitioner walkthrough)

item.title: Your Parallel Subagents All Write to the Same Checkout and Step on Each Other — `isolation: "worktree"` Routes Each Agent to Its Own Git Branch
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Set isolation: "worktree" on a Claude Code subagent to route each parallel agent to its own git branch; Edit and Write on the main checkout are blocked for that session.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `isolation: "worktree"` on a Claude Code subagent to give each parallel agent its own git branch — Edit and Write on the main checkout are blocked for that session.**
When you fan out subagents with the Agent tool (or in a Workflow script), they all share the same working tree by default. Two agents editing different files usually stay out of each other's way, but two agents touching the same file or the same generated output silently overwrite each other's work. The collision arrives at merge time, often as a lost diff.
## The fix: one parameter
```javascript // Agent tool call in a Workflow script Agent({ isolation: "worktree", prompt: "Migrate the payment module to the v3 token format" }) ```
```yaml # Or set it permanently in .claude/agents/my-agent.md frontmatter: --- isolation: worktree --- ```
Claude Code runs `git worktree add` under `.claude/worktrees/`, creates a new temporary branch, and runs the agent's entire session there. It also enforces the boundary: Edit, Write, and NotebookEdit calls that target the main checkout from within an isolated session are blocked — not advisory.
**What you get back:** when the agent completes with changes, the result includes the worktree path and branch name. When it completes with no changes, the worktree is cleaned up automatically.
## After the agents finish
Isolation guarantees no collisions *during* the run. After, you have N branches to review and merge:
```bash git worktree list # see active worktrees git diff main...<branch-name> # review one agent's work git merge <branch-name> # merge when satisfied git worktree remove .claude/worktrees/<dir> # clean up ```
Use this pattern when agents' scopes genuinely don't overlap — different modules, different features, different files. When agents need to coordinate on the same files, isolation won't help; model the dependency instead.
## Limits
- Requires Claude Code v2.1.198+. Shell commands run inside the agent's own worktree directory since v2.1.203 — check the changelog for your version, since this changed without a headline. - Each isolated session multiplies API usage proportionally to the number of parallel agents. - The N branches are yours to merge after the run. Isolation makes parallel execution safe; it does not make the merge trivial.
**Sources:** [Claude Code Worktrees — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees) · [Git worktrees with Claude Code walkthrough — BetterStack](https://betterstack.com/community/guides/ai/git-worktrees-claude/)

item.title: Your Fine-Tune Scores Higher on Your Own Test Set But Dropped Two MMLU Points — `lm_eval` Takes 10 Minutes to Measure Whether Training Helped or Regressed General Capability
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Use lm-evaluation-harness to benchmark a fine-tuned model against its base; the delta — not the absolute score — tells you whether training helped or traded general reasoning for task performance.
item.content:encoded:
**Use `lm-evaluation-harness` to run the same benchmark on the base model and your fine-tune — the delta (not the absolute score) tells you whether training improved or regressed general capability.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** benchmark a fine-tuned model against its base, catch capability regression before shipping, and read the delta rather than the absolute score.
Fine-tuning sharpens a model on your task. It also degrades general skills — what the literature calls catastrophic forgetting. A 2024 arXiv study ("Fine-Tuning or Fine-Failing?", 2406.11201) found that across most benchmark tasks, the untuned base model outperformed its fine-tuned counterpart. That's not unusual; it is the default risk of a fine-tune that isn't evaluated properly. The fix is two runs of the same benchmark, one before and one after.
## Install and run
```bash pip install lm_eval[hf] ```
**Run 1 — the base model:** ```bash lm_eval \ --model hf \ --model_args pretrained=meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B \ --tasks mmlu,hellaswag,arc_challenge \ --num_fewshot 5 \ --output_path results/base.json ```
**Run 2 — your fine-tuned model:** ```bash lm_eval \ --model hf \ --model_args pretrained=./my-finetuned-model \ --tasks mmlu,hellaswag,arc_challenge \ --num_fewshot 5 \ --output_path results/finetuned.json ```
Compare: `jq '.results' results/base.json results/finetuned.json`.
## Three things to look for
1. **Task score** (the reason you fine-tuned): confirm it went up. If not, the training data or hyperparams need work. 2. **General capability delta**: a drop of 2–4+ MMLU points after a small fine-tune is a warning sign that you've narrowed the model — check learning rate, epoch count, and dataset size. 3. **Formatting regression**: fine-tuned models sometimes produce structurally correct output but fail instruction-following for tasks outside training. HellaSwag and ARC-Challenge catch this better than MMLU alone.
## LoRA adapters: merge first
If you trained with LoRA/QLoRA, merge the adapter before evaluation:
```python from peft import PeftModel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B") model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "./my-lora-adapter") model = model.merge_and_unload() model.save_pretrained("./merged-model") ```
Point `lm_eval` at `./merged-model`. Some harness versions accept `--model_args pretrained=base,peft=adapter` directly, but merge-first is more reliable across versions.
## Limit: benchmarks measure the gap, not production quality
Standard benchmarks like MMLU are in the training data of most large models — high scores can reflect memorisation rather than capability. Use benchmark deltas to catch regressions, not to prove production quality. Pair them with a task-specific held-out eval set and an LLM-as-judge; if you use a judge model, pick one from a different model family to avoid same-family score inflation.
**Sources:** [lm-evaluation-harness quickstart — lm-evaluation-harness.readthedocs.io](https://lm-evaluation-harness.readthedocs.io/getting_started/quickstart/) · [EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness — GitHub](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness) · [Fine-Tuning or Fine-Failing? — arXiv 2406.11201](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11201)

item.title: Your Agent SDK Validation Hook Crashes Silently and the Loop Keeps Going — Set onFailure: 'block' to Stop on a Failed Check
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add onFailure: 'block' to any Agent SDK hook callback to convert a crashing or rejecting check into a hard stop — your validation gate actually closes instead of silently skipping.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR:** Add `onFailure: "block"` to any hook callback in the Claude Agent SDK to make a crashing or rejecting validator stop the agent rather than silently continue.
## What you'll be able to do after this
By the end you'll know how to wire a fail-closed validation gate so your agent actually stops when a check fails — not just logs it and keeps running.
**Key takeaways:** - By default a hook that throws or rejects is treated as a non-fatal error — the agent loop continues - `onFailure: "block"` converts that into a hard stop at the hook boundary - Use `"block"` for safety-critical checks; leave the default (`"continue"`) for logging and telemetry
---
## The problem: silent skip
The Claude Agent SDK lets you attach hook callbacks to events like `post_tool_use`. The intent is usually to validate what the agent just did before it proceeds. But if the callback throws, the default behaviour is to log the error internally and move on. Your validation gate is open.
## The fix: `onFailure: "block"`
```python from anthropic.agents import ClaudeCode
def validate_no_destructive_ops(event): if event.tool_name in ("bash", "computer") and "rm -rf" in event.tool_input.get("command", ""): raise ValueError("Destructive operation blocked by policy")
agent = ClaudeCode( system_prompt="You are a code reviewer.", hooks=[{ "event": "post_tool_use", "handler": validate_no_destructive_ops, "onFailure": "block", }] )
result = agent.run("Review this codebase for security issues.") ```
When `validate_no_destructive_ops` raises, the loop stops and surfaces the exception rather than continuing. Swap `"block"` for `"continue"` (or omit `onFailure` entirely) on a logging hook that you don't want to interrupt the run.
## Known limit
`dangerouslyDisableSandbox` can bypass `PreToolUse` hooks in some execution environments — don't rely on hooks alone as your only security boundary for untrusted inputs.
---
*Sources: [Agent SDK hooks docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks); practitioner notes at nerdleveltech.com and developersdigest.tech.*
