item.title: One Query Is What Your User Typed — MultiQueryRetriever Rephrases It Three Ways and Takes the Union, Raising Recall Without Touching Your Index
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Generate 3 query variants for each question using an LLM, run all against your vector store, and return the unique-union of results to cover different phrasings and angles.
item.content:encoded:
**TL;DR:** `MultiQueryRetriever` sends your question through an LLM to produce N rephrasings, runs all of them, and returns the unique-union — more recall, same index.
## What you'll be able to do after this
By the end you'll know how to drop `MultiQueryRetriever` into an existing LangChain retrieval chain, understand when it helps and when it's overkill, and tune it without changing your vector store.
**Key takeaways:** - Embedding similarity is phrasing-sensitive — a synonym your user didn't use can miss relevant chunks - `MultiQueryRetriever` generates N query variants, retrieves for each, and deduplicates the union - Each question costs N LLM calls + N retrieval calls; use Haiku for the rewriter to keep it cheap
---
## Why one query isn't enough
When a user asks *"How do I set up authentication?"*, your embedding space may store the answer under *"configuring OAuth"*, *"user sign-in flow"*, or *"auth middleware setup"* — none of which are lexically close to the question. Semantic similarity helps, but it's directional: the query's embedding is a single point.
`MultiQueryRetriever` sidesteps this by generating three rephrasings of the original question with an LLM, running each through the retriever independently, and returning the set-union of unique documents. The index is untouched — you're widening the probe, not reindexing.
## Code
```python from langchain.retrievers.multi_query import MultiQueryRetriever from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from langchain_chroma import Chroma from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
embedding = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5") vectorstore = Chroma(embedding_function=embedding, persist_directory="./db") base_retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5})
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-5-5", temperature=0) retriever = MultiQueryRetriever.from_llm( retriever=base_retriever, llm=llm )
docs = retriever.invoke("How do I set up authentication?") ```
`from_llm` wires up the default prompt that asks Claude to produce three alternative phrasings. It returns `List[Document]` — same interface as any other LangChain retriever, so it slots into existing `RetrievalQA` or LCEL chains with no other changes.
## Tradeoffs
| | Baseline retriever | MultiQueryRetriever | |---|---|---| | Calls per query | 1 retrieval | 1 LLM + 3 retrieval | | Latency | Low | ~2–3× higher | | Recall | Phrasing-dependent | More robust to synonyms | | Index changes needed | — | No |
Doesn't help if the index itself is sparse — if the content isn't there, more queries won't surface it. For high-volume pipelines, cache the LLM-generated variants if the same questions recur.
---
*Sources: [LangChain MultiQueryRetriever how-to](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/MultiQueryRetriever/); [LangChain query transformations](https://blog.langchain.dev/query-transformations/); James Briggs walkthrough via Class Central.*

item.title: Your Agent Unlocks New Tools Mid-Conversation — the inline-tools Beta Adds Them Without Busting the Cache
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add a fully-defined new tool to a Claude conversation after it starts, with the cache prefix preserved — the tools array stays fixed, only a tool_addition block changes.
item.content:encoded:
**Your agent can't add a brand-new tool mid-conversation without changing `tools`, and changing `tools` busts the prompt cache — until now. The `inline-tools-2026-09-15` beta header lets a `tool_addition` block carry a full tool definition so the cached prefix stays intact.**
The problem: Claude's prompt cache is keyed on the `tools` array. Add a tool mid-conversation and you rewrite the cache prefix, paying full uncached token cost on the next turn. For agents with long system prompts and many tools, that penalty compounds across every dynamic expansion.
The fix: keep `tools` fixed with at least one non-deferred tool (to establish the cache prefix), then inject new tool definitions exactly when needed via a mid-conversation system message.
**How to add a tool mid-conversation:**
```python # Initial request — tools array stays fixed for the whole session response = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", system="You are a workflow assistant.", tools=[{"name": "search_docs", ...}], # anchors the cache messages=conversation, betas=["inline-tools-2026-09-15"], )
# Later — user authenticates; unlock billing tools without touching tools[] conversation.append({ "role": "system", "content": [{ "type": "tool_addition", "tool": { "name": "submit_billing_update", "description": "Submit a billing change for the authenticated user.", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {"amount": {"type": "number"}}, "required": ["amount"] } } }] }) ```
Remove a tool that's no longer relevant with `{"type": "tool_removal", "name": "search_docs"}` in the same block shape.
**Why this matters:** agents that unlock capabilities based on context — after authentication, after a workflow step, after a user confirms scope — no longer pay cache-bust penalties on every expansion. The `tools` array establishes the cache once; `tool_addition` appends without touching it.
**Limits:** Currently Claude API only — Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud are not listed in the current docs. Requires at least one non-deferred tool in `tools` to anchor the cache. Compaction requests must include the same beta header to carry tool changes forward through context compression.
**Sources:** [Anthropic: Mid-conversation system messages](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages), [Start Debugging: Add a tool mid-conversation without breaking the cache](https://startdebugging.net/2026/11/add-a-tool-mid-conversation-without-breaking-the-claude-prompt-cache/), [ByteIota: Claude API inline tools mid-conversation](https://byteiota.com/claude-api-inline-tools-mid-conversation/)

item.title: Your Agent Loop Reviews Nothing Until the Code Is Written — Approving a Plan Before Build Runs Cuts the Cost of a Wrong Direction by an Order of Magnitude
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitHub's four-stage agentic loop — Plan, Build, Verify, Observe — restructures where human judgment enters so a direction mistake costs minutes rather than a large refactor.
item.content:encoded:
**GitHub's four-stage agentic loop — Plan, Build, Verify, Observe — restructures where human judgment enters the pipeline. A direction mistake rejected at Plan costs five minutes; the same mistake caught at Build costs hours plus a revert.**
GitHub's ["Beyond code generation" guide](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/beyond-code-generation-a-developers-guide-to-agentic-engineering/) names the principal failure mode of agent-first development: code generation accelerated, but every other part of the engineering loop — planning, review, and production investigation — did not. The fix isn't adding more reviews; it's moving judgment to the stage where it's cheapest.
**The four stages:**
**Plan** — the agent researches the codebase and proposes a spec; you approve or reject it before any code runs. Rejecting a plan costs five minutes. Redirecting an agent mid-build costs two hours plus a revert.
**Build** — the agent writes, tests, and iterates within the approved boundary. Human involvement is interrupt-on-failure, not line-by-line review. This is where most agents run today, with no approved plan behind them.
**Verify** — structured gates: type checks, unit tests, integration tests, linting. You review test results, not raw diffs. When CI is red, the agent retries; when it's consistently green, you review the diff against the plan.
**Observe** — production signals (errors, latency, feature flags) feed back into the next Plan cycle. The loop closes; you're operating a system, not maintaining code that an agent wrote.
**What this doesn't solve:** Agents can pass their own tests if the tests weren't written independently of the code. Plan approval only works when the spec is specific enough to evaluate — a vague brief still leads to a bad build. The Plan stage also slows down exploratory work where the right path isn't known until you've tried three options; reserve it for well-scoped tasks, not spikes. And the Verify stage still requires meaningful test coverage — this framework does not substitute for it.
**Sources:** [Beyond code generation: A developer's guide to agentic engineering — GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/beyond-code-generation-a-developers-guide-to-agentic-engineering/) · [From vibe coding to agentic engineering — Human Coder](https://humancoder.substack.com/p/from-vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering) · [Agentic Engineering: What Agents Need Besides the Model — Unblocked](https://getunblocked.com/blog/agentic-engineering-what-agents-need/)

item.title: Your RAG Retriever Misses Context That Spans Two Chunks Because chunk_overlap Is Zero — RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter's Two Parameters Determine Whether an Answer Survives a Split
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter cuts a document at paragraph breaks, then newlines, then words — always at a natural boundary. chunk_overlap keeps context from disappearing at every split.
item.content:encoded:
**RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter uses a priority hierarchy — paragraphs, newlines, words — so splits land at natural boundaries. `chunk_overlap` controls how many characters of context carry across each boundary; zero overlap is the most common RAG configuration mistake.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Configure `chunk_size` and `chunk_overlap` based on your embedding model's actual token limit, not arbitrary defaults - Understand why the recursive splitter performs comparably to or better than semantic chunking on most real documents - Avoid two common mistakes: zero overlap (context lost at boundaries) and character-counted chunk sizes on models with different token ratios
**The core setup:**
```python from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=1000, # characters, not tokens chunk_overlap=200, # overlap between consecutive chunks add_start_index=True, # preserves position in original document )
docs = splitter.create_documents([long_text]) # Returns list of Document(page_content=..., metadata={'start_index': N}) ```
**Why "recursive" matters:** The splitter works through a separator priority list: `["\n\n", "\n", " ", ""]`. It tries paragraph breaks first; if a paragraph is still too large, it splits at newlines; then words; finally individual characters as a last resort. A sentence is never split mid-word unless that word alone exceeds `chunk_size`.
**Setting chunk_size correctly:** `chunk_size` is in **characters**, not tokens. `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` has a 256-token limit (~1000–1300 characters); `text-embedding-3-small` handles 8191 tokens. Set your chunk size to stay comfortably under your embedding model's limit — check `model.max_seq_length` before choosing. For sentence-transformers models on English prose, 400–600 tokens (~2000–3000 characters) works well.
**Why chunk_overlap matters:** An answer that spans the boundary between two chunks will be in neither chunk at retrieval time. `chunk_overlap=200` means each chunk starts 200 characters before where the previous ended, so boundary context appears in both. Zero overlap is the default in many tutorials and the most common source of "my RAG retrieves something close but not quite right" failures.
**When RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter is good enough (which is most of the time):** A February 2026 FloTorch benchmark on 50 academic papers found fixed-size chunking within 15 percentage points of the best strategy tested — and semantic chunking underperformed it at 54% accuracy versus 69% for recursive splitting ([PremAI benchmark report](https://blog.premai.io/rag-chunking-strategies-the-2026-benchmark-guide)). An [IBM LangChain tutorial](https://www.ibm.com/think/tutorials/chunking-strategies-for-rag-with-langchain-watsonx-ai) reaches the same conclusion for structured documents. Semantic chunking adds 2–5× latency per chunk at index time by embedding each sentence before deciding where to split — that cost is rarely justified until you've measured a retrieval quality problem the recursive splitter doesn't solve.
**Where this breaks down:** RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter doesn't understand your document format. PDFs with tables, code blocks, or multi-column layouts can produce nonsense splits — use a structure-aware loader (e.g., `PyPDFLoader` with `mode="layout"`) before splitting. And `chunk_size` in characters varies by language: Chinese text at 1000 characters is 300–400 tokens; English prose at 1000 characters is typically 200–300 tokens.
**Sources:** [Recursive text splitter — LangChain Python docs](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/recursive_text_splitter) · [RAG chunking strategies benchmark — PremAI Blog](https://blog.premai.io/rag-chunking-strategies-the-2026-benchmark-guide) · [Implement RAG chunking with LangChain and watsonx.ai — IBM Think](https://www.ibm.com/think/tutorials/chunking-strategies-for-rag-with-langchain-watsonx-ai)

item.title: Every Agent Turn Runs the Same Thinking Budget Including Simple Retrieval Calls — output_config.effort in an Empty System Message Scales It Per Turn
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic's per-message effort beta (Nov 12) lets agent loops dial reasoning up or down per turn. Send the mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 beta header and an empty output_config system message.
item.content:encoded:
**Add `output_config.effort` to an empty-content system message and send the `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01` beta header to dial reasoning up or down per turn — your agent no longer has to run full thinking on tool-call confirmations.**
If your agent runs the same thinking budget on every message — including retrieval confirmations, brief summaries, and boilerplate acknowledgments — you're burning extended thinking tokens on turns that don't need them.
Anthropic's per-message effort beta (shipped November 12) lets you change the effort level mid-conversation. The mechanism: insert an empty-content system message directly before the message where the new level takes effect, and include the beta header `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01`.
```python messages = [ # ... prior turns { "role": "user", "content": [{"type": "output_config", "effort": "low"}] }, {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the retrieved context in two sentences."} ]
response = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", messages=messages, betas=["mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01"] ) ```
The practical pattern: start the session with `thinking: {budget_tokens: 20000}` at the top level, then insert low-effort markers around retrieval/formatting turns and high-effort markers around decision or synthesis turns. The override stays in effect until another empty marker changes it.
**Limits and gotchas:**
- `claude-fable-5-2` returns a 400 error — only the Claude 5.5 family (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) supports per-turn effort. - LangChain and several other proxies silently strip empty-content system messages before the request reaches the API ([issue #40892](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/issues/40892)). The feature will appear to do nothing — log the raw request body before it goes out. - The `clear_at` field, which pins when the override expires, is also dropped by some client libraries ([Bifrost #9729](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/issues/9729)).
This is most useful in long agent chains where you can clearly separate cheap turns from expensive ones. For single-turn requests, top-level `thinking` is simpler and doesn't require the beta header.
**Sources:** [Anthropic per-message effort docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort-per-message) · [LangChain issue #40892](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/issues/40892) · [Bifrost issue #9729](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/issues/9729)

item.title: Your Regenerated Artboard Overwrites the Code-Side Fixes You Already Merged — Three Questions Route Every Change to the Right Tool
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Structure changes go back to Claude Design; behavior and data wiring go to Claude Code — a three-question rule routes every iteration so the two tools stop overwriting each other.
item.content:encoded:
**Structure changes go back to Claude Design; behavior, data wiring, and component property swaps go to Claude Code — a three-question rule routes every change so the two tools stop undoing each other's work.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Route any design iteration to the right tool in 30 seconds - Stop regenerating full artboards for changes Claude Code handles in a single prompt - Keep changes from each tool from overwriting the other during active iteration
After handing off from Claude Design to Claude Code, most teams settle into one of two broken patterns: regenerating everything when they want any visual change, or making structural edits in Claude Code and wondering why the layout looks wrong. The fix is a decision rule, not a workflow hack.
**Resource:** Anthropic's [Get started with Claude Design](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design) on support.claude.com covers both the handoff and the `/design` reverse flow. The [Claude Design → Claude Code Handoff guide](https://claude-code-playbook.pages.dev/en/docs/level-4/claude-design-handoff) is a practitioner walkthrough of the same path.
**Three questions:**
1. **Does this change affect layout, component arrangement, or visual hierarchy?** → Claude Design. These changes live in the design intent; Claude Code can't reconstruct them from a text prompt without structural drift.
2. **Does this change affect behavior, state, or data wiring?** → Claude Code. Claude Design doesn't know your backend exists; ask it to generate validation logic and it generates mock logic.
3. **Is this a property swap on a component that's already in your codebase?** → Claude Code. A button variant, a color token, an icon change — Claude Code modifies the component in place; a regeneration rebuilds the visual layer and overwrites what you already fixed.
**Walk-through — a form page, one change of each type:**
``` Change A: "Add a two-column layout for address fields" → Claude Design (structural) Change B: "Show inline validation error on bad postal code" → Claude Code (behavior) Change C: "Switch submit from filled to outline variant" → Claude Code (component prop) ```
For Change B in Claude Code: `"Add inline validation for postal-code — show ValidationMessage in error state when the value isn't a valid postal code."` Claude Code knows the component; Claude Design would generate mock logic that doesn't connect to your form state.
**The reverse path:** Run `/design` in Claude Code to push an existing component into Claude Design when you want to explore a structural change without editing the artboard manually.
**Limits:** Every regeneration in Claude Design starts from the visual spec, not from your component tree. It has no awareness of code-side changes since the last handoff — if you've fixed a responsive layout or swapped a dependency, regenerating overwrites those changes. The bundle doesn't track code-side drift; merging is your responsibility.
**Sources:** [Get started with Claude Design (support.claude.com)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design) · [Claude Design handoff guide (claude-code-playbook)](https://claude-code-playbook.pages.dev/en/docs/level-4/claude-design-handoff) · [/design command docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slash-commands/design)

item.title: Claude Code v2.1.321 Patches an MCP OAuth Bug That Could Send Refresh Tokens to a Redirect Host
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: v2.1.321 (Nov 10) patches an MCP OAuth bug where token refreshes could forward credentials to a redirect host—update if you have OAuth-authenticated remote MCP servers.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code v2.1.321 (November 10) fixes an MCP OAuth vulnerability where token refreshes could follow a redirect and send credentials to the redirect target — update if you use authenticated remote MCP servers.**
The bug: when an OAuth remote MCP server responded with a redirect during token refresh, Claude Code would follow the redirect and send the refresh token (and potentially the access token) to the new host. If your MCP server or any upstream system was misconfigured or compromised, long-lived credentials could reach an unintended recipient.
**What to do:** run `claude --version` — if you're below 2.1.321, update now (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@latest`). Then check your OAuth MCP servers: `claude mcp list`. If you have any, treat the tokens as potentially exposed and re-authenticate after updating.
The same release makes Claude Fable 5.2 the new default Fable model and closes three permission gaps that allowed sandboxed processes to spawn subprocesses outside the sandbox boundary.
**Limit:** The specific fix details come from a third-party release summary (ai-tldr.dev), not official GitHub release notes — verify against the [official changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) or the v2.1.321 npm tag before acting on this.
**Why it matters:** MCP OAuth is new enough that most users haven't audited their token storage. A redirect token leak is subtle — it doesn't cause immediate breakage, it silently copies credentials. This is the class of bug that only surfaces after a security review or an incident.
**Sources:** [Claude Code 2.1.321 — ai-tldr.dev](https://ai-tldr.dev/releases/anthropic-claude-code-2-1-321/) · [Claude Code has an MCP security problem — Pulse Bot](https://www.pulse.bot/cybersecurity/news/claude-code-has-an-mcp-security-problem-and-your-developers-are-already-using-it-26088aa8-b930-4d5b-9954-f34c9a2b151e/) · [Claude Code changelog — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog)

item.title: Every Hand-Written JSON Parser in Your Claude App Is a Validation Liability — `client.messages.parse()` Returns a Typed Pydantic Object Directly
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The Anthropic Python SDK's client.messages.parse() returns a validated Pydantic object from Claude—no JSON parsing, no schema wrangling, no silent type errors downstream.
item.content:encoded:
**The Anthropic Python SDK's `client.messages.parse()` returns a validated Pydantic object — skip `json.loads()` entirely and get a typed result with schema validation built in.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** call Claude with any Pydantic model and get a typed, validated instance back — your type checker, your linter, and your downstream code all see real types, not strings.
- Under the hood, `messages.parse()` translates your Pydantic schema to a tool definition, calls Claude with it, and validates the response — all in one call. No intermediate JSON, no manual `.model_validate()`. - If Claude returns a refusal, `response.parsed_output` is `None` rather than raising an exception — guard it explicitly. - Doesn't combine with streaming (the parse waits for the full response) or with citations (use LangChain's `.with_structured_output()` for the citations case, covered [here](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-11-07-05-langchain-cited-answer-structured-output-rag-citations)).
```python from anthropic import Anthropic from pydantic import BaseModel
class PullRequestReview(BaseModel): verdict: str # "approve" | "request_changes" | "comment" summary: str blocking_issues: list[str]
client = Anthropic()
response = client.messages.parse( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, output_format=PullRequestReview, messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": f"Review this diff:\n\n{diff_text}", }], )
review = response.parsed_output if review is None: raise ValueError("Model refused to review this diff")
if review.blocking_issues: print(f"Blocking: {review.blocking_issues}") ```
**SDK version note:** `client.messages.parse()` with `output_format` is the current stable path. Code using `client.beta.messages.parse()` with a `structured-outputs-2025-11-13` beta header still works during the transition but is deprecated — migrate to the stable path.
**Sources:** [Structured outputs — Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs) · [Hands-on with Anthropic's new structured output capabilities — Towards Data Science](https://towardsdatascience.com/hands-on-with-anthropics-new-structured-output-capabilities/) · [Claude API structured outputs walkthrough — Classmethod](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/claude-api-structured-outputs/)

item.title: Your Copilot Session and Your Claude Session Are in Separate Windows — VS Code 1.145 Preview Lets You Nest Them in One Agent Run
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: VS Code 1.145 adds a preview setting that lets you nest Claude or Codex inside a running Copilot agent session, so you can delegate review and planning tasks across harnesses without switching windows.
item.content:encoded:
**VS Code 1.145 (November 4) adds a preview setting that lets you route subtasks to Claude, Codex, or other agent harnesses from inside a running Copilot session — no separate window, no context switch.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** have Copilot plan and scaffold, then drop Claude in for a code-review pass or a spec critique, all within the same VS Code workspace and without manually copying output between sessions.
VS Code's Agent Host runs agent sessions in a dedicated process separate from the editor. As of 1.144 (October 28), Copilot became the default harness for new sessions. 1.145 adds a preview on top of that: a single setting enables the ability to pick a different harness for a *nested* session — so a Copilot-driven agent loop can delegate a subtask to Claude mid-run and have its result returned inline.
**Enable the preview:**
```json // settings.json { "chat.agentHost.multipleChatProviders.enabled": true } ```
Once on, the Agents window shows a harness picker when you start a nested session. Copilot remains the outer default; Claude and Codex appear as options for inner sessions.
**Practical patterns:**
- Run a Copilot agent to draft implementation steps for a feature; then nest a Claude session to critique the plan against your existing architecture before writing any code. - Delegate code review of a generated diff to Claude while Copilot continues the scaffolding loop on another task. - Use Codex for a task that runs better on its training data, then fold the output back into the Copilot session that owns the working tree.
**Three limits worth knowing:**
1. **Enterprise-managed settings disable non-Copilot harnesses.** If your organization uses enterprise-managed Copilot policies, the Claude and Codex pickers do not appear — the setting is overridden silently. Check via `Help → Developer Tools → Console` for a blocked-harness log. 2. **Preview only — the API can change.** The `multipleChatProviders` flag is undocumented and subject to removal. If it disappears in a future update, sessions fall back to single-harness. 3. **Background cloud sessions don't carry harness choices.** Remote agent sessions started from VS Code and continued on GitHub.com or GitHub Mobile run in the Copilot harness only; the nested-harness setting applies to the local VS Code editor session exclusively.
**Sources:** [VS Code 1.145 release notes — code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_145) · [VS Code 1.145 expands remote agent workflows — Visual Studio Magazine](https://visualstudiomagazine.com/articles/2026/11/04/vs-code-1-145-expands-remote-agent-workflows-adds-cron-automations.aspx) · [VS Code 1.145 Lets You Run Claude, Codex, and Copilot in the Same Agent Session — Windows Report](https://windowsreport.com/?p=1514664)

item.title: Your Local Dev Loop Still Calls the OpenAI API on Every Test Run — Ollama Runs Any Pulled Model at `localhost:11434/v1` With a Two-Line Setup
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Ollama serves any pulled model at http://localhost:11434/v1. Point your existing openai Python client there and your app talks to a local model — no rewrite needed.
item.content:encoded:
**Ollama serves any pulled model at `http://localhost:11434/v1` — point your existing `openai` Python client there and your app talks to a local model, with no network calls and no API bill.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run your RAG chain, agent loop, or embedding pipeline entirely on-device during development — no API key rotation, no rate limits, no bill for test runs. When you're ready to ship, swap the `base_url` back to your production provider.
### Three takeaways
- Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API — same routes (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`), same JSON shape, same streaming behavior — so code written for `openai.ChatCompletion` works without modification. - The model library at [ollama.com/models](https://ollama.com/models) includes Llama 3.2, Qwen 3, Gemma 3, Mistral, and embedding models like `nomic-embed-text` — pull any of them with one command. - The API key is ignored by Ollama; pass any placeholder string to satisfy the SDK's required field.
### Walk-through
**1. Install Ollama**
```bash # macOS brew install ollama
# Linux (requires curl) curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ```
After install, Ollama starts automatically at `http://localhost:11434`. Confirm with `ollama list`.
**2. Pull a model**
```bash ollama pull llama3.2 # 2GB, 3B, fast on most laptops ollama pull nomic-embed-text # 274MB embedding model ```
The first pull downloads the GGUF weights; subsequent runs use the cache.
**3. Point your existing openai client at it**
```python from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama", # ignored, any string works )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="llama3.2", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this diff in one sentence."}], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
For embeddings, the same client and the same `base_url` work — just call `client.embeddings.create(model="nomic-embed-text", input=texts)`.
**What doesn't work:**
- **Structured outputs (`response_format: json_schema`)** — partial support; some models handle `json_object` mode but `json_schema` with strict field validation may fail depending on the model. Test before relying on it. - **Vision** — multimodal calls work only for models that include a vision encoder (e.g., `llama3.2-vision`). Sending an image to a text-only model returns an error rather than silently dropping the image. - **Tool call reliability** — function calling works on models trained for it (Qwen 3, Llama 3.2) but smaller models often hallucinate tool arguments. Use a 7B+ model for tool-use tests. - **No auth** — Ollama binds to localhost by default. Setting `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0` to expose it on your LAN means anyone on the network can call it; add a reverse proxy with auth if that matters.
**Sources:** [Ollama OpenAI compatibility — github.com/ollama](https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/openai.md) · [Ollama model library — ollama.com/models](https://ollama.com/models) · [Running Local LLMs With Ollama — KodeKloud](https://notes.kodekloud.com/docs/Running-Local-LLMs-With-Ollama/Building-AI-Applications/OpenAI-Compatibility-for-Ollama)

item.title: Your Claude Code Settings Reference `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL`, Which Is Deprecated — Pin Background-Task Model Aliases With `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` Instead
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL (the env var for Claude Code's background side-queries) is deprecated; use ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL and set all three alias vars to pin your model tier choices explicitly.
item.content:encoded:
**`ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL` — the env var that controlled which model Claude Code used for background side-queries — is deprecated. Set `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL`, and `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL` instead to pin alias resolution explicitly.**
Claude Code uses a Haiku-class model for background side-queries and certain built-in subagent tasks (file scanning, quick lookups) rather than your main session model. The original variable for that slot was `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL`. It still works but is listed as deprecated in the official env-vars reference; the replacement is `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL`.
The full trio of alias variables:
```bash export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL="claude-haiku-5-5" export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL="claude-sonnet-5-5" export ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL="claude-opus-5-5" ```
Or in `~/.claude/settings.json`:
```json { "env": { "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "claude-haiku-5-5", "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-5-5" } } ```
When you don't set these, Claude Code resolves the `haiku`, `sonnet`, and `opus` aliases to Anthropic's current defaults, which change when new models release. Setting them explicitly pins the resolution — a Haiku 5.5 model you have tested and verified keeps running even after a new Haiku releases and becomes the new default.
**Where this matters most:**
- **Bedrock and gateway deployments.** On Amazon Bedrock, the Haiku-class background model defaults to your primary Sonnet model when Haiku is not enabled in the account. Setting `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` to a Bedrock model ID you have actually enabled prevents the silent fallback and the cost increase that comes with it. - **Cost predictability.** Background tasks that run on the Haiku slot are roughly one-tenth the per-token cost of Sonnet (per Anthropic's published pricing). Pinning the alias means those tasks won't silently shift to Sonnet rates after a default rotation. - **Auditability.** Some built-in Claude Code subagents use the Haiku slot. Pinning the variable makes their model choice explicit and verifiable via `claude --verbose`.
**Limits:** Setting `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` pins the alias at the env layer, but subagents with an explicit `model:` field in their `.claude/agents/` frontmatter still override it — the per-agent setting takes precedence over the alias. The variables affect alias resolution only; they won't make a model available on a provider that hasn't enabled it in the account. The deprecated `ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL` is still read but expect it to be removed in a future release.

item.title: Every RAG Tutorial Calls `model.encode()` Without Explaining What Shape It Returns — Three Lines Show You the Float Array That Makes Semantic Search Work
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2").encode(sentences) returns a NumPy array of shape (n, 384): one fixed-length float vector per sentence where close vectors mean related meaning.
item.content:encoded:
**`SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2").encode(sentences)` returns a NumPy array of shape `(n, 384)` — one fixed-length float vector per input, where semantically similar sentences cluster close together in that space.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Load any SBERT model, encode a batch of text, and inspect the resulting embedding matrix - Compute cosine similarity between two texts without a vector database - Understand why document chunking happens before encoding — not as an optimization, but because of a hard model limit
## The three-line foundation
```bash pip install sentence-transformers ```
```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
sentences = [ "Claude Code agents can run tasks in parallel using git worktrees.", "Parallel agents on the same repo need file isolation to avoid conflicts.", "Fine-tuning a model teaches new behaviour; RAG teaches it new facts.", ]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences) print(embeddings.shape) # (3, 384) ```
The `384` is not a property of the text — it is a property of the model. `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` always produces a 384-dimensional vector regardless of input length or content. Larger models like `all-mpnet-base-v2` produce 768 dimensions; API embedding models typically produce 1024 or 3072. When you pick a model, you are also fixing the width of every column in your vector store permanently — switching models later requires re-encoding and re-indexing all stored documents.
## Similarity falls out of geometry
```python from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
# sentence 0 (parallel worktrees) vs sentence 1 (file isolation): same topic print(cosine_similarity(embeddings[:1], embeddings[1:2])) # ~0.76
# sentence 0 vs sentence 2 (fine-tuning): different topic print(cosine_similarity(embeddings[:1], embeddings[2:3])) # ~0.21 ```
Two sentences about the same thing produce vectors that point in similar directions. Cosine similarity measures that alignment: 1.0 is identical direction, 0.0 is perpendicular (unrelated). A vector database stores these embeddings and returns the rows with the highest cosine similarity to a query embedding — which is all retrieval-augmented search is doing at its core.
## The constraint that drives chunking
`all-MiniLM-L6-v2` truncates input silently at 256 tokens (~190 words). Text beyond that is dropped, not summarized or carried over. This is not a performance optimization you can tune around — it is the model's architectural limit. Document chunking therefore happens before encoding because the model cannot encode more in a single call, not as a separate speed-up. Your chunk size is partly determined by which model you choose; check `model.max_seq_length` before setting your splitter's `chunk_size`.
**Limits:** Switching models after indexing requires re-encoding and re-indexing all stored documents — the vector dimensions are fixed at index-creation time and dimensions from different models are not interchangeable. `encode()` runs on CPU by default; pass `device="cuda"` when a GPU is available, or tune `batch_size` for throughput on large corpora. Embedding quality varies significantly by domain: `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` was trained on general English and underperforms on code, medical text, and other specialized domains. Use the [MTEB Retrieval leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard) to benchmark alternatives for your specific use case before committing to an index schema.
**Sources:** [sentence-transformers quickstart — sbert.net](https://sbert.net/docs/quickstart.html) · [How to Generate and Visualize Text Embeddings in Python — thepythoncode.com](https://thepythoncode.com/article/generate-visualize-text-embeddings-python) · [Sentence Transformers: Meanings in Disguise — Pinecone Learn](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/series/nlp/sentence-embeddings/)

item.title: Your SFT Fine-Tune Knows the Facts But Ranks a Rambling Answer Equal to a Crisp One — DPO Trains Preference From Chosen/Rejected Pairs Without a Reward Model
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run Unsloth's DPO notebook to train a preference-aligned model from chosen/rejected pairs after SFT — no reward model or PPO loop needed, just contrastive fine-tuning against an SFT baseline.
item.content:encoded:
**Run Unsloth's DPO notebook to teach your fine-tuned model to prefer clearer answers over rambling ones — no reward model, no PPO loop, just contrastive training against your SFT checkpoint using (prompt, chosen, rejected) pairs.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** add a Direct Preference Optimization pass on top of an SFT checkpoint to steer response quality, using Unsloth and TRL's DPOTrainer in a single Colab session on a free GPU.
- DPO replaces the reward model and PPO with direct contrastive training: given a (prompt, chosen, rejected) triple, it increases the probability of the chosen response while decreasing the rejected one, treating your SFT checkpoint as the reference policy - The `beta` hyperparameter controls how far the model drifts from the reference — 0.1–0.3 is a stable starting range; above 0.5 training can diverge from SFT behavior - You need paired preference data: each example is a (prompt, chosen, rejected) triple. `HuggingFaceH4/ultrafeedback_binarized` is the standard starting dataset; for domain-specific use, generate pairs from your SFT outputs using Claude as the judge
**When DPO beats more SFT**
SFT teaches the model _what_ to say. If your SFT outputs are factually correct but awkwardly phrased, inconsistently structured, or prone to unnecessary hedging, more SFT on the same data doesn't fix that — it reinforces the same distribution. DPO teaches the model _which_ of two answers is better, so the preference can be orthogonal to factual correctness: same domain knowledge, better style.
**The training pattern (Unsloth + TRL)**
```python from unsloth import FastLanguageModel from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig from datasets import load_dataset
# Load your SFT checkpoint — Unsloth reuses it as both target and reference model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="your-username/your-sft-checkpoint", max_seq_length=4096, load_in_4bit=True, ) model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=64, lora_alpha=64, target_modules=["q_proj","v_proj","k_proj","o_proj"], use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", )
# Standard preference dataset: each row has prompt, chosen, rejected dataset = load_dataset( "HuggingFaceH4/ultrafeedback_binarized", split="train_prefs" )
training_args = DPOConfig( beta=0.1, # < 0.3 stays close to SFT behavior max_length=2048, max_prompt_length=512, per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=8, warmup_ratio=0.1, num_train_epochs=1, output_dir="dpo-output", )
trainer = DPOTrainer( model=model, ref_model=None, # Unsloth reuses the base as reference automatically args=training_args, train_dataset=dataset, tokenizer=tokenizer, ) trainer.train() model.push_to_hub("your-username/your-dpo-model") ```
**Limits to plan around**
- Generating quality preference pairs is harder than collecting raw demonstrations for SFT. Fewer than ~1,000 pairs often overfit to surface patterns rather than genuine quality differences. - `beta` above 0.5 can destabilize training against the reference. Evaluate against your SFT baseline before declaring improvement — DPO can degrade factual recall while improving style. - ORPO (Odds Ratio Preference Optimization) merges SFT and preference training into a single pass — Unsloth's docs cover it and it is worth trying if you are starting from a base model rather than an existing SFT checkpoint. - Preference datasets created by one judge (human or LLM) encode that judge's biases. A dataset judged by one LLM tends to prefer that LLM's own output style.
**Sources:** [Unsloth DPO, ORPO & KTO guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide/preference-dpo-orpo-and-kto) · [TRL DPOTrainer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/main/en/dpo_trainer) · [HuggingFaceH4/ultrafeedback_binarized](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceH4/ultrafeedback_binarized) · [Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model" (arXiv 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)

item.title: Your Claude Managed Agent Starts Every Session With No Memory of the Last One — Attach a Memory Store and User Context Persists as Files Under /mnt/memory/
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Attach a workspace-scoped memory store to any Managed Agents session and the agent reads and writes persistent user context as plain text files under /mnt/memory/ — preferences and prior decisions survive session restarts.
item.content:encoded:
**Attach a workspace-scoped memory store to a Managed Agents session and the agent reads and writes persistent context as plain Markdown files under `/mnt/memory/` — no separate database, no extra API calls.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** give any Claude Managed Agent a persistent workspace so it carries user preferences, prior decisions, and learned context across sessions.
- Create a durable memory store once; attach it to any number of future sessions - The agent reads and writes plain text files under `/mnt/memory/` using its existing bash and file tools - Control access per session (`read_write` or `read_only`) to prevent one agent from overwriting shared context
**Why agents forget**
Each Claude Managed Agents session starts with a fresh context by default. That is correct for stateless tasks but costly for agents doing repeated user-facing work — writing help, code review, planning — where the same context gets re-asked every session. A memory store is a filesystem volume that survives session endings and mounts automatically into the next session that attaches it.
**Create a store and attach it (Python SDK)**
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
# One-time setup per user or workspace store = client.beta.memory_stores.create( name="user-context", description="User preferences and prior session decisions. Read before responding.", )
# Attach when creating a session session = client.beta.sessions.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", beta=["managed-agents-2026-04-01"], system=( "You are a helpful assistant. Before your first response, " "check /mnt/memory/ for existing user context. " "Update relevant files at the end of each session." ), resources=[{ "type": "memory_store", "id": store.id, "access": "read_write" }] ) ```
The store mounts at `/mnt/memory/`. The agent reads and writes files there with its existing bash tools — `cat /mnt/memory/preferences.md`, `echo "..." >> /mnt/memory/decisions.md` — and those changes are there the next time you create a session using the same `store.id`.
**What to store**
Small Markdown files, one concern per file: `preferences.md`, `decisions.md`, `project-context.md`. Each file is capped at 100 KB (~25K tokens). Writes are automatically versioned, but only the latest version mounts — there is no built-in diffing between versions.
**Limits to build around**
- **Beta API**: every request requires the `managed-agents-2026-04-01` beta header; the Python and JS SDKs set it automatically. The API may change before GA. - **Prompt injection on shared stores**: a `read_write` store attached across users lets one user's input overwrite context for others. For multi-user agents, give each user a separate store, or attach shared reference stores as `read_only` and update them from application code rather than from agent tool calls. - **Workspace scope**: stores belong to the workspace, not to a user by default — a session in the same workspace can read the same store. Plan naming and access before connecting to production agents. - **No published throughput benchmarks**: each file read adds a round trip. Test at your expected concurrency before choosing memory-store reads over passing small state directly in the system prompt.
**Sources:** [Using agent memory — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory) · [Cookbook: Managed Agents that remember user preferences — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/managed-agents-cma-remember-user-preferences) · ["Agents that remember" (Code with Claude London 2026) — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=geUv4CjPpxI) · [Community walkthrough — dev.to/raxxostudios](https://dev.to/raxxostudios/claude-managed-agents-now-have-filesystem-memory-ak9)

item.title: Your First Claude Code Cloud Session Installs Dependencies From Scratch — Auto-Setup Detects What the Repo Needs, Snapshots the Disk, and Reuses That For Every Run After
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Since November 6, Claude Code cloud sessions on Pro/Max/Ultra can auto-detect a repository's dependencies and environment requirements, configure the setup script, and snapshot the result for reuse.
item.content:encoded:
**Since November 6, Claude Code cloud sessions on Pro, Max, and Ultra plans auto-detect what a repository needs, configure the environment, and snapshot the disk so every run after the first starts from a ready state.**
Previously, running a non-trivial project in a cloud session meant writing a setup script by hand: install system packages, declare external hosts, inject API keys. Now Claude inspects the repository first, drafts the setup configuration from what it finds, and runs it. When setup completes in roughly five minutes, Anthropic snapshots the filesystem — subsequent sessions start from that snapshot rather than reinstalling.
**What the snapshot preserves:** - Files written to disk during setup (installed binaries, compiled deps, downloaded models) - Environment variables injected via the environment panel
**What it does not preserve:** - Running processes (dev server, database, language runtime) — these restart each session - In-memory state
**What still needs manual configuration:** - External hosts your repo doesn't declare (private registries, internal APIs) - Secrets managed via OIDC or vault outside Claude's reach - System packages installed in a Dockerfile not visible in project config files
**Snapshot lifecycle:** the snapshot is rebuilt when you edit the setup script, change the allowed-hosts list, or after roughly seven days. Force a rebuild after any change that affects snapshottable state.
**Practical pattern:** put heavy system installs (apt packages, build tools, large model downloads) in the setup script so they land in the snapshot. Put project-level steps (`npm install`, `pip install -r requirements.txt`) in a `SessionStart` hook — that way they run identically in both local and cloud sessions and don't depend on the snapshot.
**Limits:** auto-setup is on Pro, Max, and Ultra plans only. Team plan users can still write the setup script manually using the same interface. The auto-generated script is an editable draft, not a black box — you can review and adjust it before saving.
**Sources:** [Configure cloud environments — Claude Code Docs (official)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments) · [Claude Code cloud sessions field guide — claude.dev](https://claude.dev/blog/claude-code-in-the-cloud/) · [Claude Code cloud auto-setup announcement coverage — pasqualepillitteri.it](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/en/news/30706/claude-code-cloud-automatic-setup-dependencies-api-keys)

item.title: Your Dense Retriever Returns the Wrong Chunks When Users Ask Short Questions — HyDE Generates a Hypothetical Answer First and Embeds That Instead
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) fixes vocabulary mismatch in dense retrieval: embed a generated hypothetical answer rather than the raw query so the vector lands closer to relevant chunks.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** convert a dense-retrieval pipeline that struggles with short or ambiguous queries into one that embeds a generated hypothetical answer, narrowing the vocabulary gap between user intent and document phrasing.**
Dense retrieval works well when the query uses the same language as the documents. When users ask "how do I fix this error?" but your docs say "workaround for issue #4231", cosine similarity finds wrong chunks — not because the embedding model is weak, but because the styles don't match.
HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings, Gao et al., [arXiv:2212.10496](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496)) flips the direction: instead of embedding the question, you prompt an LLM to write a fake answer, then embed that. The fake answer uses document-style language even when the query does not, so it lands closer to the right chunks in vector space. The fake document itself is discarded — only its embedding is used.
**Three-bullet takeaway:** - Real documents are embedded normally at index time; at query time the LLM writes a hypothetical answer and that gets embedded instead of the raw query. - Gains are largest when queries are short and informal but documents are long and formal (API docs, support tickets, legal text). Elastic Search Labs reported a 50% precision improvement on short-query retrieval in Elasticsearch. - **Limit:** adds one LLM call per retrieval — budget for the latency and cost. The generated text can also mislead if the LLM writes a confident but wrong hypothetical. For simple keyword lookups, the overhead is rarely worth it.
**LangChain implementation:**
```python from langchain.chains import HypotheticalDocumentEmbedder from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings, ChatOpenAI from langchain_chroma import Chroma
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini") base_embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings()
# "web_search" is a built-in prompt that tells the LLM # to write a paragraph a search result might look like. # Other prompt keys: "python_repl", "science", "fiqa", etc. hyde_embedder = HypotheticalDocumentEmbedder.from_llm( llm, base_embeddings, "web_search" )
# Use it wherever you'd pass a standard Embeddings object vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(docs, embedding=hyde_embedder) retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 4})
# At query time, the embedder generates a hypothetical answer # and embeds that instead of the raw query string docs = retriever.invoke("how do I fix authentication errors?") ```
The `HypotheticalDocumentEmbedder` wraps any LangChain `Embeddings` object. At index time it embeds real documents normally; at query time it generates a hypothetical answer, embeds that, and runs the similarity search.
**Check your import path:** in LangChain v0.3+, `HypotheticalDocumentEmbedder` lives in `langchain.chains.hyde.base`. Older tutorials may use a different path — verify against the [API reference](https://python.langchain.com/api_reference/_modules/langchain/chains/hyde/base.html) for your installed version.
**Sources:** [LangChain HyDE template docs](https://python.langchain.com/docs/templates/hyde) · [Elastic Search Labs: HyDE in Elasticsearch — 50% precision improvement on short queries](https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/hyde-semantic-search-elasticsearch) · [Original paper — Gao et al. arXiv:2212.10496](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Auto-Compacts Mid-Task at 95% Context — Run /compact Yourself at a Natural Break to Control What Gets Summarized Away
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: /compact summarizes your session and resets the context window; path-scoped CLAUDE.md rules disappear in the summary unless you anchor them in the project root or add a Compact Instructions section.
item.content:encoded:
**`/compact` summarizes your Claude Code session and resets the context window — path-scoped `CLAUDE.md` rules disappear in that summary unless you've anchored them in the project root.**
When a Claude Code session runs long — multiple file edits, repeated test runs, large tool outputs — the context fills toward its 200k-token ceiling. Auto-compaction fires automatically at 95% and summarizes the conversation. The problem: it fires mid-task when you least want the interruption, and the summary may drop early instructions you never saved to a file.
The fix: run `/compact` yourself at a natural break between subtasks.
**What survives compaction:** - The project-root `CLAUDE.md` and any unscoped rules — re-injected from disk after compaction - Your explicit task description and the most recent code snippets - Up to five recently modified files Claude touched in the session
**What gets summarized away:** - Path-scoped `CLAUDE.md` rules (anything using `paths:` frontmatter). If a rule must persist across compaction, move it to the root `CLAUDE.md` or drop the `paths:` restriction. - Detailed instructions from early in the session that weren't saved to a file.
**Steer the summary with a `Compact Instructions` section:** ```markdown ## Compact Instructions When compacting, preserve: the current task goal, any architecture decisions made this session, and the list of files already edited. ```
**Pick the right command:** - `/compact` — continuing the same task, need breathing room - `/clear` — starting a genuinely new task in the same repo - `/rewind <N>` — went down the wrong path, undo N turns
**Limit:** compacting a large session is itself a large request and costs proportionally. After a long idle break the prompt cache expires, so the compaction itself is expensive. Compact before stepping away rather than after coming back.
**Sources:** [Explore the context window — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window) · [Claude Code commands reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands) · [Claude Code context management — bestagent.dev](https://bestagent.dev/claude-code-context-management-2026/)

item.title: Your Fine-Tuned Model Is on the Hub but Calling It Means Spinning Up vLLM — Hugging Face Inference Endpoints Deploys a Managed Production API in Four Lines
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Hugging Face Inference Endpoints deploys any Hub model to a private production API backed by vLLM without managing Docker, GPU drivers, or autoscaling yourself.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** deploy any Hugging Face Hub model — including your own fine-tuned adapters — to a private HTTPS production endpoint backed by vLLM, without managing servers.
You fine-tuned a Llama adapter, pushed it to the Hub, and now you need an API. The usual next step is spinning up vLLM on a VM, writing a Dockerfile, managing GPU memory, and handling autoscaling. Inference Endpoints skips all of that.
**Three takeaways before you start:** - **vLLM is the standard engine** for chat/instruction models. The platform also supports SGLang and llama.cpp — select the one that matches your architecture. - **Private by default:** every request requires a Hugging Face token as `Authorization: Bearer`, TLS in transit. Set `type: "public"` only if you need unauthenticated access. - **Dedicated endpoints bill per hour from creation**, not per request. The Serverless Inference API is for prototyping only.
**Deploy via the Python SDK:** ```python from huggingface_hub import create_inference_endpoint
endpoint = create_inference_endpoint( "my-llama-endpoint", repository="your-username/your-fine-tuned-model", framework="pytorch", task="text-generation", accelerator="gpu", vendor="aws", region="us-east-1", instance_type="nvidia-a10g", instance_size="x1", min_replica=0, # scale to zero when idle max_replica=1, ) endpoint.wait() # blocks until RUNNING print(endpoint.url) ```
Then call it like any OpenAI-compatible endpoint: ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url=endpoint.url + "/v1", api_key="hf_…") resp = client.chat.completions.create(model="tgi", messages=[…]) ```
**UI route:** open your model on Hub, click **Deploy → Inference Endpoints**, pick hardware, click **Create**. Faster for one-offs; use the SDK for anything you want to reproduce or tear down in CI.
**Limit:** `min_replica=0` eliminates idle cost but the first request after scale-down takes ~30 seconds to cold-start. If first-hit latency matters, set `min_replica=1` and accept the per-hour cost (~$1/hr on an A10G). A forgotten endpoint at that rate adds up: set billing alerts.

item.title: Your SFT Fine-Tune Gives Generic Answers Because the Model Never Learned Your Domain — Continual Pre-Training on Raw Text First Changes That
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run Unsloth's CPT Text Completion notebook to adapt a base model to your domain on raw text before instruction fine-tuning — no labels needed, just documents.
item.content:encoded:
**Before fine-tuning on Q&A pairs, adapt the base model's weights to your domain with CPT — Unsloth's Text Completion notebook handles it in one Colab run on raw text, no labels needed.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Run a continual pre-training (CPT) pass that teaches a base model your domain's vocabulary, writing patterns, and facts, so subsequent instruction fine-tuning starts from genuine domain knowledge rather than patching over ignorance.
- **CPT keeps the original next-token prediction objective** — you feed raw documents (legal filings, codebase, medical notes); every token becomes a training target; no instruction format needed - **For CPT, full fine-tuning outperforms LoRA** — Unsloth's team reports that LoRA adapters underperform full-weight training on CPT tasks, the opposite of the typical SFT recommendation - **The right sequence:** CPT on raw domain text → SFT on instruction pairs → optional DPO/ORPO for alignment
**Walk-through (Unsloth Text Completion Colab):**
1. Install: `pip install unsloth` 2. Open [Unsloth's CPT blog and notebook links](https://unsloth.ai/blog/contpretraining) 3. Load a **base model** (not a chat model) with `FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained` 4. Format your corpus as `{"text": "raw document text"}` — no system prompt, no alpaca template 5. Use `DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(mlm=False)` for the standard CLM objective (train on all tokens) 6. Train with the full model weights — `use_gradient_checkpointing=True` to stay within VRAM 7. Save the CPT checkpoint, then run a normal SFT instruction-tuning pass on top
**Where this costs you:** Full fine-tuning at the CPT step — not LoRA — requires significantly more VRAM. Unsloth's Mistral 7B example needs at least 24 GB for 4-bit, more for 16-bit. Free Colab T4 (16 GB) limits you to smaller models or quantized CPT, which Unsloth flags as lower quality than full CPT. LoRA CPT is still better than skipping CPT entirely when VRAM is constrained.
**Sources:** [Unsloth CPT blog + notebooks](https://unsloth.ai/blog/contpretraining) · [Unsloth CPT docs](https://docs.unsloth.ai/basics/continued-pretraining) · [Continuing Pre-Training on Raw Text — Chris McCormick ML](https://mccormickml.com/2025/01/18/continuing-pre-training-on-raw-text/)
