item.title: Your CLAUDE.md Has Instructions Written for a Model You No Longer Use — `/claude-api prompt-audit` Finds and Removes Them
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run /claude-api prompt-audit in Claude Code to scan your CLAUDE.md, skills, and tool descriptions for instructions written for older models that hurt performance or waste tokens on current ones.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `/claude-api prompt-audit` to scan your project's CLAUDE.md, skill files, and tool descriptions for instructions written for older Claude models that confuse or bloat context on current ones.**
Claude's models change how they interpret instructions. Patterns that helped older models — explicit "think step by step" nudges, repeated capability reminders, verbose tool description padding, model-name-specific hedging — can confuse or waste context on Fable 5.2 and Sonnet 5.5. The `claude-api` skill includes a `prompt-audit` subcommand that scans your project for these.
**What it checks:** Your CLAUDE.md, any `.claude/skills/` files, tool descriptions in application code, and agent harness prompts. It identifies patterns from older Claude generations that the current release handles better without guidance — or handles worse with it.
**Run it:**
``` /claude-api prompt-audit ```
No arguments audits the working directory. Target a specific file:
``` /claude-api prompt-audit ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md ```
**Output:** Reports findings by file and line, with proposed rewrites. It never modifies files automatically — you review and accept each change.
**What practitioners report:** Teams running the audit on established projects find legacy "you are an X assistant" framing, model-specific hedging ("as Claude 3.5 Sonnet, you..."), and tool descriptions that over-explain what the model already infers. Removing those patterns tightened context. Anthropic's own write-up reports a 9% additional cost reduction on top of caching improvements — that's their measurement on their workload; your results will differ based on how much cruft has accumulated.
**Where it falls short:** The command checks prompts, skills, and inline API calls, but won't catch model-specific assumptions baked into UI text, test fixtures, or hardcoded few-shot examples elsewhere in a codebase. Those need manual review.
**Sources:** [Reducing cost and improving performance — claude.com](https://claude.com/resources/articles/reducing-cost-and-improving-performance-with-claude-platform) · [We audited our Claude Code setup — DEV Community](https://dev.to/pponali/we-audited-our-claude-code-setup-against-anthropics-own-context-engineering-rules-heres-what-we-3mme) · [CLAUDE.md anti-patterns — jwatte.com](https://jwatte.com/blog/claude-md-anti-patterns/) · [How to audit CLAUDE.md for newer models — Aident AI](https://aident.ai/blog/audit-claude-md-for-newer-models)

item.title: Your FAISS Index Lives in RAM and Disappears at Process Exit — ChromaDB's `PersistentClient` Survives Restarts and Grows Without Reloading All Documents
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db") stores your vector collection to SQLite on disk; add documents across runs, query them, and migrate to a server without changing your collection code.
item.content:encoded:
**`chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")` stores your vector collection to SQLite on disk — add documents incrementally across script runs and migrate to a production server without touching your query code.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** persist a vector store between runs, add documents incrementally without reloading all embeddings, and move from local dev to a hosted Chroma server when you outgrow single-process storage.
**Three takeaways:** - Use `EphemeralClient()` for in-memory test fixtures, `PersistentClient(path=...)` for anything that needs to survive a restart - Use `get_or_create_collection()` instead of `create_collection()` — it's idempotent and safe to call on every run - Production migration is one line: swap `PersistentClient(...)` for `HttpClient(host=..., port=8000)` — your collection name, add, and query code stay the same
**Walk-through:**
```bash pip install chromadb sentence-transformers ```
```python import chromadb from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions
ef = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction( model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2" )
# Local SQLite persistence — data survives process exit client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db")
# Idempotent — safe to call each run collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="docs", embedding_function=ef)
# add() skips duplicate IDs; use upsert() to overwrite collection.add( documents=["Chroma stores vectors in SQLite on disk."], ids=["doc-1"] )
results = collection.query(query_texts=["local vector storage"], n_results=1) print(results["documents"]) ```
**Production migration:** When you need concurrent access or remote storage, run `chroma run --path ./chroma_db` to start the Chroma server, then swap the client:
```python client = chromadb.HttpClient(host="localhost", port=8000) # collection.add() and collection.query() code unchanged ```
**Gotcha — SQLite version:** Chroma requires SQLite ≥ 3.35. If you hit a `RuntimeError` about SQLite, run `python -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)"`. Python 3.11 ships a newer SQLite than 3.9 on most Linux distros; upgrading Python is usually the fix. Alternatively, `pip install pysqlite3-binary` overrides the system version.
**Where FAISS still wins:** FAISS is faster for large-scale ANN search and doesn't need a separate process for multi-writer concurrency. Use Chroma when you want metadata filtering, incremental adds, or the HTTP server handoff — it trades raw ANN throughput for a more usable operational model.
**Sources:** [ChromaDB docs — Getting Started](https://docs.trychroma.com/getting-started) · [DataCamp ChromaDB step-by-step tutorial](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/chromadb-tutorial-step-by-step-guide) · [Local RAG with ChromaDB + Ollama — BestLLMFor](https://bestllmfor.com/guide/rag-chromadb-ollama-python/)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Hangs Forever When an Unattended Agent Hits a Permission Prompt — `denyInsteadOfPrompting` Makes It Fail Fast Instead
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Set "denyInsteadOfPrompting": true under permissions in .claude/settings.json to convert any unapproved tool call into an immediate denial rather than an indefinite hang during unattended or CI runs.
item.content:encoded:
**Set `"denyInsteadOfPrompting": true` under `permissions` in `.claude/settings.json` to convert any unapproved tool call into an immediate denial rather than an indefinite hang during unattended or CI runs.**
By default, when Claude Code hits a tool call it hasn't been given explicit permission for, it pauses and waits for you to approve or deny it. In an interactive session that's correct. In a background agent, a subagent, or a CI step — it means the process hangs indefinitely, often for hours, until someone notices the terminal.
`permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting`, added in v2.1.319, converts that pause into a fast failure: the call is denied immediately, the turn continues with an error result visible to Claude, and the agent can either recover or report cleanly.
**Configuration:**
```json // .claude/settings.json (project-level) or ~/.claude/settings.json (user-level) { "permissions": { "denyInsteadOfPrompting": true, "allow": [ "Bash(npm test:*)", "Bash(git status:*)", "Read(**)" ] } } ```
Explicit `allow` rules are unaffected — those calls still execute without prompting or denial. Only calls that *would have asked* get denied instead.
**Side effects to plan for:**
- The `/ask` tool is unavailable with this setting on. Claude cannot pause to request confirmation; it must commit to a direction or report that it cannot proceed. - MCP elicitation requests are cancelled automatically, unless you have an `Elicitation` hook that answers them programmatically.
**When to use it:** Any unattended agent that must fail fast rather than hang: CI validation runs, scheduled agents, backend automation triggered by webhooks. It also surfaces permission gaps quickly during development — run your agent once against a new task, watch what it tries to do, and add allow rules for the legitimate calls.
**Limits:** The setting does not change which calls require approval — it only changes the response when approval is missing. Explicit allow rules always take precedence; this setting only fires when no matching allow or deny rule applies.
**Sources:** [SmartScope: denyInsteadOfPrompting (v2.1.319)](https://smartscope.blog/en/blog/claude-code-automatic-permission-prompt-denial-denyinsteadofprompting-v2-2026/) · [DevelopersDigest: Deny Instead of Prompting](https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/claude-code-deny-instead-of-prompting-2026) · [AgentPatterns: Deny-Fallback Permissions for Unattended Agents](https://agentpatterns.ai/patterns/agent-design/deny-fallback-unattended-permissions/)

item.title: Your Manual Tool Loop Calls the API, Checks stop_reason, Builds the Next Message, and Repeats — `client.beta.messages.tool_runner` Does That With a `for` Loop and Two Decorators
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Annotate your Python functions with @beta_tool, pass them to client.beta.messages.tool_runner(), and iterate — the SDK handles the call/result loop automatically, without manual message assembly.
item.content:encoded:
**Annotate your Python functions with `@beta_tool`, pass them to `client.beta.messages.tool_runner()`, and iterate — the SDK calls the API, invokes matching tools, and feeds results back automatically.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Build a multi-step tool-using agent (search → fetch → compute → format) without writing the message-assembly loop yourself.
A manual tool-calling loop requires: call the API, check `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, extract each `tool_use` block by id, call the matching function, build a `tool_result` content block with the right structure, append it to the messages list, repeat until `stop_reason == "end_turn"`. That's roughly 30 lines of message-assembly bookkeeping before your first real function does anything useful.
The Anthropic Python SDK's `ToolRunner` (currently in beta) wraps that loop:
```python from anthropic import Anthropic from anthropic.lib.tools import beta_tool
client = Anthropic()
@beta_tool def get_weather(location: str, unit: str = "celsius") -> str: """Get the current weather for a location.""" return f"22°C in {location}" # your real implementation
@beta_tool def convert_currency(amount: float, from_currency: str, to_currency: str) -> str: """Convert an amount between currencies.""" return f"{amount * 1.08} {to_currency}" # your real implementation
runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", tools=[get_weather, convert_currency], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris and 100 USD in euros?"}], )
# Iterate through all turns (including tool call/result turns): for message in runner: pass
# Or skip intermediate turns and get the final message directly: final = runner.until_done() print(final.content[0].text) ```
`@beta_tool` builds the JSON schema automatically from Python type hints and the function's docstring — no manual `{"name": ..., "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {...}}}` block required.
**Limits:**
- The tool runner is in beta (`client.beta`), so the interface may change before it graduates to stable. - It does not support human-in-the-loop approval inside the loop. If you need a "confirm this action?" step before an action runs, use the manual loop instead. - Async is supported: use `async for` on the async client's `tool_runner`. - The SDK does not handle client-side context compaction for long runs — trim your messages manually if the context grows large.
**Sources:** [Tool Runner (SDK) — Anthropic Docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-runner) · [tools_runner.py SDK example](https://sources.debian.org/src/anthropic-sdk-python/0.76.0-1/examples/tools_runner.py)

item.title: Your Anthropic API Calls Block Until the Full Response Arrives — `client.messages.stream()` Gives You Token-by-Token Text for Any Streaming UI
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Replace client.messages.create() with the client.messages.stream() context manager and iterate stream.text_stream — tokens arrive as they generate instead of blocking on the full response, so a FastAPI SSE endpoint can forward each token to the browser immediately.
item.content:encoded:
**What changes:** replace `client.messages.create()` with the `client.messages.stream()` context manager, then iterate `stream.text_stream` — tokens arrive as they generate instead of blocking on the full response.
```python import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
# Blocking — waits for the full response message = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain vector search."}] ) print(message.content[0].text)
# Streaming — tokens arrive as they generate with client.messages.stream( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain vector search."}] ) as stream: for text in stream.text_stream: print(text, end="", flush=True) final = stream.get_final_message() # full Message object with usage counts ```
The context manager handles connection lifecycle. `stream.get_final_message()` returns the complete `Message` object with `usage.input_tokens` and `usage.output_tokens`, so you still have token counts after streaming.
## Wire it to a FastAPI SSE endpoint
```python from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse import anthropic
app = FastAPI() client = anthropic.Anthropic()
@app.get("/chat") def chat(prompt: str): def token_stream(): with client.messages.stream( model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] ) as stream: for text in stream.text_stream: yield f"data: {text}\n\n" yield "data: [DONE]\n\n" return StreamingResponse(token_stream(), media_type="text/event-stream") ```
The browser side reads via `EventSource` or a `fetch` reader loop against `/chat?prompt=...`.
## Limits
- **NGINX / load balancer timeouts**: the default read timeout is 60 s. A slow generation on large `max_tokens` can still time out upstream. Set `proxy_read_timeout 300s;` or equivalent on any reverse proxy between your app and the client. - **Cloudflare Workers free tier**: the CPU time limit is 10 ms per request; holding a Worker context open for a streaming response does not work on the free tier. Use Cloudflare's `fetch()` with `ReadableStream` instead of a blocking SDK loop inside a Worker. - **Cloudflare Workers paid (Unbound)**: the wall-clock limit is 30 s for a Workers-to-origin request. If your LLM call streams beyond 30 s, the client gets a truncated response with no error. Stream shorter outputs or proxy through a Durable Object. - **`get_final_message()` placement**: call it outside the `with` block after iteration finishes, not inside it. Inside the block it blocks until all tokens arrive, defeating the purpose of streaming in a generator context.
**Sources:** [Anthropic streaming docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/build-with-claude/streaming) · [Python SDK source (Debian sources mirror)](https://sources.debian.org/src/python-anthropic/) · [Streaming responses with Claude API in Python (dev.to, 2026)](https://dev.to/kalyna_pro/streaming-responses-with-claude-api-in-python-2026-44la)

item.title: Your Inference Code Calls Three Different SDKs for Three Different Providers — Cloudflare Workers AI's OpenAI-Compatible Endpoint Cuts That to One SDK
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Cloudflare Workers AI exposes an OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint: point the openai Python SDK at api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{id}/ai/v1 with a Workers AI token and call Llama 3.3, Mistral, Gemma, and others with the same code that calls OpenAI GPT.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** call Llama 3.3, Mistral, Gemma, and other models on Cloudflare Workers AI using the standard `openai` Python SDK — the same code that calls OpenAI GPT works against Workers AI by changing three lines.
- Use one SDK for every inference provider instead of maintaining separate `anthropic`, `openai`, and `google.generativeai` import paths - Run inference from Python scripts against Workers AI's hosted fleet without opening a provider account for each model - Stream tokens the same way you already do with the OpenAI client
## Setup
```bash pip install openai ```
```python import os from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI( api_key=os.environ["CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN"], base_url=( f"https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/" f"{os.environ['CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID']}/ai/v1" ) )
response = client.chat.completions.create( model="@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain HNSW indexing in three sentences."}] ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) ```
`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` = an API token with the **Workers AI Read** permission (not your Global API key). `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` appears in the Cloudflare dashboard URL bar.
## Streaming
```python stream = client.chat.completions.create( model="@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain HNSW indexing."}], stream=True, ) for chunk in stream: delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content if delta: print(delta, end="", flush=True) ```
## Available models
Browse the full catalog at [developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/). Common picks:
| Model | Workers AI name | |---|---| | Llama 3.3 70B (fast) | `@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast` | | Mistral 7B Instruct | `@cf/mistral/mistral-7b-instruct-v0.2-lora` | | Gemma 7B | `@cf/google/gemma-7b-it` | | Qwen 2.5 Coder 15B | `@cf/qwen/qwen2.5-coder-15b-instruct` |
## Limits
- **Free tier — neurons**: Workers AI free tier gives 10,000 neurons/day. The 70B model costs roughly 7–10 neurons per output token, so ~1,000–1,400 output tokens before hitting the daily cap. The 7B–8B models cost fewer neurons per token. Neuron cost is listed on each model's page in the catalog. - **Latency**: Workers AI runs inference at Cloudflare's edge. From a standalone Python script on your laptop, that is an extra round-trip compared to calling the model's native API. The endpoint is fastest when your code runs inside a Cloudflare Worker, colocated with the inference fleet. - **Model availability**: not every model in the catalog is available in every region at every time — a 503 from the endpoint means the model is at capacity. Build retry logic for production use. - **OpenAI API surface parity**: Workers AI implements `chat/completions` and embeddings. It does not implement function calling, fine-tuning, files, or assistants — if your code uses those OpenAI features, it will not work against this endpoint.
**Sources:** [Workers AI OpenAI compatibility docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/configuration/open-ai-compatibility/) · [Workers AI model catalog](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/) · [Cloudflare Workers AI tutorial (mecanik.dev)](https://mecanik.dev/en/posts/cloudflare-workers-ai-tutorial/) · [Workers AI with Agno (agno.com docs)](https://docs.agno.com/examples/models/cloudflare/basic)

item.title: Your Anthropic SDK Calls Run in a Black Box — `AnthropicInstrumentor` Puts Every Generation, Token Count, and Latency Into a Trace You Can Inspect
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: AnthropicInstrumentor() from opentelemetry-instrumentation-anthropic captures every Claude API call automatically; @observe groups multi-step functions into a single trace tree in Langfuse without changing any business logic.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** instrument your Python app so every Claude API call appears as a trace with its full prompt, response, token counts, and latency — without touching your existing API call code.
- See input/output for every generation, plus model name and token usage, in a shareable trace UI - Group multi-step functions into a single trace tree so a failure tells you exactly which call caused it - Filter traces by user ID or session ID to debug production issues for specific users
## Setup
```bash pip install langfuse opentelemetry-instrumentation-anthropic ```
Configure Langfuse and call `instrument()` once before any API call:
```python import os os.environ["LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY"] = "pk-lf-..." os.environ["LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY"] = "sk-lf-..." os.environ["LANGFUSE_HOST"] = "https://cloud.langfuse.com" # or self-hosted
from langfuse import observe, get_client from opentelemetry.instrumentation.anthropic import AnthropicInstrumentor import anthropic
AnthropicInstrumentor().instrument() # one line, all SDK calls now traced client = anthropic.Anthropic() ```
Every `client.messages.create(...)` call from this point is automatically captured as a **generation** span — model, prompt, response, tokens, latency. No changes to your existing API calls.
## Group calls with `@observe`
```python @observe() def handle_support_ticket(ticket: str) -> dict: category = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=64, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"One-word category: {ticket}"}] ).content[0].text
reply = client.messages.create( model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=256, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Draft reply for a {category} issue: {ticket}"}] ).content[0].text
return {"category": category, "reply": reply} ```
Each `handle_support_ticket()` call appears as one trace in Langfuse containing two nested generations. Nested `@observe`-decorated functions are linked automatically — no manual span management.
## Limits
- **SDK version:** Langfuse v3 Python SDK requires a Langfuse server at v4.59.0+ for self-hosting. If your instance is older, stay on the v2 SDK (`from langfuse.decorators import observe`). - **Short-lived scripts:** Traces are sent asynchronously. Add `get_client().flush()` at the end of scripts that exit immediately or the last trace can be dropped. - **Self-hosting:** The Docker Compose stack is documented at langfuse.com/self-hosting. Cloud-hosted Langfuse rate-limits high-volume trace ingestion — for production workloads generating thousands of traces per minute, plan for self-hosting. - **Anthropic SDK auto-instrumentation caveat:** `AnthropicInstrumentor` captures generations correctly for `messages.create`. Streaming responses and tool use blocks may have partial capture depending on the instrumentation package version — test your specific call patterns before relying on completeness.

item.title: Your Claude Code "Yes, Don't Ask Again" Saves the Full Shell Command — Including Any Password or API Key Inline in It
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Choosing "Yes, don't ask again" stores the full shell command as a plaintext allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json. If the command contained a credential, the credential is now in that file. Apiiro found 1,122+ public repos with exposed secrets.
item.content:encoded:
**Choosing "Yes, don't ask again" stores the full shell command — including any inline credential — in `.claude/settings.local.json`. Apiiro found 1,122+ public repos with exposed secrets.**
When Claude Code asks permission to run a shell command and you pick "Yes, and don't ask again," it records the exact command string as an allow rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`. Commands like `PGPASSWORD=s3cr3t psql -U app prod` or `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" ...` where `$TOKEN` was expanded before you ran it get stored verbatim.
## Why the existing protection isn't enough
Claude Code adds `.claude/settings.local.json` to your global git excludes (usually `~/.gitignore_global`). That protects the developer's current machine — but global git excludes do not travel with the repository. A collaborator who clones on a different machine has no protection, and the file can be committed and pushed. In many of the 1,122 cases Apiiro found, Claude Code itself was listed as the commit co-author.
Secrets remain in git history and in every clone and fork even after the file is deleted.
## Three things to do now
**1. Add it to your project's `.gitignore`:**
``` # .gitignore .claude/settings.local.json ```
This protects all collaborators, not just the original developer. The committed `.claude/settings.json` (team-shared allow rules) is fine; it's the `.local` variant that shouldn't travel.
**2. Never inline credentials in a "don't ask again" command.** Use environment variables that Claude Code can reference rather than values:
```bash # Fine — the allow rule records the reference, not the secret PGPASSWORD="$DB_PASS" psql -U app prod
# Dangerous — the allow rule stores the literal string PGPASSWORD=s3cr3t psql -U app prod ```
**3. Audit your existing history.** Check whether the file was ever committed:
```bash git log --all --oneline -- .claude/settings.local.json ```
If it shows up, rotate every credential that appeared in an allow rule there. Deleting the file from HEAD is not enough — secrets stay in git history, forks, and clones.
**One limit:** Pre-commit secret scanners that check for known key formats (GitHub PAT, AWS keys) may not detect a database password stored inside a shell command string. After adding the file to `.gitignore`, also consider a scanner that flags credential patterns inside any command block.
**Sources:** [Apiiro security report — aviatrix.ai threat research center](https://aviatrix.ai/threat-research-center/claude-code-dont-ask-again-settings-local-json-passwords-keys-1122-github-2026/) · ["Don't ask again" leaks developer secrets — iTnews](https://www.itnews.com.au/news/dont-ask-again-in-anthropics-claude-code-leaks-developer-secrets-630203) · [Claude Code GitHub issue #5544](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/5544)

item.title: Every RAG Tutorial Starts With `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` — Use the MTEB Leaderboard's Retrieval Tab to Find Out If That's Still the Right Call
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The overall MTEB average misleads for RAG — filter to the retrieval tab to compare models on actual retrieval tasks, then test your top candidates on your own data before committing.
item.content:encoded:
**Filter the MTEB leaderboard to the retrieval tab — not the overall average — to compare embedding models on actual RAG recall, then test your top candidates on your own documents.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Navigate the [MTEB leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard) and filter it to the retrieval task instead of the overall average - Identify the trade-off between model size and retrieval score for three common tiers - Run a lightweight A/B comparison against your own documents before committing to a model
---
Most RAG tutorials reach for `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` without explaining why. It was near the top of the leaderboard when the tutorials were written — small, fast, and good enough. MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) is the benchmark that tells you whether it still is for your use case.
MTEB scores hundreds of embedding models across 56 datasets covering retrieval, reranking, clustering, classification, and other tasks. The key rule before reading any ranking: **filter to the retrieval tab, not the overall average**. A model that wins the overall leaderboard can sit mid-pack on retrieval — the overall score folds in classification and clustering tasks that have nothing to do with RAG recall.
## Three common size tiers and what you trade
| Model | Params | Dims | Approximate retrieval score | |---|---|---|---| | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | 22M | 384 | ~56 on BEIR retrieval | | `bge-base-en-v1.5` | 110M | 768 | ~63 on BEIR retrieval | | `bge-large-en-v1.5` | 335M | 1024 | ~65 on BEIR retrieval |
The jump from MiniLM to bge-base is roughly 7 retrieval points at ~5× the embedding time. Whether that matters depends on your query volume and latency budget. Scores above are approximate BEIR averages; check the live leaderboard for current figures.
## A practical selection workflow
**1. Open the leaderboard and filter to task: retrieval.** Sort descending. This gives you a list ranked on the datasets that matter — NQ, HotpotQA, MSMARCO, FEVER, and others from the BEIR benchmark suite.
**2. Flag contamination risk.** Models trained after 2023 may have seen parts of the BEIR datasets. A model card that lists MTEB scores without saying whether the benchmark corpora were excluded from training should be treated with caution. The [premai.io comparison](https://blog.premai.io/best-embedding-models-for-rag-2026-ranked-by-mteb-score-cost-and-self-hosting) calls this out for several 2025–2026 models.
**3. Test on your own corpus.** MTEB tells you how models rank on public datasets. Your documents are different. Per [Zilliz's analysis](https://zilliz.com/blog/choose-embedding-model-rag-2026), the 11th-ranked MTEB model outperformed the top-ranked one on their actual documents. After shortlisting from the leaderboard, embed 200–500 of your own chunks with each candidate and run a small retrieval eval:
```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer import numpy as np
model_a = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5") model_b = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
# Embed your eval queries and chunks, then compare hit@3 or MRR ```
**One limit:** MTEB primarily covers single-language English text retrieval. If your documents are multilingual, switch to the MTEB Multilingual tab — the rankings shift substantially. For code retrieval, check the code retrieval task filter. Neither the English nor multilingual tab reflects performance on structured data, tables, or very long documents.
**Sources:** [MTEB Leaderboard — huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard) · [Best Embedding Models for RAG 2026 — premai.io](https://blog.premai.io/best-embedding-models-for-rag-2026-ranked-by-mteb-score-cost-and-self-hosting) · [How to Choose the Best Embedding Model for RAG — Zilliz](https://zilliz.com/blog/choose-embedding-model-rag-2026) · [Top embedding models on the MTEB leaderboard — Modal](https://modal.com/blog/mteb-leaderboard-article)

item.title: Your `claude -p` Script Gets the Final Answer and Loses Every Tool Call — `--output-format stream-json` Streams Each Event as Parseable NDJSON
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run claude --output-format stream-json and each tool call, result, and final answer arrives as its own JSON line — so CI scripts can inspect every step, not just the last sentence.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `claude -p` with `--output-format stream-json` and every tool call, result, and final answer arrives as its own JSON line (NDJSON) — so CI scripts can inspect what Claude did, not just what it said.**
When you wire `claude -p "..."` into a build pipeline today, you get a text blob: Claude's final answer. If the session made tool calls to gather context — reading files, running searches, checking git history — those steps are invisible. `--output-format stream-json` changes that: each session event streams as a JSON object on its own line as it happens, making the full execution trace parseable.
## The three output modes
| Flag | Use case | |---|---| | (none) or `--output-format text` | Human-readable terminal output — the default | | `--output-format json` | Full session as a single JSON object after completion — includes `total_cost_usd`, tool call history, final result | | `--output-format stream-json` | NDJSON stream: each event appears as it happens. Best for long tasks where `json` mode would time out the CI runner |
## Streaming events in a CI job
```bash # Log each tool call in real time; act on the final result claude -p "Audit all TypeScript files for console.log calls that weren't removed before prod." \ --output-format stream-json \ --allowedTools "Glob,Read,Bash" \ | while IFS= read -r event; do type=$(echo "$event" | jq -r '.type // empty') case "$type" in tool_use) echo "→ $(echo "$event" | jq -r '.name')" ;; result) echo "Session complete" ;; esac done ```
The [headless docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless) define the full event schema; event types you don't recognise are safe to skip — treat them as informational.
## Getting cost and session data from `--output-format json`
```bash # Run a code review and capture cost output=$(claude -p "Review the diff and output JSON only: {\"issues\": [], \"severity\": \"none|low|critical\"}" \ --output-format json \ --allowedTools "Read" < diff.txt)
cost=$(echo "$output" | jq -r '.cost_usd // .total_cost_usd // "unknown"') echo "Review cost: \$cost" ```
The JSON output includes `total_cost_usd` and `session_id` — pass the session ID to `--resume` in a follow-up `claude -p` call to continue the same conversation from a script.
## Practical patterns
- **Cost gate:** Extract `total_cost_usd` from the final JSON object and fail the job if Claude exceeded a per-task budget — useful when you fan out many parallel reviews - **Fail on critical finding:** Ask Claude to output structured JSON with a severity field, parse it with `jq`, and `exit 1` if severity is `critical` - **Audit trail:** Pipe `stream-json` to a log file alongside the CI artifact; every tool call is there if you need to replay what Claude did
**One limit:** `--output-format json` waits for the session to finish before writing anything to stdout. For tasks that might run for minutes, use `stream-json` instead — the CI runner won't time out, and you get progress. Neither mode supports interactive prompts; both require `--print` / `-p` mode.
**Sources:** [Headless mode — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless) · [Claude Code automation and stream-json — The Prompt Shelf](https://thepromptshelf.dev/blog/claude-code-print-mode-stream-json-automation-2026/) · [Headless mode CI/CD guide — SFEIR Institute](https://institute.sfeir.com/en/claude-code/claude-code-headless-mode-and-ci-cd/tutorial/)

item.title: Your Model Gives Generic Answers Even After Fine-Tuning — Three Questions Diagnose Whether the Fix Is RAG or Behavior Training
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: RAG injects knowledge at query time; fine-tuning changes model behavior permanently. Three diagnostic questions tell you which one actually solves your problem.
item.content:encoded:
**RAG injects knowledge at query time; fine-tuning changes model behavior permanently. The most common applied-AI mistake is using fine-tuning to fix a knowledge gap — here's the three-question test that tells them apart.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Diagnose any model output problem as either a knowledge gap (needs RAG) or a behavior gap (needs fine-tuning) in under two minutes, and avoid the most expensive mistake in applied AI: running a fine-tuning job on a problem only retrieval can solve.
**Three takeaways:** 1. Fine-tuning changes *how* the model responds — format, style, tone, reasoning structure. It does not reliably add new facts; it bakes in training signal the model may surface without grounding. 2. RAG changes *what* the model knows at query time. It's debuggable (inspect the retrieved chunks), reversible (remove a document and it's gone), and always current. 3. The two compose: fine-tune once to lock in output format and domain vocabulary, then add RAG to inject changing facts at query time.
## The three diagnostic questions
**1. If you pasted the right information into the prompt, would the model answer correctly?**
Test it in under a minute:
```python import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic()
# Failing without context response = client.messages.create( model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=256, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is our Q3 refund policy for enterprise customers?"}] ) # Probably: "I don't have access to your company's policies..."
# Now paste the relevant document with open("policies/q3-enterprise-refund.md") as f: policy_text = f.read()
response = client.messages.create( model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=256, messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": f"Policy:\n{policy_text}\n\nWhat is the Q3 refund policy for enterprise customers?" }] ) # If this answers correctly: the fix is RAG, not fine-tuning ```
**→ Answers correctly with context → RAG.** The model has the capability; it lacks the information. **→ Still wrong even with context → Fine-tuning candidate.** The model doesn't know *how* to respond, even when given the facts.
**2. Does the information change, or do you need to cite a source?**
A model fine-tuned on last month's docs will confidently cite outdated numbers with no way to tell. Meta's own guidance is explicit: "If the problem requires access to a dynamic corpus of data, fine-tuning may not be the right approach, as the knowledge of the LLM can soon become stale."
→ Changing or citable data → **RAG.**
**3. Is the problem about *how* it responds, not *what* it says?**
- Always outputs a specific JSON schema - Always replies in a particular language or voice - Always reasons through a fixed structure before answering - Consistent domain vocabulary across a narrow task
These are behavior/format changes that a system prompt alone can be inconsistent about at scale.
→ Output format, style, reasoning structure → **Fine-tuning** (try a detailed system prompt with few-shot examples first).
## The practical hybrid
Most production systems end up using both. Fine-tune to lock in output behavior — the JSON schema your API consumers depend on — then add RAG to inject current facts at query time. The fine-tuned model processes retrieved context more reliably because it already knows what shape the answer should take:
```python # Fine-tuned model: always outputs {"answer": "...", "sources": [...]} # RAG: injects the current facts at query time context_chunks = retrieve_top_k(query, vector_store, k=5) response = client.messages.create( model="your-fine-tuned-checkpoint", max_tokens=512, system='You are a support assistant. Output only valid JSON: {"answer": string, "sources": [string]}', messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{chr(10).join(context_chunks)}\n\nQuestion: {query}" }] ) ```
## When fine-tuning genuinely wins alone
- Output format compliance at scale (consistent JSON schema without long few-shot examples per prompt) - Domain vocabulary and tone consistency (legal, medical, brand voice) - Latency/cost: a fine-tuned smaller model can outperform prompting a larger one for a narrow task - Teaching a reasoning *pattern* where training examples fully specify correct behavior
**Common mistakes to avoid:** - Fine-tuning to fix hallucinations → usually makes the model more *confidently* wrong - Fine-tuning on knowledge you'll need to update → no diff, no rollback, stale weights with no indicator - Fine-tuning before trying prompting → always test system prompts and few-shot examples first
**Sources:** [To fine-tune or not to fine-tune — Meta AI Blog](https://ai.meta.com/blog/when-to-fine-tune-llms-vs-other-techniques/) · [Methods for adapting LLMs — Meta AI](https://ai.meta.com/blog/adapting-large-language-models-llms/) · [Fine-tuning vs RAG in 2026: A Practical Decision Framework — Tian Pan](https://tianpan.co/forum/t/fine-tuning-vs-rag-in-2026-a-practical-decision-framework-for-production-llm-systems/995)

item.title: Your Long-Running MCP Tool Call Holds Claude's Attention — The `/tasks` Panel and an Env Var Give You Back Control
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.319 backgrounds long-running MCP tool calls immediately. Here's how to observe, test, and control this behavior — with the escape hatch for tools that need to stay in the main thread.
item.content:encoded:
**Since v2.1.319, Claude Code backgrounds long-running MCP tool calls immediately instead of holding the main thread — here's how to observe, test, and control this in your servers.**
Before v2.1.319, a slow MCP tool call either held Claude Code's focus during execution or was auto-backgrounded at the 2-minute timeout. The new behavior is immediate and explicit: tool calls that Claude Code classifies as long-running are moved to the background at the start, freeing Claude to continue working while the tool runs.
**What you can do with running tasks:** - Open `/tasks` (alias `/bashes`) to see all running MCP tasks and their status - A counter appears in the status line while a task runs - Claude resumes with the full tool result once the task completes
**Testing your server:** Run your tools with `/tasks` open and verify they appear there. If a fast tool (under 1 second) is being backgrounded unexpectedly, check the classification — the official changelog has the heuristic.
**Opting out:** Set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND=1` in your environment if a tool call needs to block the main thread — for example, when testing a tool interactively or when it streams intermediate output you need to watch in real time.
**Where this doesn't help:** Tools that need Claude to poll for completion after returning a task handle still require a polling tool on your server. Tools that return in under a second are unaffected.
The earlier 2-minute auto-background threshold (from v2.1.212) remains as a catch-all for any MCP call that hasn't finished in time — this new behavior runs earlier than that.
**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog v2.1.319](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog), [v2.1.319 release notes](https://ai-tldr.dev/releases/anthropic-claude-code-2-1-319/), [MCP progress notification tracking](https://claudeissues.com/issue/86464-bug-mcp-progress-notifications-are-received-but-discarded-once-a-call-is-auto-ba)

item.content:encoded:
**Two changes in Claude Code v2.1.319 (Nov 6) affect anyone running MCP servers or deploying Claude Code in enterprise LLM gateway environments.**

**Why it matters:** If your team uses Claude Code behind a gateway and recently noticed more permission prompts after upgrading, this is the cause — the fix is explicit allow rules, not reverting to an older version.

item.title: Your v0 Component Uses shadcn Defaults, Not Your Design System — `npx shadcn add` + Claude Code Closes That Gap

item.description: v0's "Add to Codebase" CLI command drops a generated component into your Next.js project in seconds; Claude Code then adapts it to your design tokens and component library in one pass.
item.content:encoded:
**v0's "Add to Codebase" CLI command drops a generated component into your Next.js project in seconds; Claude Code then adapts it to your design tokens and component library in one pass.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Generate a complex UI component in v0 — a data table, settings panel, or chart wrapper — and land it in your existing project using your color tokens, your `<Button>`, and your TypeScript types, not shadcn/ui defaults.
**Three takeaways:** - `npx shadcn@latest add <v0-url>` installs the component and any missing shadcn primitives directly into `components/ui/` — no copy-paste required. - The main failure modes are missing CSS variables and server/client component boundary errors, both fixable with a focused Claude Code prompt. - v0 output assumes shadcn/ui; if your project uses a different library or custom tokens, Claude Code can adapt it in one pass rather than you rewriting every import manually.
**The workflow:**
1. Build and iterate your component on [v0.dev](https://v0.dev) until it looks right. 2. Click **Add to Codebase** → copy the `npx shadcn@latest add <url>` command. Run it at your project root — it installs the component into `components/ui/` and any shadcn primitives it depends on. 3. Import the component in a page. Run `tsc --noEmit` and your dev server to catch missing CSS vars (`--background`, `--foreground`, `--primary`) and boundary errors. 4. Open Claude Code: `"This component uses shadcn tokens and imports from 'shadcn/ui'. Adapt it to use our design system (see CLAUDE.md tokens section) and replace shadcn primitives with components from @/components."` One pass usually covers it. 5. Re-run your type checker and spot-check the rendered output.
**Where it breaks:** shadcn's default styling bleeds through when your CSS token set doesn't cover the full range the component uses. Keep your token list in CLAUDE.md so Claude Code knows what variables are available. If your project doesn't use shadcn/ui at all, include which component library you do use in the adaptation prompt.
**Sources:** [v0 official guide](https://vercel.com/blog/maximizing-outputs-with-v0-from-ui-generation-to-code-creation), [v0-to-Next.js integration walkthrough](https://dev.to/brandon-vibestart/from-v0-output-to-production-nextjs-in-90-minutes-a-6-step-integration-workflow-2026-4c60), [shadcn/ui CLI docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/cli)

item.title: Your RAG Chain Passes Its Unit Tests But Still Hallucinates — DeepEval Scores Faithfulness, Contextual Precision, and Recall as Pytest Assertions
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: DeepEval turns RAG evaluation into pytest assertions — Contextual Precision, Contextual Recall, and Faithfulness are LLM-as-judge metrics you gate CI on, not prose you read manually.
item.content:encoded:
**DeepEval turns RAG evaluation into pytest: three LLM-as-judge metrics score whether retrieved chunks were ranked well, whether the answer stayed inside them, and whether the right chunks came back at all.**
Your RAG pipeline passes every unit test and still hallucinates. The problem is that existing tests check plumbing — retriever returns something, LLM responds — not quality: were the right chunks promoted? Did the answer stay inside the context?
**What you'll be able to do after this:** write pytest assertions that catch retrieval ranking problems, groundedness failures, and coverage gaps before they reach production — using the same LLM you already call.
**Three takeaways:** - `ContextualPrecisionMetric` catches ranking problems: were the most relevant chunks promoted above noise? - `FaithfulnessMetric` catches generation drift: does the answer include claims not in the retrieved context? - `ContextualRecallMetric` catches coverage holes: did the retriever surface all the facts the question needed?
**The walkthrough:**
```bash pip install -U deepeval ```
```python from deepeval import evaluate from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase from deepeval.metrics import ( ContextualPrecisionMetric, ContextualRecallMetric, FaithfulnessMetric, )
case = LLMTestCase( input="What is the refund policy for digital goods?", actual_output=your_chain.invoke("What is the refund policy for digital goods?"), # your retriever's returned chunks, in ranking order retrieval_context=["Digital goods are non-refundable after download.", ...], # used by Precision and Recall to judge coverage expected_output="Digital goods cannot be refunded once downloaded.", )
evaluate( test_cases=[case], metrics=[ ContextualPrecisionMetric(threshold=0.5), ContextualRecallMetric(threshold=0.5), FaithfulnessMetric(threshold=0.5), ], ) ```
Each metric uses a configured LLM as judge — by default OpenAI, [configurable to any provider](https://deepeval.com/docs/metrics-introduction#using-a-custom-llm-as-judge) including Anthropic models. Scores are 0–1; a test case passes only when every metric clears its threshold.
**Running in pytest:**
```python # test_rag.py def test_refund_policy(): case = LLMTestCase(input=..., actual_output=..., retrieval_context=[...], expected_output=...) assert_test(case, [ContextualPrecisionMetric(), FaithfulnessMetric()]) ```
```bash pytest test_rag.py -v ```
**Limits:** Each evaluation turn calls your judge LLM — a full suite over hundreds of question-answer pairs has real API cost. DeepEval can use a local Ollama model as judge (lower cost, noisier on nuanced faithfulness checks). A 0.5 threshold flags clear failures; production gates typically need 0.7+, which you calibrate against a labeled set. The LlamaIndex integration guide notes that judge-model defaults point to `gpt-4o`, so check the config before billing surprises arrive.

item.title: Your Team's CLAUDE.md Is Committed but Your Personal Preferences Aren't — CLAUDE.local.md Is the Gitignored Per-Developer Override That Loads Every Session
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: CLAUDE.local.md sits alongside your committed CLAUDE.md, loads automatically every session, takes precedence when rules conflict, and never gets checked into the repo.
item.content:encoded:
**`CLAUDE.local.md` is a gitignored per-developer file that loads alongside the committed `CLAUDE.md` and wins on any conflict — the right place for personal tool paths, debug preferences, and machine-specific facts your team doesn't need.**
Your project's `CLAUDE.md` is committed and shared. That's correct — team conventions, codebase structure, and deploy steps should be consistent. But some instructions only apply to you: your virtualenv path, your preference to never use `sudo`, the fact that your machine maps `python` to 3.12 while CI uses 3.11, your note to always print the SQL query during this debugging session.
Putting those in the shared file is noise for your teammates. Keeping them only in your head means every new Claude Code session starts without them.
**`CLAUDE.local.md` is the per-developer override.** It sits in the project root alongside `CLAUDE.md`. Claude Code reads it on startup, adds it to `.gitignore` automatically, and never stages it. When instructions conflict with the shared file, the local file wins.
**What it's for — a short checklist:**
```markdown # My local overrides for this project - Use ~/.venvs/myproject/bin/python, not the system python - Never use sudo — ask me first if you need elevated access - My machine is on macOS ARM; avoid x86-only tools - When debugging DB issues, print the full SQL query before executing - I'm working on the payments module this week — focus suggestions there ```
**How to create it:**
```bash # Create in project root (Claude Code gitignores it automatically) touch CLAUDE.local.md # Verify — if it was missed: grep -q 'CLAUDE.local.md' .gitignore || echo 'CLAUDE.local.md' >> .gitignore ```
**The companion: `.claude/settings.local.json`** does the same for settings — it's also gitignored and takes precedence over the committed `.claude/settings.json`. If you have been pasting personal `allow` rules (tool permissions, `Bash` patterns) into the shared settings file, move them here.
```json { "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(pnpm run:*)", "Bash(node scripts/:*)"] } } ```
**Limits:** `CLAUDE.local.md` only helps the person who wrote it — shared team conventions still belong in `CLAUDE.md`. It loads every turn, so keep it short; a 400-line personal file bleeds context budget the same as a 400-line shared one. For one-session context (a debugging hypothesis, a temporary constraint), use a `/memory` note instead — it doesn't persist to disk.
**Sources:** [Claude Code memory and CLAUDE.md hierarchy — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) · [CLAUDE.md hierarchy and local overrides — morphllm.com](https://www.morphllm.com/claude-md-guide) · [settings.local.json reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)

item.title: Your Team's Deploy Checklist Exists Only in Slack — Encode It in `.claude/commands/name.md` and `/name` Runs It Every Time
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Drop a Markdown file in .claude/commands/, type /filename <args>, and Claude Code runs the encoded prompt with $ARGUMENTS and inline shell output — no copy-pasting, no forgetting a step.
item.content:encoded:
**A Markdown file in `.claude/commands/` becomes a slash command at startup — `$ARGUMENTS` injects whatever you type after the name, and backtick lines starting with `!` run shell commands before Claude sees the prompt.**
Claude Code loads every `.md` file in `.claude/commands/` as a project-scoped slash command. The filename (without `.md`) is the command name. The file content is the prompt Claude receives. Commit the directory and the whole team shares it.
**The authoring format:**
```markdown <!-- .claude/commands/check-pr.md --> --- allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Grep --- Review PR #$ARGUMENTS for security issues.
First, fetch the diff: `!gh pr diff $ARGUMENTS`
Then check each changed file for: - Unparameterized SQL in raw query strings - Missing input validation at API boundaries - Credentials or secrets in new config keys
Report findings as `file:line — issue` entries. ```
Type `/check-pr 42` and Claude Code fetches the diff for PR #42, injects it inline, and runs the review against your three criteria.
**Three mechanics worth knowing:**
1. **`$ARGUMENTS`** — the string after the command name, dropped in wherever `$ARGUMENTS` appears in the file. `/check-pr 42` passes `42`; `/deploy staging v2.1.3` passes `staging v2.1.3`. It is a single variable — split inside a shell block if you need parts. 2. **Backtick lines with `!`** — `` `!command` `` runs a shell command before Claude processes the prompt; the output is injected inline. Claude sees live data (the actual diff, the CI log, the recent commits), not a placeholder you forgot to fill. 3. **`allowed-tools` frontmatter** — restricts which tools this command can invoke. A code-review command that should never write files gets `Bash, Read, Grep` only. Without it, the command inherits the full tool set.
**When a custom command earns its file:** - Steps that always happen in the same order: fetch diff → grep for a pattern → analyze → report - Context-gathering that takes several manual steps before Claude has what it needs - Shared quality gates — security scan, release-notes generation, test-failure triage — that need a consistent, versioned prompt
**Limits:** Commands are Markdown files in the repo — a new team member does not have them until they clone, and changes go through code review like any other source file. For personal or exploratory prompts, `~/.claude/commands/` stores per-user commands that do not commit. `$ARGUMENTS` interpolates the whole string after the command name; there is no positional-argument syntax (`$1`, `$2`) built in — parse it in the shell block if you need separate parts.
**Sources:** [Custom slash commands — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slash-commands) · [Project configuration — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/project-overview) · [Claude Code custom commands in practice — AI Engineer Guide](https://aiengineerguide.com/til/claude-code-custom-command/)

item.title: Your Fine-Tuned LoRA Adapters Each Need Their Own vLLM Instance — `--enable-lora --lora-modules` Serves Dozens of Adapters on One Base Model
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: --enable-lora --lora-modules name=path lets one vLLM server switch between LoRA adapters per-request; clients select an adapter by passing its registered name as the model ID.
item.content:encoded:
**`--enable-lora --lora-modules name=path` lets one vLLM server switch between LoRA adapters per-request — one copy of the base weights in VRAM, dozens of fine-tunes accessible by name.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Serve multiple fine-tuned LoRA adapters from a single base model and GPU allocation, without spinning up a separate vLLM instance per fine-tune.
**Three things this unlocks:**
1. Clients use the same OpenAI-compatible API; they select an adapter (or the unmodified base) by passing its name as the `model=` value 2. `--max-loras N` controls how many adapters stay in GPU memory simultaneously — misses swap from disk (LRU cache), not an error 3. All adapters must share the same base model; serving adapters for different base models requires separate server instances
**How to set it up:**
```bash pip install vllm
# Adapters must be in PEFT format (adapter_config.json + adapter_model.safetensors) # -- the output of model.save_pretrained() or model.push_to_hub()
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \ --enable-lora \ --lora-modules customer_support=/models/cs-adapter \ code_review=/models/cr-adapter \ --max-loras 2 \ --max-lora-rank 64 ```
If you pushed your adapter to the Hub with `model.push_to_hub()`, pass the Hub path (`username/cs-adapter`) instead of a local directory.
**Selecting an adapter from client code:**
```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="x")
# customer_support adapter resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="customer_support", # name from --lora-modules messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I return an order?"}] )
# base model, no adapter resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain HNSW indexing."}] ) ```
`curl http://localhost:8000/v1/models` lists all registered adapters alongside the base model.
**Limits:** An adapter whose rank exceeds `--max-lora-rank` is rejected at load time — set the flag to match your largest adapter. `--max-loras` is a VRAM budget: too high and you exhaust GPU memory, too low and cache misses spike latency (not fatal, but measurable). Runtime adapter loading/unloading is available but requires `VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=True`, which the vLLM docs flag as a production risk. All adapters in one server instance must share the same base model — mixing base models requires separate instances.
**Sources:** [vLLM LoRA adapters — docs.vllm.ai](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/models/lora.html) · [Multi-LoRA serving guide — docs.anyscale.com](https://docs.anyscale.com/llm/serving/multi-lora)

item.title: Your Claude Code Session Keeps Solving the Wrong Problem After an Hour of Tool Calls — `/goal` Locks the Session to One Explicit Objective and Loops Until It's Met
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: `/goal <text>` turns Claude Code into an autonomous loop that keeps working until a machine-checkable condition is true; added in v2.1.139 as a research preview for unattended tasks.
item.content:encoded:
**`/goal <condition>` pins an explicit objective to the session and loops Claude Code until the condition is verifiably true — added in v2.1.139 (May 2026) as a research preview.**
Long sessions drift. After 20 tool calls and two compaction cycles the model is still technically "on task," but its working definition of "done" has drifted from what you meant at the start. `/goal` is a session directive, not a prompt: set it once and the session loops — running tools, checking its own output, trying again — until it can demonstrate that the stated condition holds.
**Usage:**
``` /goal "All 47 unit tests pass and eslint returns zero errors" ```
The objective persists across tool calls and compaction for the life of the session. Claude evaluates whether the condition is satisfied after each significant action and continues if it is not.
For unattended runs with the CLI:
```bash claude --dangerously-skip-permissions \ -p '/goal "migrate auth module to new token format; existing session tests stay passing"' ```
The session exits when it judges the goal met, or when it hits a blocker it cannot resolve.
**Where it works:**
- CI-style gates: "all tests pass," "lint returns zero errors," "build succeeds" - Refactors with a verifiable before/after state: "all usages of the old API replaced and the type checker is clean" - Autonomous scripted pipelines you would otherwise have to babysit
**Where it breaks down:**
- **Needs a machine-checkable condition.** Vague goals ("improve the code quality") give the model an easy exit — it will decide it succeeded. The goal must be something the session can evaluate without asking you. - **Research preview.** The `/goal` command is not in the stable API. Behavior around compaction and subagents is not officially documented and may change. - **Full blast radius with write access.** `--dangerously-skip-permissions` lets the loop run file edits, shell commands, and git commits without pausing. Scope the goal and the directory carefully.
**Sources:** [MindStudio: Claude Code /goal command](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/claude-code-goal-command-autonomous-tasks) · [startupfortune.com: Claude adds /goal](https://startupfortune.com/claude-adds-goal-to-keep-working-until-the-job-is-done/) · [Stork.ai: /goal guide](https://www.stork.ai/blog/claudes-goal-command-will-change-how-you-work)

item.title: Claude Enterprise Nov 5: Security Center Shows Policy Gaps, Admin API Gets Session Revocation, Developer Platform Adds IP Allowlisting
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Anthropic's Nov 5 enterprise release adds a security center that flags configuration gaps against Anthropic's recommendations, Admin API session revocation, and IP allowlisting for the Developer Platform — all in beta.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic's Nov 5 enterprise release includes a security center for configuration gap analysis, Admin API session revocation, and IP allowlisting for the Developer Platform — all currently in beta.**
Three additions shipped together on November 5:
**Security center (beta).** A new dashboard in the Claude.ai admin panel audits your organization's configuration against Anthropic's security recommendations and surfaces gaps. The recommendations are Anthropic's own judgment, not a third-party benchmark — treat the flagged items as a prioritized checklist, not a compliance report.
**Admin API: session revocation.** Admins can now invalidate active Claude.ai sessions via the Admin API. Useful for responding to a compromised account or offboarding without waiting for session expiry. Revoke a session:
```bash curl -X DELETE https://api.anthropic.com/v1/admin/sessions/<session_id> \ -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN_API_KEY" ```
(Exact endpoint shape from release notes — verify against current Admin API docs before wiring into automation.)
**Developer Platform IP allowlisting (beta).** Organizations can now restrict API key usage to a declared list of IP ranges. Keys used from outside the allowlist are rejected. Applies to the Developer Platform (direct API access), not to Claude.ai web sessions.
**Inference hooks — background.** The release notes also reference inference hook visibility improvements. Inference hooks (beta since Aug 5, 2026) let an organization route every prompt and response through its own HTTPS security server before and after inference; the security server can allow or deny the request but cannot rewrite it. The Nov 5 update improves hook status visibility in the admin panel.
**Where it breaks down:**
- All three features are still in beta — APIs and UI may change. - Security center recommendations reflect Anthropic's defaults; your organization's risk model may differ. - Inference hooks can only allow or deny requests, not rewrite them — DLP use cases that require redaction need a different approach.
**Sources:** [Claude Enterprise release notes — Anthropic support](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12138966-release-notes) · [Anthropic puts inline DLP inside Claude Enterprise — Unite.AI](https://www.unite.ai/anthropic-puts-inline-data-loss-prevention-inside-claude-enterprise/) · [Claude Enterprise inference hooks: a protocol review — mint.security](https://www.mint.security/blog/claude-enterprise-inference-hooks-a-protocol-review)

item.title: Every Claude Client Gets Its Own Hard-Coded Tool Integration Until You Build One MCP Server — `@mcp.tool()` Exposes Any Python Function to All Clients Without Duplication
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Define tools and resources once in a Python MCP server with `@mcp.tool()` and `@mcp.resource()` decorators; test with the MCP Inspector via `mcp dev server.py`, then register with Claude Code using one command.
item.content:encoded:
**Write a Python function, decorate it with `@mcp.tool()`, and every MCP-compatible client — including Claude Code — can call it without a separate integration per client.**
Before MCP, connecting an internal API to Claude Code meant a custom tool definition in every session config. Connect it to Cursor, same thing. Connect it to a Claude-powered agent, another integration. MCP flips that: you build the server once, and clients discover it over a standard protocol.
**Install and scaffold:**
```bash uv add "mcp[cli]" ```
```python from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP # SDK v1.x; check official docs for v2 import path
mcp = FastMCP("my-tools")
@mcp.tool() def get_latest_metrics(service: str, hours: int = 24) -> str: """Return the last N hours of p99 latency for a service.""" # Replace with a real metrics API call return f"p99 for {service}: 42ms (last {hours}h)"
@mcp.resource("docs://{path}") def get_internal_doc(path: str) -> str: """Return an internal doc by path.""" return open(f"docs/{path}").read()
if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run() ```
The docstring is the tool description Claude sees when deciding whether to call it — write it as you would a function signature comment.
**Test with the MCP Inspector:**
```bash mcp dev server.py ```
This starts a local web UI at `http://localhost:5173` where you can invoke tools and resources interactively before wiring up any client. It's the fastest feedback loop for catching schema errors.
**Register with Claude Code:**
```bash claude mcp add my-tools --transport stdio -- uv run python server.py ```
Claude Code starts the server as a subprocess on `stdio` and injects the declared tools into every session automatically.
**Where it breaks down:**
- **stdio = local only.** The stdio transport connects one server to one client on the same machine. Sharing a server across machines or running it as a persistent service requires the Streamable HTTP transport (`mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")`), which is newer and less widely supported. - **Startup cost per session.** Claude Code starts the server fresh each session. Cold start for a Python server with heavy imports adds latency to the first tool call. - **Permission prompts still apply.** MCP tool calls go through Claude Code's standard permission model — Claude will still ask before running destructive tools unless you've pre-allowed them.
**Sources:** [Build an MCP server — official quickstart](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/build-server) · [python-sdk — GitHub](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk) · [MCP quickstart resources — GitHub](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/quickstart-resources)

item.title: Your CI Eval Loop Waits for Each Inference Call Before Starting the Next — Anthropic's Message Batches API Submits All Requests at Once and Returns Results at Half Cost
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Submit up to 100k requests as a single batch job; Anthropic charges 50% of standard rates and returns results as a .jsonl file. Good for eval runs, bulk classification, and document pipelines.
item.content:encoded:
**Anthropic reports 50% cost reduction on the Message Batches API for async workloads — submit up to 100k requests in one call, pick up results as a `.jsonl` file when the batch completes.**
A synchronous eval loop — one inference call per test case, waiting for each before the next — is the most expensive way to run evaluations. The Message Batches API submits every request in one call and handles rate-limit queuing on Anthropic's side. Per Anthropic's pricing page, all usage on the Batches API is billed at 50% of standard rates; that discount stacks with prompt caching.
**How it works:**
```python import anthropic, time
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
# 1. Build request list (same params as a standard Messages call) requests = [ { "custom_id": f"eval-{i}", "params": { "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "max_tokens": 512, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Classify: {text}"}], } } for i, text in enumerate(test_cases) ]
# 2. Submit batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)
# 3. Poll until complete while batch.processing_status == "in_progress": time.sleep(60) batch = client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id)
# 4. Stream results (.jsonl, arbitrary order) for result in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id): if result.result.type == "succeeded": print(result.custom_id, result.result.message.content[0].text) ```
`custom_id` ties each result back to your input — results arrive in arbitrary order, so keep it meaningful (e.g. the test-case id, the document path).
**Good fits:** CI eval pipelines, nightly document classification or extraction, bulk summarization, offline enrichment jobs — anything where waiting an hour for the full batch beats paying double for real-time throughput.
**Where it breaks down:**
- **Not eligible for Zero Data Retention.** Per the official docs, data is retained under the standard retention policy for the feature. If ZDR is a compliance requirement, batch mode won't satisfy it — use the standard Messages API instead. - **Batches expire after 24 hours.** Most complete in under an hour, but Anthropic publishes no SLA for completion time. Don't schedule batch jobs without a timeout handler. - **No streaming.** Results arrive as a completed `.jsonl` file. Partial progress isn't visible until the batch ends, so this isn't a fit for anything that surfaces incremental output to a user. - **Rate limits still apply.** You can't bypass per-minute limits by batching; the batch endpoint itself has its own limits. See the current batch processing guide for the per-account caps.
**Sources:** [Message Batches API — Anthropic docs](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/message-batches) · [Batch processing guide — platform.claude.com](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing.md) · [Message Batching: when 50% off is worth the latency — DEV Community](https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/anthropic-message-batching-when-50-off-is-worth-the-latency-4jfc)

item.title: Your Complex Claude Code Session Ends When You Close the Terminal — `/rename` It Before You Finish and `--resume` Gets You Back Instantly
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: /rename stores a session by name before you close; claude --resume <name> reopens it in any directory with its full history intact. Flags like --mcp-config must be passed again.
item.content:encoded:
**`/rename <name>` stores a session by name before you close; `claude --resume <name>` or `claude --continue` reopens it in any directory with its full history intact.**
When a Claude Code session builds up real value — an hour of debugging context, accumulated file insights, a decision trail — closing the terminal forgets it. By default `claude --continue` reopens the most recent session in that directory. That breaks the moment you switch directories or the most recent session isn't the one you want.
**Name a session before you close it:**
``` /rename auth-debug-session ```
Claude Code stores it in the session table. Next session:
```bash claude --resume auth-debug-session # exact name claude --resume # pick from a list ```
Inside a running session, `/resume` opens the same picker without leaving the terminal.
**What carries over:** - Full conversation history (or its compact summary if idle compaction ran) - The session's model and agent type - Permission mode (can be overridden: `claude --resume <name> --permission-mode default`)
**What you must pass again on resume:** `--mcp-config`, `--settings`, `--plugin-dir`, `--add-dir`, and `--fallback-model` don't persist — they aren't part of the session record. Keep a wrapper shell alias for sessions with non-default flags so you don't have to remember them.
**Limit:** Sessions launched via `claude -p` (headless print mode) or through the Agent SDK are excluded from the picker and from `--continue`. They run non-interactively and don't appear in `claude --resume`.
**Sources:** [Manage sessions — Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions) · [Claude Code headless mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless) · [Session flags, community testing — claudeissues.com](https://claudeissues.com)

item.title: Your RAG Chain Returns Plain Text and Users Can't Verify Which Source Backs Each Claim — Add a `CitedAnswer` Schema and Every Fact Gets Its Document Index
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Define a CitedAnswer Pydantic schema with an answer string and a list of integer indices; pass it to .with_structured_output() and the LLM cites its sources in every response.
item.content:encoded:
**What you'll be able to do after this:** modify your existing LangChain RAG chain to return a structured `CitedAnswer` object — an answer string plus a list of citation indices — so every claim can be traced back to a retrieved source chunk.
Currently most RAG answers are plain text: the LLM summarizes or misremembers something, and there is no way to tell which chunk it drew from. Citations close that gap by forcing the model to reference document IDs inline.
**Step 1 — Define the schema:**
```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
class CitedAnswer(BaseModel): answer: str = Field( description="The answer, with inline [N] markers referencing source indices" ) citations: list[int] = Field( description="0-based indices of the retrieved documents that support the answer" )
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-5-5").with_structured_output(CitedAnswer) ```
**Step 2 — Label the retrieved chunks before passing them to the LLM:**
```python def format_docs_with_ids(docs): return "\n\n".join( f"[{i}] {doc.page_content}\nSource: {doc.metadata.get('source', '')}" for i, doc in enumerate(docs) )
context = format_docs_with_ids(retrieved_docs) prompt = f"""Answer using ONLY the provided context. Cite each fact as [N] where N is the document index.
Context: {context}
Question: {question}"""
result = llm.invoke(prompt) # result.answer: "HNSW uses an M parameter to control edges [0]. Higher ef_construction improves recall [1]." # result.citations: [0, 1] ```
**Step 3 — Surface the sources:**
```python for idx in result.citations: print(f"[{idx}] {retrieved_docs[idx].metadata['source']}") ```
**Three takeaways:** - `.with_structured_output()` calls the tool/function-calling API — the model fills in the schema rather than guessing JSON format - Claude Sonnet 5.5 and other Anthropic models support this via `langchain-anthropic` - LangChain's how-to describes five citation methods; the tool-calling approach above is recommended first because it is most reliable
**Limits:** `.with_structured_output()` does not stream — the full `CitedAnswer` object returns once at the end, increasing perceived latency for long answers. The LLM can still cite a source index that does not support the claim; surface the actual chunk alongside the answer so users can verify.
**Sources:** [How to get a RAG application to add citations — LangChain docs](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/qa_citations) · [Citation-aware RAG in Python — netjstech.com (April 2026)](https://www.netjstech.com/2026/04/citation-aware-rag-application-in.html)
